title: al-ʿIzzī
author: ʿIzz al-Dīn al-Zanjānī
subject: sarf
summary: Al-Taṣrīf, known after its author ʿIzz al-Dīn al-Zanjānī as al-ʿIzzī, is the ṣarf book read after the Amthila, the Binā and the Maqṣūd in the Ottoman madrasa, and in many other madrasas besides. In a few pages it sets out the patterns of the bare and augmented verb, transitivity, the conjugation of the sound verb with the jussive, the naṣb, the command and the two nūns of emphasis, the participles, and then each kind of verb that is not sound: the doubled, the mithāl, the hollow, the defective, the two lafīfs and the hamzated, ending with the nouns of time, place, instrument, once and manner. It is short and exact, and its rules are given with their reasons. The lessons follow its order and give every weak form as the print gives it.

parts.title: Taṣrīf and the patterns of the verb

lessons.title: What taṣrīf is, and the divisions of the verb
body: Al-ʿIzzī opens with a definition in two halves. In the language taṣrīf is “change” (al-taghyīr); in the craft (al-ṣināʿa) it is “turning a single origin into different forms, for intended meanings that are obtained only through them”. Every word of the second half counts: one origin, many forms (amthila), and each form there for a meaning that no other form gives.

Take one origin, ḍarb, “hitting”. From it come ḍaraba, “he hit”, yaḍribu, “he hits”, iḍrib, “hit!”, ḍārib, “one who hits”, and maḍrūb, “one who is hit”. Past time, present time, a command, the doer, the one done to: each meaning is reached only by its own form. The commentators on al-ʿIzzī take this single origin to be the maṣdar, as the Baṣrans do. This is what the whole book will teach: how the forms are built and how they change.

Then three divisions, each in two. The verb is triliteral or quadriliteral, by the number of its radical letters; each is bare (mujarrad) or augmented (mazīd fīhi), by whether letters are added to the radicals; and each is sound (sālim) or not sound. Three divisions of two give eight kinds, the same eight with which the Binā closed.

The sound verb is defined exactly: it is the verb “whose radical letters, which are matched with the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām, are free of the letters of weakness, of the hamza and of doubling”. The radicals are measured on f-ʿ-l: in naṣara the nūn is the fāʾ, the ṣād the ʿayn, the rāʾ the lām. So saʾala, with a hamza, madda, with doubling, and waʿada, with a wāw, are not sālim, though only waʿada has a weak letter.

A beginner's trap: soundness looks only at the radicals. Akrama has a hamza, but its hamza is added, not radical; its radicals k-r-m are free of all three, so akrama is a sound, augmented triliteral. The order of the book follows these divisions: first the sound verb in all its patterns, then each kind that is not sound.

tasks.prompt: Name five forms that come from the origin naṣr, “helping”, and the meaning each one gives.
tasks.answer: Naṣara, “he helped” (past); yanṣuru, “he helps” (present); unṣur, “help!” (command); nāṣir, “a helper” (doer); manṣūr, “helped” (one done to). Each meaning is reached only through its own form.

tasks.prompt: Which of these is sālim, and why are the others not: akrama, saʾala, madda, waʿada?
tasks.answer: Only akrama: its radicals k-r-m are free of weak letters, hamza and doubling; its hamza is added. Saʾala has a radical hamza, madda a doubled radical, waʿada a weak letter (wāw).

tasks.prompt: Akrama has four letters in its past. Why is it still a triliteral verb?
tasks.answer: The division into triliteral and quadriliteral counts the radicals, and akrama has three: k-r-m. The hamza is added, so akrama is an augmented triliteral whose past happens to have four letters.

quiz.prompt: What is taṣrīf in the language?
quiz.explanation: Al-taghyīr, change; the technical sense is a kind of change: one origin turned into many forms.

quiz.prompt: In the craft, taṣrīf turns one origin into…
quiz.explanation: “For intended meanings that are obtained only through them”: each form carries its own meaning.

quiz.prompt: How many two-way divisions of the verb does al-ʿIzzī give?
quiz.explanation: Triliteral or quadriliteral, bare or augmented, sound or not: three divisions, eight kinds together.

quiz.prompt: Which verb is sālim?
quiz.explanation: The radicals n-ṣ-r have no weak letter, hamza or doubling; saʾala has a hamza, madda doubling, waʿada a wāw.

quiz.prompt: Akrama is…
quiz.explanation: Three radicals, k-r-m, and an added hamza: augmented triliteral.

quiz.prompt: The radical letters are matched with…
options: the hamza, nūn, yāʾ and tāʾ
the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām
quiz.explanation: On the measure f-ʿ-l the first radical is the fāʾ, the second the ʿayn, the third the lām.

quiz.prompt: Which radicals keep a verb from being sālim?
options: A weak letter, a hamza or a doubled letter
quiz.explanation: Sālim is narrower than “not weak”: the hamza and doubling also exclude it.

text.original: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ. الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، وَالصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَى سَيِّدِنَا مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ أَجْمَعِينَ. اعْلَمْ أَنَّ التَّصْرِيفَ فِي اللُّغَةِ التَّغْيِيرُ، وَفِي الصِّنَاعَةِ تَحْوِيلُ الْأَصْلِ الْوَاحِدِ إِلَى أَمْثِلَةٍ مُخْتَلِفَةٍ لِمَعَانٍ مَقْصُودَةٍ لَا تَحْصُلُ إِلَّا بِهَا.
text.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and blessing and peace upon our master Muḥammad and upon all his family. Know that taṣrīf in the language is change, and in the technical usage it is turning a single origin into different forms, for intended meanings that are obtained only through them.

text.original: ثُمَّ الْفِعْلُ إِمَّا ثُلَاثِيٌّ وَإِمَّا رُبَاعِيٌّ، وَكُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا إِمَّا مُجَرَّدٌ وَإِمَّا مَزِيدٌ فِيهِ، وَكُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا إِمَّا سَالِمٌ أَوْ غَيْرُ سَالِمٍ. وَنَعْنِي بِالسَّالِمِ مَا سَلِمَتْ حُرُوفُهُ الْأَصْلِيَّةُ الَّتِي تُقَابَلُ بِالْفَاءِ وَالْعَيْنِ وَاللَّامِ مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْعِلَّةِ وَالْهَمْزَةِ وَالتَّضْعِيفِ.
text.en: Further, the verb is either triliteral or quadriliteral; each of them is either bare (mujarrad) or augmented (mazīd fīhi); and each of them is either sound (sālim) or not sound. By the sound we mean that whose radical letters, which are matched with the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām, are free of the letters of weakness, of the hamza and of doubling.

lessons.title: The bābs of the bare triliteral
body: The bare sound triliteral is sorted by the vowel of its ʿayn, first in the past and then in the present. A past on faʿala, with fatḥa on the ʿayn, has its present on yafʿulu or yafʿilu: naṣara yanṣuru, “to help”, and ḍaraba yaḍribu, “to hit”. Which of the two a verb takes is not given by a rule; it is learnt from use and the dictionary.

A third present is possible for faʿala: yafʿalu, with fatḥa, “when the ʿayn or the lām of its verb is one of the letters of the throat”. These are six: the hamza, the hāʾ, the ʿayn, the ḥāʾ, the ghayn and the khāʾ. So saʾala yasʾalu, “to ask”, with a hamza as ʿayn, and manaʿa yamnaʿu, “to prevent”, with an ʿayn as lām. Abā yaʾbā, “to refuse”, is irregular (shādhdh): its hamza is the fāʾ, and neither its ʿayn nor its lām is a throat letter.

The rule works in one direction only. A throat letter allows yafʿalu but does not require it: dakhala yadkhulu, “to enter”, has a khāʾ as its ʿayn and is still on yafʿulu. What al-ʿIzzī rules out is yafʿalu without a throat letter, and abā yaʾbā is the exception he names.

A past on faʿila has its present on yafʿalu: ʿalima yaʿlamu, “to know”, “except what is irregular, such as ḥasiba yaḥsibu and its sisters”, with kasra in both: naʿima yanʿimu and waritha yarithu. A past on faʿula has its present on yafʿulu, with the ḍamma kept: ḥasuna yaḥsunu, karuma yakrumu. The grammarians add that faʿula is the bāb of lasting qualities, and is intransitive.

Together this gives the six bābs every madrasa student knows: faʿala yafʿulu, faʿala yafʿilu, faʿala yafʿalu, faʿila yafʿalu, faʿila yafʿilu and faʿula yafʿulu. Al-ʿIzzī does not number them as the Maqṣūd does; he groups them by the past, and gives the reason for each.

tasks.prompt: What do saʾala yasʾalu and manaʿa yamnaʿu share that allows their present on yafʿalu?
tasks.answer: A letter of the throat in the ʿayn or the lām: the hamza is the ʿayn of saʾala, the ʿayn is the lām of manaʿa.

tasks.prompt: Why does al-ʿIzzī call abā yaʾbā irregular?
tasks.answer: Its present is on yafʿalu, though neither its ʿayn (the bāʾ) nor its lām is a throat letter. Its hamza is the fāʾ, and the rule looks only at the ʿayn and the lām.

tasks.prompt: Dakhala has a khāʾ as its ʿayn, yet its present is yadkhulu. Does it break the rule?
tasks.answer: No. The rule says that yafʿalu comes only with a throat letter, not that every verb with one takes yafʿalu. The throat letter is a condition, not a cause.

tasks.prompt: Give the present of ʿalima, ḥasiba and karuma, each with its bāb.
tasks.answer: Yaʿlamu (faʿila yafʿalu, the rule); yaḥsibu (faʿila yafʿilu, the irregular group); yakrumu (faʿula yafʿulu).

quiz.prompt: When can faʿala take a present on yafʿalu?
options: When its fāʾ is a throat letter
When its ʿayn or lām is a throat letter
quiz.explanation: Saʾala yasʾalu, manaʿa yamnaʿu; a throat letter in the fāʾ does not count.

quiz.prompt: How many letters of the throat does al-ʿIzzī count?
quiz.explanation: The hamza, the hāʾ, the ʿayn, the ḥāʾ, the ghayn and the khāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Which present is irregular?
quiz.explanation: It is on yafʿalu with no throat letter in its ʿayn or lām.

quiz.prompt: The regular present of faʿila is…
quiz.explanation: ʿAlima yaʿlamu; ḥasiba yaḥsibu and its sisters are the exceptions.

quiz.prompt: Ḥasiba yaḥsibu is…
quiz.explanation: With kasra in past and present, like naʿima yanʿimu and waritha yarithu.

quiz.prompt: The present of faʿula is…
quiz.explanation: Ḥasuna yaḥsunu, karuma yakrumu: the ḍamma of the past stays in the present.

quiz.prompt: Which pair are sisters of ḥasiba?
quiz.explanation: They share its kasra in both past and present.

text.original: أَمَّا الثُّلَاثِيُّ الْمُجَرَّدُ السَّالِمُ فَإِنْ كَانَ مَاضِيهِ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ عَلَى فَعَلَ فَمُضَارِعُهُ يَفْعُلُ أَوْ يَفْعِلُ بِضَمِّ الْعَيْنِ أَوْ كَسْرِهَا، نَحْوُ: نَصَرَ يَنْصُرُ، وَضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ. وَيَجِيءُ مُضَارِعُهُ عَلَى وَزْنِ يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ إِذَا كَانَ عَيْنُ فِعْلِهِ أَوْ لَامُهُ حَرْفًا مِنْ حُرُوفِ الْحَلْقِ، وَهِيَ سِتَّةٌ: الْهَمْزَةُ وَالْهَاءُ وَالْعَيْنُ وَالْحَاءُ وَالْغَيْنُ وَالْخَاءُ، نَحْوُ: سَأَلَ يَسْأَلُ، وَمَنَعَ يَمْنَعُ، وَأَبَى يَأْبَى شَاذٌّ.
text.en: As for the bare, sound triliteral: if its past has fatḥa on the ʿayn, on the pattern faʿala, its muḍāriʿ is yafʿulu or yafʿilu, with ḍamma or kasra on the ʿayn, as naṣara yanṣuru “to help” and ḍaraba yaḍribu “to hit”. Its muḍāriʿ comes on the measure yafʿalu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn, when the ʿayn or the lām of its verb is one of the letters of the throat (ḥurūf al-ḥalq), which are six: the hamza, the hāʾ, the ʿayn, the ḥāʾ, the ghayn and the khāʾ, as saʾala yasʾalu “to ask” and manaʿa yamnaʿu “to prevent”; and abā yaʾbā “to refuse” is irregular (shādhdh).

text.original: فَإِنْ كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى فَعِلَ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ فَمُضَارِعُهُ يَجِيءُ عَلَى يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: عَلِمَ يَعْلَمُ، إِلَّا مَا شَذَّ، نَحْوُ: حَسِبَ يَحْسِبُ وَأَخَوَاتِهِ، مِثْلُ: نَعِمَ يَنْعِمُ، وَوَرِثَ يَرِثُ. وَإِنْ كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى فَعُلَ مَضْمُومِ الْعَيْنِ فَمُضَارِعُهُ يَفْعُلُ بِضَمِّ الْعَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: حَسُنَ يَحْسُنُ، وَكَرُمَ يَكْرُمُ.
text.en: If its past is on faʿila, with kasra on the ʿayn, its muḍāriʿ comes on yafʿalu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn, as ʿalima yaʿlamu “to know”, except what is irregular, as ḥasiba yaḥsibu “to reckon” and its sisters, such as naʿima yanʿimu “to live in comfort” and waritha yarithu “to inherit”. If its past is on faʿula, with ḍamma on the ʿayn, its muḍāriʿ is yafʿulu, with ḍamma on the ʿayn, as ḥasuna yaḥsunu “to be good” and karuma yakrumu “to be noble”.

lessons.title: The bare quadriliteral; augmented pasts of four and five letters
body: The bare quadriliteral “has one pattern: faʿlala yufaʿlilu faʿlalatan wa-fiʿlālan, as daḥraja yudaḥriju daḥrajatan”, “to roll”. The pattern carries two maṣdars, faʿlala and fiʿlāl; the print gives the example with the first only. Four radicals, none added: the pattern repeats the lām to stand for the fourth.

The augmented triliteral is sorted, not by what is added, but by the number of letters in its past. Pasts of four letters are three: afʿala, as akrama yukrimu ikrāman, “to honour”; faʿʿala, as farraḥa yufarriḥu tafrīḥan, “to gladden”; and fāʿala, as qātala yuqātilu muqātalatan wa-qitālan, “to fight”, with two maṣdars.

Pasts of five letters are five, in two groups. Two begin with the tāʾ: tafaʿʿala, as takassara yatakassaru takassuran, “to break into pieces”, and tafāʿala, as tabāʿada, “to move apart”. Three begin with the hamza: infaʿala, as inqaṭaʿa yanqaṭiʿu inqiṭāʿan, “to be cut off”; iftaʿala, as ijtamaʿa yajtamiʿu ijtimāʿan, “to come together”; and ifʿalla, as iḥmarra yaḥmarru iḥmirāran, “to turn red”.

Why count the letters of the past? Because the count decides the vowels, as the next lessons show: every verb whose past has four letters, bare or augmented, gives its present a ḍamma on the prefix (yudaḥriju, yukrimu, yufarriḥu, yuqātilu), and every other verb a fatḥa (yatakassaru, yanqaṭiʿu). The four-letter group is the key.

A trap: the hamza of akrama and the hamza of inqaṭaʿa are not the same. The first is part of the pattern and is always said; the second is a hamza of joining (waṣl), said only when one begins with the word and dropped in connected speech. Al-ʿIzzī will say so when he comes to the past.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الرُّبَاعِيُّ الْمُجَرَّدُ فَلَهُ بِنَاءٌ وَاحِدٌ، فَهُوَ فَعْلَلَ يُفَعْلِلُ فَعْلَلَةً وَفِعْلَالًا، كَدَحْرَجَ يُدَحْرِجُ دَحْرَجَةً.
text.en: As for the bare quadriliteral, it has one pattern: faʿlala yufaʿlilu faʿlalatan wafiʿlālan, as daḥraja yudaḥriju daḥrajatan “to roll”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الثُّلَاثِيُّ الْمَزِيدُ فِيهِ فَهُوَ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْسَامٍ: الْأَوَّلُ مَا كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ، كَأَفْعَلَ نَحْوُ: أَكْرَمَ يُكْرِمُ إِكْرَامًا، وَفَعَّلَ نَحْوُ: فَرَّحَ يُفَرِّحُ تَفْرِيحًا، وَفَاعَلَ نَحْوُ: قَاتَلَ يُقَاتِلُ مُقَاتَلَةً وَقِتَالًا.
text.en: As for the augmented triliteral, it is of three kinds. The first is that whose past has four letters: such as afʿala, as akrama yukrimu ikrāman “to honour”; faʿʿala, as farraḥa yufarriḥu tafrīḥan “to gladden”; and fāʿala, as qātala yuqātilu muqātalatan waqitālan “to fight”.

text.original: وَالثَّانِي مَا كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى خَمْسَةِ أَحْرُفٍ: إِمَّا أَوَّلُهُ التَّاءُ مِثْلُ تَفَعَّلَ نَحْوُ: تَكَسَّرَ يَتَكَسَّرُ تَكَسُّرًا، وَتَفَاعَلَ نَحْوُ: تَبَاعَدَ، وَإِمَّا أَوَّلُهُ الْهَمْزَةُ مِثْلُ انْفَعَلَ نَحْوُ: انْقَطَعَ يَنْقَطِعُ انْقِطَاعًا، وَافْتَعَلَ نَحْوُ: اجْتَمَعَ يَجْتَمِعُ اجْتِمَاعًا، وَافْعَلَّ نَحْوُ: احْمَرَّ يَحْمَرُّ احْمِرَارًا.
text.en: The second is that whose past has five letters. Either it begins with the tāʾ, such as tafaʿʿala, as takassara yatakassaru takassuran “to break into pieces”, and tafāʿala, as tabāʿada “to move apart from each other”; or it begins with the hamza, such as infaʿala, as inqaṭaʿa yanqaṭiʿu inqiṭāʿan “to be cut off”, iftaʿala, as ijtamaʿa yajtamiʿu ijtimāʿan “to come together”, and ifʿalla, as iḥmarra yaḥmarru iḥmirāran “to turn red”.

lessons.title: Pasts of six letters; the augmented quadriliteral
body: The third kind of augmented triliteral has six letters in its past, and all six patterns begin with a hamza of joining. Istafʿala: istakhraja yastakhriju istikhrājan, “to bring out”. Ifʿālla: iḥmārra yaḥmārru iḥmīrāran, “to turn deep red”. Ifʿawwala: ijlawwadha yajlawwidhu ijliwwādhan, “to go on swiftly”. Ifʿawʿala: iʿshawshaba yaʿshawshibu iʿshīshāban, “to be thick with grass”.

The last two add a nūn: ifʿanlala, as iqʿansasa yaqʿansisu iqʿinsāsan, “to hang back”, and ifʿanlā, as islanqā yaslanqī islinqāʾan, “to lie on one's back”. In islanqā the last radical is a yāʾ, shown as alif in the past and as yāʾ in the present: these weak forms are given as the print gives them, and their rules come later.

The augmented quadriliteral has three patterns: tafaʿlala, as tadaḥraja yatadaḥraju tadaḥrujan, “to roll along”; ifʿanlala, as iḥranjama yaḥranjimu iḥrinjāman, “to crowd together”; and ifʿalalla, as iqshaʿarra yaqshaʿirru iqshiʿrāran, “to shudder”.

One pattern appears twice: ifʿanlala. Iqʿansasa is triliteral, from q-ʿ-s, with the nūn added and the sīn repeated; iḥranjama is quadriliteral, from ḥ-r-j-m, with only the nūn added. The pattern word is the same, the roots are not. To tell them apart, count the different radicals: three in iqʿansasa, four in iḥranjama.

The count is now complete: the augmented triliteral has fourteen patterns (three of four letters, five of five, six of six), the bare quadriliteral one, the augmented quadriliteral three. With the six bābs of the bare triliteral these are all the patterns the book will conjugate.

terms.en: the augmented quadriliteral
the hamza of joining, at the start of the longer patterns
the pattern with an added nūn, for three or four radicals

examples.en: istakhraja yastakhriju istikhrājan, “to bring out”
iḥmārra yaḥmārru iḥmīrāran, “to turn deep red”
iqʿansasa, “to hang back”: ifʿanlala on a triliteral root
iḥranjama, “to crowd together”: ifʿanlala on a quadriliteral root

tasks.prompt: Give the present and the maṣdar of istakhraja, iʿshawshaba and iqshaʿarra, as the book gives them.
tasks.answer: Istakhraja yastakhriju istikhrājan; iʿshawshaba yaʿshawshibu iʿshīshāban; iqshaʿarra yaqshaʿirru iqshiʿrāran.

tasks.prompt: Iqʿansasa and iḥranjama are both on ifʿanlala. Why is one triliteral and the other quadriliteral?
tasks.answer: Iqʿansasa has three different radicals, q-ʿ-s, with the nūn added and the sīn repeated; iḥranjama has four, ḥ-r-j-m, with only the nūn added.

tasks.prompt: How many augmented patterns does al-ʿIzzī give for the triliteral and for the quadriliteral?
tasks.answer: Fourteen for the triliteral (three with four letters in the past, five with five, six with six) and three for the quadriliteral.

quiz.prompt: How do all the six-letter patterns begin?
quiz.explanation: Istafʿala, ifʿālla, ifʿawwala, ifʿawʿala, ifʿanlala, ifʿanlā.

quiz.prompt: Iʿshawshaba, “to be thick with grass”, is on…
quiz.explanation: The ʿayn is repeated with a wāw between: iʿshawshaba yaʿshawshibu.

quiz.prompt: Which pattern is iḥmārra on?
quiz.explanation: Iḥmārra yaḥmārru iḥmīrāran: an alif before the doubled lām.

quiz.prompt: How many patterns has the augmented quadriliteral?
quiz.explanation: Tafaʿlala, ifʿanlala and ifʿalalla.

quiz.prompt: Tadaḥraja is on…
quiz.explanation: Daḥraja with a tāʾ added: tadaḥraja yatadaḥraju tadaḥrujan.

quiz.prompt: Which pattern is shared by a triliteral and a quadriliteral example?
quiz.explanation: Iqʿansasa from q-ʿ-s, iḥranjama from ḥ-r-j-m.

quiz.prompt: How many augmented patterns has the triliteral in al-ʿIzzī?
quiz.explanation: Three with four letters, five with five, six with six.

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ مَا كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى سِتَّةِ أَحْرُفٍ، مِثْلُ اسْتَفْعَلَ نَحْوُ: اسْتَخْرَجَ يَسْتَخْرِجُ اسْتِخْرَاجًا، وَافْعَالَّ نَحْوُ: احْمَارَّ يَحْمَارُّ احْمِيرَارًا، وَافْعَوَّلَ نَحْوُ: اجْلَوَّذَ يَجْلَوِّذُ اجْلِوَّاذًا، وَافْعَوْعَلَ نَحْوُ: اعْشَوْشَبَ يَعْشَوْشِبُ اعْشِيشَابًا، وَافْعَنْلَلَ نَحْوُ: اقْعَنْسَسَ يَقْعَنْسِسُ اقْعِنْسَاسًا، وَافْعَنْلَى نَحْوُ: اسْلَنْقَى يَسْلَنْقِي اسْلِنْقَاءً.
text.en: The third is that whose past has six letters, such as istafʿala, as istakhraja yastakhriju istikhrājan “to bring out”; ifʿālla, as iḥmārra yaḥmārru iḥmīrāran “to turn deep red”; ifʿawwala, as ijlawwadha yajlawwidhu ijliwwādhan “to go on swiftly”; ifʿawʿala, as iʿshawshaba yaʿshawshibu iʿshīshāban “to be thick with grass”; ifʿanlala, as iqʿansasa yaqʿansisu iqʿinsāsan “to hang back”; and ifʿanlā, as islanqā yaslanqī islinqāʾan “to lie on one's back”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الرُّبَاعِيُّ الْمَزِيدُ فِيهِ فَأَمْثِلَتُهُ: تَفَعْلَلَ كَتَدَحْرَجَ يَتَدَحْرَجُ تَدَحْرُجًا، وَافْعَنْلَلَ نَحْوُ: احْرَنْجَمَ يَحْرَنْجِمُ احْرِنْجَامًا، وَافْعَلَلَّ نَحْوُ: اقْشَعَرَّ يَقْشَعِرُّ اقْشِعْرَارًا.
text.en: As for the augmented quadriliteral, its patterns are: tafaʿlala, as tadaḥraja yatadaḥraju tadaḥrujan “to roll along”; ifʿanlala, as iḥranjama yaḥranjimu iḥrinjāman “to crowd together”; and ifʿalalla, as iqshaʿarra yaqshaʿirru iqshiʿrāran “to shudder”.

parts.title: The conjugation of the sound verb

lessons.title: Transitive and intransitive
body: A short note (tanbīh) before the paradigms. The verb is either transitive (mutaʿaddī), “the one that passes over to the direct object”, as ḍaraba Zaydan, “he hit Zayd”, also called “falling” (wāqiʿ) because its action falls on someone, and “passing beyond” (mujāwiz); or intransitive, “the one that does not pass beyond the doer”, as ḥasuna Zaydun, “Zayd was good”, called lāzim, “clinging” to its doer, and “not falling”.

The test is simple: does the action need someone or something it is done to? Hitting needs one hit; being good needs no one but the one who is good. In ḍaraba Zaydan, Zayd is the object, in naṣb; in ḥasuna Zaydun, Zayd is the doer, in rafʿ.

An intransitive verb can be made transitive. In the bare triliteral this is done “by doubling the ʿayn and by adding the hamza”: fariḥa, “to be glad”, gives farraḥtu Zaydan, “I gladdened Zayd”; jalasa, “to sit”, gives ajlastuhu, “I seated him”. These are faʿʿala and afʿala, the first two patterns of four letters, and the Binā named taʿdiya first among their meanings.

“And in all [kinds] by a preposition”: dhahabtu bi-Zaydin, “I went away with Zayd”, that is, I took him away; inṭalaqtu bi-hi, “I set off with him”. A preposition leaves the verb as it is, so it can serve any verb, bare or augmented: inṭalaqa is infaʿala. Doubling and the hamza change the pattern, so they belong to the bare triliteral.

This note matters for what follows: the passive (lesson 6) and the passive participle (lesson 12) are made from verbs that have an object, and al-ʿIzzī will show how an intransitive verb with a preposition makes its passive participle.

terms.en: transitive: passing over to the object
intransitive: not passing beyond the doer
making a verb transitive
the direct object

ḥasuna Zaydun, “Zayd was good”: intransitive
farraḥtu Zaydan wa-ajlastuhu: by doubling the ʿayn and by the hamza

tasks.prompt: Is ḥasuna transitive? Explain with the book's definition.
tasks.answer: No. It does not pass beyond its doer: Zayd is good, and no one else is touched by the action. It is lāzim, “not falling”.

tasks.prompt: Name the means of taʿdiya in: farraḥtu Zaydan; ajlastuhu; dhahabtu bi-Zaydin.
tasks.answer: Doubling the ʿayn (faʿʿala); adding the hamza (afʿala); a preposition (bi-).

tasks.prompt: Why does the preposition work “in all”, but doubling and the hamza only in the bare triliteral?
tasks.answer: Doubling and the hamza turn the bare verb into a new pattern, faʿʿala or afʿala. A preposition leaves the verb as it is, so it can follow any verb, bare or augmented, as inṭalaqtu bi-hi with inṭalaqa, which is infaʿala.

quiz.prompt: The transitive verb is the one that…
options: passes over to the direct object
quiz.explanation: As ḍaraba Zaydan: the hitting falls on Zayd.

quiz.prompt: Which name is NOT given to the transitive verb?
quiz.explanation: Lāzim is the intransitive: it clings to its doer.

quiz.prompt: In ḥasuna Zaydun, Zayd is…
quiz.explanation: The verb does not pass beyond him, so he is the doer, in rafʿ.

quiz.prompt: Farraḥtu Zaydan is made transitive by…
quiz.explanation: Fariḥa becomes farraḥa, on faʿʿala.

quiz.prompt: Ajlastuhu is made transitive by…
quiz.explanation: Jalasa becomes ajlasa, on afʿala: “I seated him”.

quiz.prompt: Which means can make any verb transitive?
quiz.explanation: “And in all by a preposition”: dhahabtu bi-Zaydin, inṭalaqtu bi-hi.

quiz.prompt: Dhahabtu bi-Zaydin means…
options: I went away with Zayd, took him away
quiz.explanation: With bi- the going falls on Zayd too.

text.original: الْفِعْلُ إِمَّا مُتَعَدٍّ، وَهُوَ الَّذِي يَتَعَدَّى إِلَى الْمَفْعُولِ بِهِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدًا، وَيُسَمَّى أَيْضًا وَاقِعًا وَمُجَاوِزًا، وَإِمَّا غَيْرُ مُتَعَدٍّ، وَهُوَ الَّذِي لَمْ يُجَاوِزِ الْفَاعِلَ، كَقَوْلِكَ: حَسُنَ زَيْدٌ، وَيُسَمَّى لَازِمًا وَغَيْرَ وَاقِعٍ.
text.en: The verb is either transitive (mutaʿaddī), which is the one that passes over to the direct object (al-mafʿūl bihi), as when you say ḍaraba Zaydan “he hit Zayd”; it is also called “falling” (wāqiʿ) and “passing beyond” (mujāwiz). Or it is not transitive, which is the one that does not pass beyond the doer, as when you say ḥasuna Zaydun “Zayd was good”; it is called intransitive (lāzim) and “not falling” (ghayr wāqiʿ).

text.original: وَيُعَدِّيهِ فِي الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ تَضْعِيفُ الْعَيْنِ وَزِيَادَةُ الْهَمْزَةِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: فَرَّحْتُ زَيْدًا وَأَجْلَسْتُهُ، وَحَرْفُ الْجَرِّ فِي الْكُلِّ، نَحْوُ: ذَهَبْتُ بِزَيْدٍ وَانْطَلَقْتُ بِهِ.
text.en: In the bare triliteral it is made transitive by doubling the ʿayn and by adding the hamza, as when you say farraḥtu Zaydan “I gladdened Zayd” and ajlastuhu “I made him sit”; and in all [kinds] by a preposition (ḥarf al-jarr), as dhahabtu bi-Zaydin “I went away with Zayd” and inṭalaqtu bi-hi “I set off with him”.

lessons.title: The past, built for the doer and for the one done to
body: The past “is that which indicates a meaning that took place in past time”. Its form built for the doer has a fatḥa on its first letter, “and likewise the first vowelled letter in it has fatḥa”: naṣara naṣarā naṣarū, and so on through the persons. The same holds for faʿlala, tafaʿlala, infaʿala, iftaʿala, istafʿala and the rest.

Why add “the first vowelled letter”? Because of the alifs at the start of the longer patterns. “The vowels of the alifs at the beginning are not taken into account, for they are additional: they stand when one begins with them and drop in connected speech.” In inqaṭaʿa the first letter, the hamza of joining, does not count; the first vowelled letter is the qāf, and it has fatḥa.

The form built for the one done to, “whose doer is not named”, has a ḍamma on its first letter: fuʿila, ufʿila, fūʿila, tufuʿʿila, tufūʿila, fuʿlila, tufuʿlila; or on its first vowelled letter: uftuʿila, ustufʿila, “and the hamza of joining follows this letter in having ḍamma”. In every case “the letter before its last always has kasra”: nuṣira Zaydun, “Zayd was helped”, ustukhrija al-mālu, “the money was brought out”.

Watch the long vowels. In fūʿila the alif of fāʿala, after a ḍamma, is said as ū: qātala gives qūtila. In tufuʿʿila both the tāʾ and the fāʾ take a ḍamma: takassara gives tukussira. In ustufʿila the sīn is quiescent, so the ḍamma falls on the tāʾ, and the hamza of joining takes a ḍamma with it: istakhraja gives ustukhrija.

A trap: the hamza of akrama is part of the pattern and takes the ḍamma itself, ukrima, as the first letter; the hamza of istakhraja is a hamza of joining and only follows the ḍamma of the tāʾ. They look alike in ukrima and ustukhrija, but for different reasons.

built for the one done to: the passive, whose doer is not named

tasks.prompt: Make the passive of akrama, qātala and istakhraja, and say which letter takes the ḍamma.
tasks.answer: Ukrima: the first letter, the hamza of afʿala. Qūtila: the first letter, with the alif said as ū. Ustukhrija: the first vowelled letter, the tāʾ, with the hamza of joining following it in ḍamma. In all three the letter before the last has kasra.

tasks.prompt: Why is the vowel of the hamza in inqaṭaʿa not counted?
tasks.answer: It is a hamza of joining: added, said only when one begins with the word and dropped in connected speech. So the first vowelled letter that counts is the qāf, with its fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: In nuṣira Zaydun, what does “built for the one done to” mean?
tasks.answer: The verb's doer is not named. Zayd is the one helped, and he stands in rafʿ in the place of the doer.

quiz.prompt: In the active past, the first letter has…
quiz.explanation: And so does the first vowelled letter: naṣara, inqaṭaʿa.

quiz.prompt: Why are the vowels of the opening alifs not counted?
options: They are added and drop in connected speech
quiz.explanation: The hamza of joining stands at the start of speech and falls in the middle.

quiz.prompt: In the passive past, the letter before the last has…
quiz.explanation: Nuṣira, ukrima, ustukhrija: the kasra before the last is the mark of the passive past.

quiz.prompt: The passive of qātala is…
quiz.explanation: Fūʿila: after the ḍamma the alif is said as ū.

quiz.prompt: In ustukhrija, which letter carries the ḍamma that counts?
options: The tāʾ, the first vowelled letter
quiz.explanation: The hamza of joining only follows it.

quiz.prompt: Which passive pattern has a ḍamma on two letters before the doubled ʿayn?
quiz.explanation: Takassara gives tukussira: the tāʾ and the fāʾ both take ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: The passive is called the verb…
quiz.explanation: Alladhī lam yusamma fāʿiluhu: the one done to takes the doer's place.

text.original: أَمَّا الْمَاضِي فَهُوَ الَّذِي دَلَّ عَلَى مَعْنًى وُجِدَ فِي الزَّمَانِ الْمَاضِي، فَالْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْفَاعِلِ مِنْهُ مَا كَانَ أَوَّلُهُ مَفْتُوحًا، وَكَذَا أَوَّلُ مُتَحَرِّكٍ مِنْهُ مَفْتُوحًا، مِثَالُهُ: نَصَرَ نَصَرَا نَصَرُوا إِلَخْ. وَقِسْ عَلَى هَذَا فَعْلَلَ وَتَفَعْلَلَ وَانْفَعَلَ وَافْتَعَلَ وَاسْتَفْعَلَ وَافْعَالَّ وَافْعَوْعَلَ وَافْعَنْلَلَ وَافْعَنْلَى وَافْعَوَّلَ، وَلَا تُعْتَبَرُ حَرَكَاتُ الْأَلِفَاتِ فِي الْأَوَائِلِ؛ فَإِنَّهَا زَائِدَةٌ تَثْبُتُ فِي الِابْتِدَاءِ وَتَسْقُطُ فِي الدَّرْجِ.
text.en: As for the past, it is that which indicates a meaning that took place in past time. Its form built for the doer (al-mabnī li-al-fāʿil) is the one whose first letter has fatḥa, and likewise the first voweled letter in it has fatḥa. Its example: naṣara naṣarā naṣarū etc. Measure on this faʿlala, tafaʿlala, infaʿala, iftaʿala, istafʿala, ifʿālla, ifʿawʿala, ifʿanlala, ifʿanlā and ifʿawwala. The vowels of the alifs at the beginning are not taken into account, for they are additional: they stand when one begins with them and drop in connected speech.

text.original: وَالْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْمَفْعُولِ مِنْهُ، وَهُوَ الَّذِي لَمْ يُسَمَّ فَاعِلُهُ، وَهُوَ مَا كَانَ أَوَّلُهُ مَضْمُومًا، كَفُعِلَ وَأُفْعِلَ وَفُوعِلَ وَتُفُعِّلَ وَتُفُوعِلَ وَفُعْلِلَ وَتُفُعْلِلَ، أَوْ كَانَ أَوَّلُ مُتَحَرِّكٍ مِنْهُ مَضْمُومًا، مِثْلُ افْتُعِلَ وَاسْتُفْعِلَ، وَهَمْزَةُ الْوَصْلِ تَتْبَعُ هَذَا الْمَضْمُومَ فِي الضَّمِّ، وَمَا قَبْلَ آخِرِهِ يَكُونُ مَكْسُورًا أَبَدًا، كَقَوْلِكَ: نُصِرَ زَيْدٌ، وَاسْتُخْرِجَ الْمَالُ.
text.en: Its form built for the one done to (al-mabnī li-al-mafʿūl), which is the one whose doer is not named, is that whose first letter has ḍamma, as fuʿila, ufʿila, fūʿila, tufuʿʿila, tufūʿila, fuʿlila and tufuʿlila; or whose first voweled letter has ḍamma, as uftuʿila and ustufʿila, and the hamza of connection follows this letter in having ḍamma. The letter before its last always has kasra, as when you say nuṣira Zaydun “Zayd was helped” and ustukhrija al-mālu “the money was brought out”.

lessons.title: The muḍāriʿ and its letters
body: The muḍāriʿ is the verb with one of four added letters at its start: the hamza, the nūn, the yāʾ and the tāʾ, gathered in atayna, anaytu or naʾtī. The hamza is for the speaker alone; the nūn for the speaker with another; the tāʾ for the one addressed, any number, masculine or feminine, and for the absent woman, singular and dual; the yāʾ for the absent man, any number, and for the plural of absent women.

It serves two times: yafʿalu al-āna, “he is doing now”, the present (ḥāl), and yafʿalu ghadan, “he will do tomorrow”, the future (mustaqbal). With sa- or sawfa it is reserved for the future: sa-yafʿalu, sawfa yafʿalu.

Built for the doer, its prefix has fatḥa, “except the verb whose past has four letters: in it the letter of the muḍāriʿ always has ḍamma”: yudaḥriju, yukrimu, yufarriḥu, yuqātilu. Here the count of lesson 3 pays: daḥraja, akrama, farraḥa and qātala all have four letters. “The sign that these four are built for the doer is that the letter before the last always has kasra.” Every other verb has fatḥa on its prefix: yanṣuru, yatakassaru, yanqaṭiʿu, yastakhriju, yatadaḥraju.

Built for the one done to, “the letter of the muḍāriʿ has ḍamma and the letter before the last has fatḥa”: yunṣaru, yudaḥraju, yukramu, yufarraḥu, yuqātalu, yustakhraju. So in the four-letter verbs the prefix is the same in both voices, and only the vowel before the last tells them apart: yukrimu, “he honours”, yukramu, “he is honoured”.

Two traps. First, the tāʾ serves both “you” and “she”: tanṣuru is “you help” or “she helps”, and only the sentence decides. Second, the yāʾ serves the plural of absent women too: yanṣurna, “they (women) help”, with a yāʾ, though the singular is tanṣuru.

terms.en: the letters of the muḍāriʿ: hamza, nūn, yāʾ, tāʾ
the present and the future
particle that reserves the muḍāriʿ for the future, like sa-

examples.en: atayna, anaytu, naʾtī: words that gather the four letters
sa-yafʿalu, sawfa yafʿalu: reserved for the future
ḍamma on the prefix: pasts of four letters
the passive: ḍamma on the prefix, fatḥa before the last

tasks.prompt: Which letter and which person: anṣuru, nanṣuru, tanṣuru, yanṣurna?
tasks.answer: Anṣuru: the hamza, “I help”. Nanṣuru: the nūn, “we help”. Tanṣuru: the tāʾ, “you help” or “she helps”. Yanṣurna: the yāʾ, “they (women) help”.

tasks.prompt: Why does yudaḥriju have a ḍamma on its prefix and yatadaḥraju a fatḥa?
tasks.answer: Daḥraja has four letters in its past, and every such verb has ḍamma on the prefix of its active muḍāriʿ. Tadaḥraja has five, so its prefix takes fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Tell active from passive: yukrimu, yukramu, yastakhriju, yustakhraju.
tasks.answer: Yukrimu active, yukramu passive: the prefix is the same, the kasra or fatḥa before the last decides. Yastakhriju active (fatḥa on the prefix, kasra before the last), yustakhraju passive (ḍamma on the prefix, fatḥa before the last).

tasks.prompt: What does sa- do to yanṣuru?
tasks.answer: It reserves it for the future: sa-yanṣuru, “he will help”, can no longer mean “he is helping now”.

quiz.prompt: Which letters begin the muḍāriʿ?
quiz.explanation: Gathered in atayna, anaytu or naʾtī.

quiz.prompt: The nūn is for…
quiz.explanation: The nūn is for the speaker with another: nanṣuru, “we help”; the hamza is for the speaker alone.

quiz.prompt: Tanṣuru can mean…
quiz.explanation: The tāʾ serves the one addressed and the absent woman.

quiz.prompt: What restricts the muḍāriʿ to the future?
quiz.explanation: Sa- and sawfa reserve it for the future: sa-yafʿalu, sawfa yafʿalu, “he will do”.

quiz.prompt: Which active muḍāriʿ has a ḍamma on its prefix?
quiz.explanation: Qātala has four letters in its past.

quiz.prompt: The passive muḍāriʿ has…
options: ḍamma on the prefix, fatḥa before the last
fatḥa on the prefix, kasra before the last
quiz.explanation: Yunṣaru, yukramu, yustakhraju.

quiz.prompt: What tells yukrimu from yukramu?
options: The vowel before the last letter
quiz.explanation: Kasra for the doer, fatḥa for the one done to.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُضَارِعُ فَهُوَ مَا كَانَ فِي أَوَّلِهِ إِحْدَى الزَّوَائِدِ الْأَرْبَعِ، وَهِيَ الْهَمْزَةُ وَالنُّونُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالتَّاءُ، يَجْمَعُهَا «أَتَيْنَ» أَوْ «أَنَيْتُ» أَوْ «نَأْتِي». فَالْهَمْزَةُ لِلْمُتَكَلِّمِ وَحْدَهُ، وَالنُّونُ لَهُ إِذَا كَانَ مَعَهُ غَيْرُهُ، وَالتَّاءُ لِلْمُخَاطَبِ مُفْرَدًا أَوْ مُثَنًّى أَوْ مَجْمُوعًا، مُذَكَّرًا كَانَ أَوْ مُؤَنَّثًا، وَلِلْغَائِبَةِ الْمُفْرَدَةِ وَالْمُثَنَّاةِ، وَالْيَاءُ لِلْغَائِبِ الْمُذَكَّرِ مُفْرَدًا أَوْ مُثَنًّى أَوْ مَجْمُوعًا، وَلِجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ الْغَائِبَةِ.
text.en: As for the muḍāriʿ, it is that which has at its beginning one of the four additional letters, which are the hamza, the nūn, the yāʾ and the tāʾ; they are gathered in atayna or anaytu or naʾtī. The hamza is for the speaker alone; the nūn is for him when another is with him; the tāʾ is for the one addressed, singular, dual or plural, masculine or feminine, and for the absent feminine, singular and dual; and the yāʾ is for the absent masculine, singular, dual or plural, and for the plural of the absent feminine.

text.original: وَهَذَا يَصْلُحُ لِلْحَالِ وَالِاسْتِقْبَالِ، تَقُولُ: يَفْعَلُ الْآنَ، وَيُسَمَّى حَالًا وَحَاضِرًا، وَيَفْعَلُ غَدًا، وَيُسَمَّى مُسْتَقْبَلًا. فَإِذَا أَدْخَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ السِّينَ أَوْ سَوْفَ فَقُلْتَ: سَيَفْعَلُ، أَوْ سَوْفَ يَفْعَلُ، اخْتَصَّ بِزَمَانِ الِاسْتِقْبَالِ.
text.en: This [form] serves for the present and the future. You say yafʿalu al-āna “he is doing now”, and it is called present (ḥāl, ḥāḍir), and yafʿalu ghadan “he will do tomorrow”, and it is called future (mustaqbal). When you put the sīn or sawfa before it and say sa-yafʿalu or sawfa yafʿalu “he will do”, it is reserved for future time.

text.original: فَالْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْفَاعِلِ مِنْهُ مَا كَانَ حَرْفُ الْمُضَارَعَةِ مِنْهُ مَفْتُوحًا، إِلَّا مَا كَانَ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ؛ فَإِنَّ حَرْفَ الْمُضَارَعَةِ مِنْهُ يَكُونُ مَضْمُومًا أَبَدًا، نَحْوُ: يُدَحْرِجُ وَيُكْرِمُ وَيُفَرِّحُ وَيُقَاتِلُ، وَعَلَامَةُ بِنَاءِ هَذِهِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ لِلْفَاعِلِ كَوْنُ الْحَرْفِ الَّذِي قَبْلَ الْآخِرِ مَكْسُورًا أَبَدًا.
text.en: Its form built for the doer is the one in which the letter of the muḍāriʿ (ḥarf al-muḍāraʿa) has fatḥa, except the verb whose past has four letters: in it the letter of the muḍāriʿ always has ḍamma, as yudaḥriju, yukrimu, yufarriḥu and yuqātilu. The sign that these four are built for the doer is that the letter before the last always has kasra.

text.original: مِثَالُهُ مِنْ يَفْعُلُ: يَنْصُرُ يَنْصُرَانِ يَنْصُرُونَ إِلَخْ. وَقِسْ عَلَى هَذَا: يَضْرِبُ، وَيَعْلَمُ، وَيُدَحْرِجُ، وَيُكْرِمُ، وَيُفَرِّحُ، وَيُقَاتِلُ، وَيَتَكَسَّرُ، وَيَتَبَاعَدُ، وَيَنْقَطِعُ، وَيَجْتَمِعُ، وَيَحْمَرُّ، وَيَحْمَارُّ، وَيَسْتَخْرِجُ، وَيَعْشَوْشِبُ، وَيَجْلَوِّذُ، وَيَقْعَنْسِسُ، وَيَسْلَنْقِي، وَيَتَدَحْرَجُ، وَيَحْرَنْجِمُ، وَيَقْشَعِرُّ.
text.en: Its example from yafʿulu: yanṣuru yanṣurāni yanṣurūna etc. Measure on this yaḍribu, yaʿlamu, yudaḥriju, yukrimu, yufarriḥu, yuqātilu, yatakassaru, yatabāʿadu, yanqaṭiʿu, yajtamiʿu, yaḥmarru, yaḥmārru, yastakhriju, yaʿshawshibu, yajlawwidhu, yaqʿansisu, yaslanqī, yatadaḥraju, yaḥranjimu and yaqshaʿirru.

text.original: وَالْمَبْنِيُّ لِلْمَفْعُولِ مِنْهُ مَا كَانَ حَرْفُ الْمُضَارَعَةِ مِنْهُ مَضْمُومًا، وَمَا قَبْلَ الْآخِرِ مِنْهُ مَفْتُوحًا، نَحْوُ: يُنْصَرُ، وَيُدَحْرَجُ، وَيُكْرَمُ، وَيُفَرَّحُ، وَيُقَاتَلُ، وَيُسْتَخْرَجُ، وَقِسِ الْبَوَاقِيَ عَلَى هَذِهِ.
text.en: Its form built for the one done to is the one in which the letter of the muḍāriʿ has ḍamma and the letter before the last has fatḥa, as yunṣaru, yudaḥraju, yukramu, yufarraḥu, yuqātalu and yustakhraju; measure the rest on these.

lessons.title: Negation, the jussive, the naṣb, the lām of command and the prohibition
body: The negating mā and lā come before the muḍāriʿ “and do not change its form”: lā yanṣuru lā yanṣurāni lā yanṣurūna, “he does not help…”. The verb stays in rafʿ.

The jussive particles (al-jawāzim) do change it: they take away “the vowel of the singular, and the nūn of the dual, of the masculine plural and of the feminine singular addressed”: lam yanṣur, lam yanṣurā, lam yanṣurū, lam tanṣurī. The nūn of the feminine plural is not taken away, “because it is a pronoun, like the wāw in the masculine plural”: lam yanṣurna. A pronoun is part of the meaning and cannot be dropped; the other nūns are only signs of rafʿ.

The particle of naṣb “replaces the ḍamma with the fatḥa and drops the nūns other than the nūn of the feminine plural”: lan yanṣura, lan yanṣurā, lan yanṣurū. So naṣb and jazm look the same wherever a nūn drops; they differ only in the singular persons and the first persons, fatḥa against sukūn.

Two jussive particles make commands. The lām of command gives the command to the absent: li-yanṣur, “let him help”, li-yaḍrib, li-yaʿlam, li-yudaḥrij. The lā of prohibition forbids: lā yanṣur, “let him not help”, to the absent, and lā tanṣur, “do not help!”, to the one present.

A trap in writing: lā yanṣuru, “he does not help”, and lā yanṣur, “let him not help”, are the same letters with one vowel's difference. The first lā negates and leaves the verb in rafʿ; the second forbids and puts it in jazm. The vowel of the last letter tells you which lā you are reading.

terms.en: the jussive particles
a particle of naṣb, such as lan
the lām of command
the lā of prohibition

tasks.prompt: Why does the nūn of yanṣurna stay after lam, when the nūn of yanṣurūna drops?
tasks.answer: The nūn of yanṣurna is a pronoun, the doer, like the wāw of yanṣurūna; a pronoun cannot be dropped. The nūn of yanṣurūna is only the sign of rafʿ, so the jussive takes it away.

tasks.prompt: Put tanṣurīna after lan and after lam. Why are the two the same?
tasks.answer: Lan tanṣurī and lam tanṣurī. Both particles drop the nūn of the woman addressed; where the nūn is the sign, naṣb and jazm look alike.

tasks.prompt: Read lā yanṣuru and lā yanṣur, and say which lā each has.
tasks.answer: Lā yanṣuru, “he does not help”: the negating lā, the verb in rafʿ. Lā yanṣur, “let him not help”: the lā of prohibition, the verb in jazm.

quiz.prompt: What do mā and lā of negation do to the muḍāriʿ?
options: Nothing: they do not change its form
quiz.explanation: Negation leaves the form unchanged: lā yanṣuru stays in rafʿ, with its ḍamma.

quiz.prompt: What does the jussive take from the singular?
quiz.explanation: The jussive takes the vowel of the singular: yanṣuru becomes lam yanṣur.

quiz.prompt: Why is the nūn of the feminine plural kept in jazm?
options: It is the sign of rafʿ
quiz.explanation: Like the wāw of the masculine plural, it is the doer itself.

quiz.prompt: Lan yanṣurū: what did lan do?
quiz.explanation: The nāṣib drops the nūns other than the women's.

quiz.prompt: Li-yanṣur means…
quiz.explanation: The lām of command, a jussive particle: the command to the absent.

quiz.prompt: Lā tanṣur is…
options: the prohibition to the one present
quiz.explanation: The lā of prohibition puts the verb in jazm.

quiz.prompt: Where do naṣb and jazm differ in form?
options: Where no nūn drops: fatḥa against sukūn
quiz.explanation: Lan yanṣura, lam yanṣur; but lan yanṣurā and lam yanṣurā are the same.

text.original: اعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يَدْخُلُ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ مَا وَلَا النَّافِيَتَانِ فَلَا تُغَيِّرَانِ صِيغَتَهُ، تَقُولُ: لَا يَنْصُرُ لَا يَنْصُرَانِ لَا يَنْصُرُونَ إِلَخْ.
text.en: Know that the negating mā and lā come before the muḍāriʿ and do not change its form; you say lā yanṣuru lā yanṣurāni lā yanṣurūna “he does not help, they two do not help, they do not help” etc.

text.original: وَيَدْخُلُ الْجَوَازِمُ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ فَيُحْذَفُ حَرَكَةُ الْوَاحِدِ، وَنُونُ التَّثْنِيَةِ وَالْجَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ وَالْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَلَا يُحْذَفُ نُونُ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ ضَمِيرٌ كَالْوَاوِ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ، فَتَقُولُ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ: لَمْ يَنْصُرْ لَمْ يَنْصُرَا لَمْ يَنْصُرُوا إِلَخْ.
text.en: The jussive particles (al-jawāzim) come before the muḍāriʿ, and then the vowel of the singular is deleted, and the nūn of the dual, of the masculine plural and of the feminine singular addressed. The nūn of the feminine plural is not deleted, because it is a pronoun, like the wāw in the masculine plural. So you say in every case: lam yanṣur lam yanṣurā lam yanṣurū “he did not help, they two did not help, they did not help” etc.

text.original: وَيَدْخُلُ عَلَيْهِ النَّاصِبُ فَيُبْدِلُ مِنَ الضَّمَّةِ الْفَتْحَةَ، وَيُسْقِطُ النُّونَاتِ سِوَى نُونِ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ، فَتَقُولُ: لَنْ يَنْصُرَ لَنْ يَنْصُرَا لَنْ يَنْصُرُوا إِلَخْ.
text.en: The particle of the naṣb (al-nāṣib) comes before it: it replaces the ḍamma with the fatḥa and drops the nūns other than the nūn of the feminine plural. You say lan yanṣura lan yanṣurā lan yanṣurū “he will not help, they two will not help, they will not help” etc.

text.original: وَمِنَ الْجَوَازِمِ لَامُ الْأَمْرِ، فَتَقُولُ فِي أَمْرِ الْغَائِبِ: لِيَنْصُرْ لِيَنْصُرَا لِيَنْصُرُوا إِلَخْ، وَكَذَلِكَ لِيَضْرِبْ وَلِيَعْلَمْ وَلِيُدَحْرِجْ وَغَيْرُهَا. وَمِنْهَا لَا النَّاهِيَةُ، فَتَقُولُ فِي نَهْيِ الْغَائِبِ: لَا يَنْصُرْ لَا يَنْصُرَا لَا يَنْصُرُوا إِلَخْ، وَفِي نَهْيِ الْحَاضِرِ: لَا تَنْصُرْ لَا تَنْصُرَا لَا تَنْصُرُوا إِلَخْ، وَهَكَذَا قِيَاسُ سَائِرِ الْأَمْثِلَةِ.
text.en: Among the jussive particles is the lām of command. You say in the command to the absent: li-yanṣur li-yanṣurā li-yanṣurū “let him help, let them two help, let them help” etc., and likewise li-yaḍrib, li-yaʿlam, li-yudaḥrij and the others. Among them is the lā of prohibition. You say in the prohibition to the absent: lā yanṣur lā yanṣurā lā yanṣurū “let him not help, let them two not help, let them not help” etc., and in the prohibition to the one present: lā tanṣur lā tanṣurā lā tanṣurū “do not help!” etc. The rule for all the other forms goes in the same way.

lessons.title: The command to the one present
body: The command to the one present is called “the command by the form” (al-amr bi-l-ṣīgha): it is made by a form of its own, not by a particle like the lām of li-yanṣur. It “runs on the wording of the jussive muḍāriʿ”: take tanṣuru, put it in jazm, tanṣur, and change only its beginning. What happens at the beginning depends on the letter after the prefix.

If that letter has a vowel, drop the prefix and keep the rest as it is in jazm. From tudaḥriju: daḥrij daḥrijā daḥrijū daḥrijī daḥrijā daḥrijna, “roll!”. So too farriḥ, qātil, takassar, tabāʿad, tadaḥraj: in each the letter after the prefix is vowelled, and the command begins with it.

If that letter is quiescent, drop the prefix and add a hamza of joining, since a word cannot begin with a quiescent letter. The hamza has kasra, “unless the ʿayn of its muḍāriʿ has ḍamma: then you give it ḍamma”: unṣur unṣurā unṣurū, “help!”, but iḍrib, iʿlam, inqaṭiʿ, ijtamiʿ, istakhrij. The vowel follows the ʿayn of the present, not of the past: naṣara has fatḥa in its past, yet unṣur takes ḍamma because of yanṣuru; ʿalima yaʿlamu has fatḥa in its present, so the hamza keeps the usual kasra, iʿlam.

Akrim, “honour!”, is the exception. Its hamza has fatḥa and is never dropped, “building on the rejected original form, for the original of tukrimu is tuʾakrimu”. The hamza of afʿala was dropped from the muḍāriʿ; take the prefix away from tuʾakrimu and the pattern's own hamza comes back. It is not a hamza of joining but part of afʿala.
A check that catches most mistakes: say the command in the middle of a sentence. Fa-nṣur and wa-stakhrij lose their hamza; fa-akrim keeps it. If the hamza stays, it belongs to the pattern.

the command to the one present
the rejected original, tuʾakrimu

tasks.prompt: Make the command to one man from tuqātilu, tastakhriju and tanqaṭiʿu, and say whether a hamza is needed.
tasks.answer: Qātil: no hamza, the qāf after the prefix is vowelled. Istakhrij and inqaṭiʿ: a hamza of joining with kasra, because the letter after the prefix is quiescent and the ʿayn of the present has kasra.

tasks.prompt: Why is it unṣur with ḍamma, but iʿlam with kasra?
tasks.answer: The hamza follows the ʿayn of the muḍāriʿ: yanṣuru has ḍamma, so unṣur; yaʿlamu has fatḥa, so the hamza takes the usual kasra: iʿlam.

tasks.prompt: Why is the hamza of akrim said with fatḥa and kept in connected speech?
tasks.answer: It is not a hamza of joining but the hamza of afʿala. The muḍāriʿ dropped it, but its rejected original is tuʾakrimu; with the prefix taken away the hamza of the pattern returns, with its fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Give the command of daḥraja in the six persons.
tasks.answer: Daḥrij, daḥrijā, daḥrijū, daḥrijī, daḥrijā, daḥrijna.

quiz.explanation: Daḥrij, farriḥ, qātil, takassar.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْأَمْرُ بِالصِّيغَةِ، وَهُوَ أَمْرُ الْحَاضِرِ، فَهُوَ جَارٍ عَلَى لَفْظِ الْمُضَارِعِ الْمَجْزُومِ؛ فَإِنْ كَانَ مَا بَعْدَ حَرْفِ الْمُضَارَعَةِ مُتَحَرِّكًا فَتُسْقِطُ مِنْهُ حَرْفَ الْمُضَارَعَةِ وَتَأْتِي بِصُورَةِ الْبَاقِي مَجْزُومًا، فَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ الْحَاضِرِ مِنْ تُدَحْرِجُ: دَحْرِجْ دَحْرِجَا دَحْرِجُوا دَحْرِجِي دَحْرِجَا دَحْرِجْنَ، وَهَكَذَا قِيَاسُ سَائِرِ الْأَمْثِلَةِ، تَقُولُ: فَرِّحْ وَقَاتِلْ وَتَكَسَّرْ وَتَبَاعَدْ وَتَدَحْرَجْ.
text.en: As for the command by the form (al-amr bi-al-ṣīgha), which is the command to the one present, it runs on the wording of the jussive muḍāriʿ. If the letter after the letter of the muḍāriʿ is voweled, you drop the letter of the muḍāriʿ and bring what remains in its jussive shape. So you say in the command to the one present from tudaḥriju: daḥrij daḥrijā daḥrijū daḥrijī daḥrijā daḥrijna “roll!”; the rule for the other forms goes in the same way: you say farriḥ, qātil, takassar, tabāʿad and tadaḥraj.

text.original: فَإِنْ كَانَ سَاكِنًا فَتَحْذِفُ مِنْهُ حَرْفَ الْمُضَارَعَةِ وَتَأْتِي بِصُورَةِ الْبَاقِي مَجْزُومًا مَزِيدًا فِي أَوَّلِهِ هَمْزَةُ وَصْلٍ مَكْسُورَةً، إِلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ عَيْنُ الْمُضَارِعِ مِنْهُ مَضْمُومًا فَتَضُمُّهَا، تَقُولُ: اُنْصُرْ اُنْصُرَا اُنْصُرُوا، وَكَذَلِكَ اضْرِبْ وَاعْلَمْ وَانْقَطِعْ وَاجْتَمِعْ وَاسْتَخْرِجْ. وَفَتَحُوا هَمْزَةَ أَكْرِمْ بِنَاءً عَلَى الْأَصْلِ الْمَرْفُوضِ؛ فَإِنَّ أَصْلَ تُكْرِمُ تُؤَكْرِمُ.
text.en: If it has a sukūn, you delete the letter of the muḍāriʿ and bring what remains in its jussive shape, with a hamza of connection added at its beginning, with kasra, unless the ʿayn of its muḍāriʿ has ḍamma: then you give it ḍamma. You say unṣur unṣurā unṣurū “help!”, and likewise iḍrib, iʿlam, inqaṭiʿ, ijtamiʿ and istakhrij. They gave the hamza of akrim “honour!” a fatḥa, building on the rejected original form, for the original of tukrimu is tuʾakrimu.

lessons.title: Two tāʾs, and the changes of iftaʿala
body: In the muḍāriʿ of tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala two tāʾs meet when the prefix is a tāʾ: that of the prefix and that of the pattern. Both may be kept, as tatajannabu, “you keep away”, tatabāʿadu, tatadaḥraju; or one may be dropped, as in the Qurʾān: fa-anta lahu taṣaddā, “to him you give your attention” (80:6), nāran talaẓẓā, “a fire that blazes” (92:14), and tanazzalu al-malāʾikatu, “the angels descend” (97:4).

Here is a trap for the reader of the Qurʾān. With one tāʾ dropped, the muḍāriʿ looks like the past of the same pattern. Tanazzalu ends in ḍamma, the rafʿ of a muḍāriʿ; the past would be tanazzala, or tanazzalat with a feminine subject. The last vowel shows that the verse speaks of what the angels do, not what they did.

When the fāʾ of iftaʿala is one of the four letters ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ, ẓāʾ, its tāʾ becomes ṭāʾ: from al-ṣulḥ, iṣṭalaḥa, “to make peace”; from al-ḍarb, iḍṭaraba; from al-ṭard, iṭṭarada; from al-ẓulm, iẓẓalama. The change runs through all the forms: iṣṭalaḥa yaṣṭaliḥu iṣṭilāḥan, muṣṭaliḥ, muṣṭalaḥ, iṣṭaliḥ, lā taṣṭaliḥ.

When the fāʾ is dāl, dhāl or zāy, the tāʾ becomes dāl: iddaraʾa, iddakara, izdajara, from al-darʾ, al-dhikr, al-zajr; in iddakara the dhāl has gone into the dāl. When the fāʾ is wāw, yāʾ or thāʾ, the fāʾ itself becomes tāʾ and is merged into the tāʾ of iftaʿala: ittaqā, “to guard oneself”, ittasara, ittaghara.

The book gives the rules without their reason; the commentators give it as ease of speech. The ṭāʾ shares the heavy, “covered” sound of ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ and ẓāʾ; the dāl shares the voice of dāl, dhāl and zāy, which the tāʾ lacks. A practical result: ittaqā is found in the dictionary under w-q-y, iṣṭalaḥa under ṣ-l-ḥ, izdajara under z-j-r. Never look for a root with a ṭāʾ or a dāl that is only the tāʾ of iftaʿala.

tasks.prompt: Form iftaʿala from al-ṣulḥ and give all its forms as the book does.

tasks.prompt: Why is izdajara written with a dāl, though iftaʿala has a tāʾ?
tasks.answer: Its fāʾ is a zāy, and when the fāʾ of iftaʿala is dāl, dhāl or zāy, the tāʾ is turned into a dāl.

tasks.prompt: In tanazzalu al-malāʾikatu (Q 97:4), is tanazzalu past or present? How do you know?
tasks.answer: Present: it is the muḍāriʿ of tanazzala with one of the two tāʾs dropped. Its final ḍamma is the rafʿ of the muḍāriʿ; the past would end in fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: What is the root of ittaqā, and where did its first radical go?
tasks.answer: W-q-y. The wāw, as fāʾ of iftaʿala, was turned into a tāʾ and merged into the tāʾ of the pattern: hence the doubled tāʾ.

quiz.prompt: In which patterns can two tāʾs meet at the start of the muḍāriʿ?
quiz.explanation: Their own tāʾ meets the tāʾ of the prefix.

quiz.explanation: A muḍāriʿ of tafaʿʿala: “a fire that blazes”.

quiz.prompt: After which letters as fāʾ does the tāʾ of iftaʿala become ṭāʾ?
quiz.explanation: Iṣṭalaḥa, iḍṭaraba, iṭṭarada, iẓẓalama.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ إِذَا اجْتَمَعَ تَاءَانِ فِي أَوَّلِ مُضَارِعِ تَفَعَّلَ وَتَفَاعَلَ وَتَفَعْلَلَ فَيَجُوزُ إِثْبَاتُهُمَا، نَحْوُ: تَتَجَنَّبُ وَتَتَبَاعَدُ وَتَتَدَحْرَجُ، وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُ إِحْدَاهُمَا كَمَا فِي التَّنْزِيلِ: ﴿فَأَنْتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى﴾، وَ﴿نَارًا تَلَظَّى﴾، وَ﴿تَنَزَّلُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ﴾.
text.en: Know that when two tāʾs come together at the beginning of the muḍāriʿ of tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala, both may be kept, as tatajannabu “you keep away”, tatabāʿadu “you move away” and tatadaḥraju “you roll along”; and one of them may be deleted, as in the Revelation: fa-anta lahu taṣaddā “to him you give your attention” [80:6], nāran talaẓẓā “a fire that blazes” [92:14] and tanazzalu al-malāʾikatu “the angels descend” [97:4].

text.original: وَمَتَى كَانَ فَاءُ افْتَعَلَ صَادًا أَوْ ضَادًا أَوْ طَاءً أَوْ ظَاءً قُلِبَتْ تَاؤُهُ طَاءً، فَتَقُولُ فِي افْتَعَلَ مِنَ الصُّلْحِ: اصْطَلَحَ، وَمِنَ الضَّرْبِ: اضْطَرَبَ، وَمِنَ الطَّرْدِ: اطَّرَدَ، وَمِنَ الظُّلْمِ: اظَّلَمَ. وَكَذَلِكَ سَائِرُ مُتَصَرِّفَاتِهِ، نَحْوُ: اصْطَلَحَ يَصْطَلِحُ اصْطِلَاحًا فَهُوَ مُصْطَلِحٌ وَذَاكَ مُصْطَلَحٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ اصْطَلِحْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَصْطَلِحْ.
text.en: When the fāʾ of iftaʿala is ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ or ẓāʾ, its tāʾ is changed into ṭāʾ. So you say in iftaʿala from al-ṣulḥi “peace”: iṣṭalaḥa “to make peace”; from al-ḍarbi “hitting”: iḍṭaraba “to be agitated”; from al-ṭardi “driving away”: iṭṭarada “to run on regularly”; and from al-ẓulmi “wrong”: iẓẓalama “to bear a wrong”. So too all its other derived forms, as iṣṭalaḥa yaṣṭaliḥu iṣṭilāḥan, so he is muṣṭaliḥun “one who makes peace” and that is muṣṭalaḥun “agreed upon”; the command is iṣṭaliḥ and the prohibition lā taṣṭaliḥ.

text.original: وَمَتَى كَانَ فَاءُ افْتَعَلَ دَالًا أَوْ ذَالًا أَوْ زَاءً قُلِبَتْ تَاؤُهُ دَالًا، فَتَقُولُ فِي افْتَعَلَ مِنَ الدَّرْءِ وَالذِّكْرِ وَالزَّجْرِ: ادَّرَأَ وَادَّكَرَ وَازْدَجَرَ. وَمَتَى كَانَ فَاءُ افْتَعَلَ وَاوًا أَوْ يَاءً أَوْ ثَاءً قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالثَّاءُ تَاءً، ثُمَّ أُدْغِمَتِ التَّاءُ فِي تَاءِ افْتَعَلَ، نَحْوُ: اتَّقَى وَاتَّسَرَ وَاتَّغَرَ.
text.en: When the fāʾ of iftaʿala is dāl, dhāl or zāy, its tāʾ is changed into dāl. So you say in iftaʿala from al-darʾi “warding off”, al-dhikri “remembering” and al-zajri “restraining”: iddaraʾa “to ward off”, iddakara “to remember” and izdajara “to be restrained”. When the fāʾ of iftaʿala is wāw, yāʾ or thāʾ, the wāw, the yāʾ and the thāʾ are changed into tāʾ, and then this tāʾ is merged into the tāʾ of iftaʿala, as ittaqā “to guard oneself”, ittasara “to play at maysir” and ittaghara “to cut one's front teeth”.

lessons.title: The two nūns of emphasis
body: Two nūns of emphasis attach “to the verb other than the past and the present”: so to the command, the prohibition and the muḍāriʿ with a future sense. The light one has sukūn; the heavy one has fatḥa, except in the verb of the two and of the group of women, where it has kasra: idhhabānni, “go, you two!”, idhhabnānni, “go, you women!”. In the second an alif is put after the nūn of the women “to separate the nūns”, which would otherwise be three in a row.

The light nūn does not attach to these two, “because it would bring two sukūns together outside their limit”. Two quiescent letters may meet only “when the first is a letter of prolongation and the second is merged”, as in dābbatin, “an animal”, where the long ā is followed by a doubled bāʾ. Idhhabānni keeps to this: ā and then a doubled nūn. With the light nūn the ā would meet a single quiescent nūn, which is not allowed.

With both nūns the nūn of the five forms (yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna, tafʿalīna) is dropped, as with the jussive. The wāw of the men's plural and the yāʾ of the woman addressed are dropped too, “except when the letter before them has fatḥa”: lā takhshawunna, “do not fear!”, la-tublawunna, “you will surely be tried” (Q 3:186), immā tarayinna, “if you should see” (Q 19:26). There the wāw or yāʾ takes a vowel instead of dropping.

The last letter of the verb then takes a vowel that tells the person: fatḥa for the singular and the absent woman, ḍamma for the group of men, kasra for the woman addressed. The ḍamma and the kasra are the traces of the dropped wāw and yāʾ: unṣurunna, “do help! (men)”, from unṣurū; unṣurinna, “do help! (woman)”, from unṣurī.

The paradigms: li-yanṣuranna li-yanṣurānni li-yanṣurunna li-tanṣuranna li-tanṣurānni li-yanṣurnānni, and with the light nūn li-yanṣuran li-yanṣurun li-tanṣuran; unṣuranna unṣurānni unṣurunna unṣurinna unṣurānni unṣurnānni, and unṣuran unṣurun unṣurin. Read them in pairs: only the vowel before the nūn separates unṣuranna, said to one man, from unṣurunna, said to many.

terms.en: the heavy and the light nūn of emphasis
the five forms with a final nūn
two quiescent letters meeting within their limit: a long vowel and a merged letter

examples.en: idhhabānni, idhhabnānni: kasra on the heavy nūn, after an alif
dābbatin: a long vowel before a merged letter, the allowed meeting
the wāw and yāʾ kept, with a vowel, after a fatḥa
the command to the absent with the heavy nūn

tasks.prompt: Why does the light nūn not attach to the verb of the two?
tasks.answer: The alif of the dual would meet a single quiescent nūn. Two quiescent letters may meet only when the first is a long vowel and the second is merged, as in dābbatin; the heavy nūn is merged, the light one is not.

tasks.prompt: Explain the vowel before the nūn in unṣuranna, unṣurunna and unṣurinna.
tasks.answer: Fatḥa for one man. Ḍamma for the men: the wāw of unṣurū was dropped and its ḍamma left. Kasra for the woman: the yāʾ of unṣurī was dropped and its kasra left.

tasks.prompt: Why is the wāw kept in lā takhshawunna but dropped in unṣurunna?
tasks.answer: In takhshaw the letter before the wāw has fatḥa, so the wāw is kept and given a ḍamma. In unṣurū the letter before it has ḍamma, so it drops and the ḍamma stands for it.

tasks.prompt: Why is there an alif in idhhabnānni?
tasks.answer: To separate the nūns: without it the nūn of the women would stand directly before the doubled nūn of emphasis, three nūns in a row.

quiz.prompt: To which verbs do the nūns of emphasis attach?
options: Not to the past or the present
quiz.explanation: To the command, the prohibition and the muḍāriʿ of the future.

quiz.prompt: The heavy nūn has kasra in…
options: the dual and the women's plural
quiz.explanation: Idhhabānni, idhhabnānni; elsewhere it has fatḥa.

quiz.prompt: Why is the light nūn not used in the dual?
options: Two sukūns would meet outside their limit
quiz.explanation: Only a long vowel before a merged letter is allowed, as in dābbatin.

quiz.prompt: What is dropped from tanṣurūna before the heavy nūn?
quiz.explanation: As in jazm the nūn goes, then the wāw for the two sukūns: li-yanṣurunna, unṣurunna.

quiz.prompt: Unṣurinna is said to…
quiz.explanation: The kasra stands for the dropped yāʾ of unṣurī.

quiz.prompt: In immā tarayinna (Q 19:26), the yāʾ is…
options: kept with a kasra, after a fatḥa
quiz.explanation: The letter before it has fatḥa, so it takes a vowel instead of dropping.

quiz.prompt: The light nūn is…
quiz.explanation: The light nūn has sukūn: unṣuran, unṣurun, unṣurin; the heavy one is doubled.

text.original: وَتَلْحَقُ الْفِعْلَ غَيْرَ الْمَاضِي وَالْحَالِ نُونَانِ لِلتَّأْكِيدِ: خَفِيفَةٌ سَاكِنَةٌ، أَوْ ثَقِيلَةٌ مَفْتُوحَةٌ إِلَّا فِيمَا تَخْتَصُّ بِهِ، وَهُوَ فِعْلُ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَجَمَاعَةِ النِّسَاءِ، فَهِيَ مَكْسُورَةٌ فِيهِمَا، تَقُولُ: اذْهَبَانِّ لِلِاثْنَيْنِ، وَاذْهَبْنَانِّ لِلنِّسْوَةِ، فَتُدْخِلُ الْأَلِفَ بَعْدَ نُونِ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ لِتَفْصِلَ بَيْنَ النُّونَاتِ.
text.en: Two nūns of emphasis attach to the verb other than the past and the present: a light one with sukūn, and a heavy one with fatḥa, except in what is particular to it, namely the verb of the two and of the group of women: in these two it has kasra. You say idhhabānni “go, you two!” for the two, and idhhabnānni “go, you women!” for the women: you put the alif after the nūn of the feminine plural, to separate the nūns.

text.original: وَلَا تُدْخِلُهُمَا الْخَفِيفَةَ؛ لِأَنَّهُ يَلْزَمُ الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ عَلَى غَيْرِ حَدِّهِ؛ فَإِنَّ الْتِقَاءَ السَّاكِنَيْنِ إِنَّمَا يَجُوزُ إِذَا كَانَ الْأَوَّلُ حَرْفَ مَدٍّ وَالثَّانِي مُدْغَمًا فِيهِ، نَحْوُ: دَابَّةٍ.
text.en: The light one is not attached to these two, because it would bring two sukūns together outside their limit; for two sukūns may meet only when the first is a letter of prolongation and the second is merged, as dābbatin “an animal”.

text.original: وَتَحْذِفُ مِنَ الْفِعْلِ مَعَهُمَا النُّونَ فِي الْأَمْثِلَةِ الْخَمْسَةِ كَمَا يُحْذَفُ مَعَ الْجَازِمِ، وَهِيَ: يَفْعَلَانِ وَتَفْعَلَانِ وَيَفْعَلُونَ وَتَفْعَلُونَ وَتَفْعَلِينَ، وَتَحْذِفُ وَاوَ يَفْعَلُونَ وَتَفْعَلُونَ وَيَاءَ تَفْعَلِينَ إِلَّا إِذَا انْفَتَحَ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، نَحْوُ: لَا تَخْشَوُنَّ، وَلَتُبْلَوُنَّ، وَإِمَّا تَرَيِنَّ.
text.en: With them you delete from the verb the nūn in the five forms (al-amthila al-khamsa), as it is deleted with the jussive particle; they are yafʿalāni, tafʿalāni, yafʿalūna, tafʿalūna and tafʿalīna. You also delete the wāw of yafʿalūna and tafʿalūna and the yāʾ of tafʿalīna, except when the letter before them has fatḥa, as lā takhshawunna “do not fear!”, la-tublawunna “you will surely be tried” and immā tarayinna “if you should see”.

text.original: وَتَفْتَحُ آخِرَ الْفِعْلِ إِذَا كَانَ فِعْلَ الْوَاحِدِ وَالْوَاحِدَةِ الْغَائِبَةِ، وَتَضُمُّهُ إِذَا كَانَ فِعْلَ جَمَاعَةِ الذُّكُورِ، وَتَكْسِرُهُ إِذَا كَانَ فِعْلَ الْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ، فَتَقُولُ فِي أَمْرِ الْغَائِبِ مُؤَكَّدًا بِالنُّونِ الثَّقِيلَةِ: لِيَنْصُرَنَّ لِيَنْصُرَانِّ لِيَنْصُرُنَّ لِتَنْصُرَنَّ لِتَنْصُرَانِّ لِيَنْصُرْنَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: لِيَنْصُرَنْ لِيَنْصُرُنْ لِتَنْصُرَنْ.
text.en: You give the last letter of the verb fatḥa when it is the verb of the singular and of the absent feminine singular, ḍamma when it is the verb of the group of men, and kasra when it is the verb of the feminine singular addressed. So you say in the command to the absent, emphasised with the heavy nūn: li-yanṣuranna li-yanṣurānni li-yanṣurunna li-tanṣuranna li-tanṣurānni li-yanṣurnānni “let him surely help” etc.; and with the light one: li-yanṣuran li-yanṣurun li-tanṣuran.

text.original: وَفِي أَمْرِ الْحَاضِرِ مُؤَكَّدًا بِالنُّونِ الثَّقِيلَةِ: اُنْصُرَنَّ اُنْصُرَانِّ اُنْصُرُنَّ اُنْصُرِنَّ اُنْصُرَانِّ اُنْصُرْنَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: اُنْصُرَنْ اُنْصُرُنْ اُنْصُرِنْ، وَقِسْ عَلَى هَذَا نَظَائِرَهُ.
text.en: And in the command to the one present, emphasised with the heavy nūn: unṣuranna unṣurānni unṣurunna unṣurinna unṣurānni unṣurnānni “do help!”; and with the light one: unṣuran unṣurun unṣurin. Measure its like on this.

lessons.title: The active and the passive participle
body: From the bare triliteral the active participle “mostly” comes on fāʿil: nāṣir nāṣirāni nāṣirūna, “helper”; the passive participle on mafʿūl: manṣūr manṣūrāni manṣūrūna manṣūra manṣūratāni manṣūrāt, with a broken plural besides, manāṣir. “Mostly”, because the adjectives of faʿula and faʿila have other patterns, which the Maqṣūd listed.

An intransitive verb that takes its object through a preposition makes its passive participle in a special way: mamrūrun bi-hi, mamrūrun bi-himā, mamrūrun bi-him, mamrūrun bi-hā, mamrūrun bi-himā, mamrūrun bi-hinna, “passed by”. The participle stays masculine singular; it is the pronoun after the preposition that is made dual, plural and feminine. The one passed by is not the subject of mamrūr; he is reached through bi-.

Faʿīl sometimes has the meaning of the doer, as al-raḥīm, “the merciful”, and sometimes of the one done to, as al-qatīl, “the slain”, meaning al-maqtūl. One pattern, two senses: the meaning must be learnt word by word.

For every verb of more than three letters there is one rule: take the muḍāriʿ, put a mīm with ḍamma in the place of the prefix, and give the letter before the last a kasra for the doer and a fatḥa for the one done to: mukrim and mukram, mudaḥrij and mudaḥraj, mustakhrij and mustakhraj. It is the muḍāriʿ of lesson 7 again: yukrimu gives mukrim, yukramu gives mukram.

“Sometimes the wording of the active and the passive participle is the same”: muḥābb, mujāb, mukhtār, muḍṭarr, muʿtadd, munṣabb fīhi, mutaḥābb, mutaḥābb ʿanhu; “the underlying form differs”. In mukhtār the yāʾ has become alif, so the kasra or fatḥa before it is gone; the commentators restore mukhtayir for the one who chooses and mukhtayar for the one chosen. Where the letter before the last is doubled or has become alif, the vowel that tells doer from done to cannot be seen, and only the sense decides.

terms.en: the active participle: the doer
the passive participle: the one done to
faʿīl with a passive sense, as qatīl
the underlying form, not heard but restored

tasks.prompt: Make the active and passive participle of istakhraja and explain the rule.
tasks.answer: Mustakhrij and mustakhraj. Take yastakhriju, put a mīm with ḍamma for the prefix, and give the letter before the last kasra for the doer, fatḥa for the one done to.

tasks.prompt: Why does one say mamrūrun bi-him, not mamrūrūna bi-him?
tasks.answer: The verb reaches the ones passed by only through the preposition. The participle is not their description; the pronoun after bi- is made plural instead.

tasks.prompt: Mukhtār can be the doer or the one done to. How is that possible?
tasks.answer: Its underlying forms differ, mukhtayir for the doer and mukhtayar for the one done to; the yāʾ became alif and took away the vowel that tells them apart, so the two sound the same.

tasks.prompt: Al-raḥīm and al-qatīl are both faʿīl. What is the difference?
tasks.answer: Al-raḥīm has the sense of the doer, the one who shows mercy; al-qatīl the sense of the one done to, the one killed, al-maqtūl.

quiz.prompt: The active participle of the bare triliteral mostly comes on…
quiz.explanation: Nāṣir, nāṣirāni, nāṣirūna; “mostly”, because some adjectives take other patterns.

quiz.prompt: Which is a broken plural of manṣūr given by the book?
quiz.explanation: Beside the sound plural manṣūrāt the book gives the broken plural manāṣir.

quiz.prompt: In mamrūrun bi-hinna, what shows the feminine plural?
quiz.explanation: The participle stays masculine singular.

quiz.prompt: Al-qatīl means…
quiz.explanation: Faʿīl in the meaning of the one done to: al-maqtūl.

quiz.prompt: Above three letters, the participle takes the muḍāriʿ and…
options: puts a mīm with ḍamma for the prefix
quiz.explanation: Then kasra or fatḥa before the last.

quiz.prompt: Mudaḥraj is…
quiz.explanation: Mudaḥraj has fatḥa before the last letter, the mark of the one done to; mudaḥrij is the doer.

quiz.prompt: Why do mukhtār and muʿtadd serve for both participles?
options: The vowel before the last cannot be seen
quiz.explanation: An alif or a merged letter hides the kasra or fatḥa; the underlying forms differ.

text.original: وَأَمَّا اسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ فَالْأَكْثَرُ أَنْ يَجِيءَ اسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ مِنْهُ عَلَى وَزْنِ فَاعِلٍ، تَقُولُ: نَاصِرٌ نَاصِرَانِ نَاصِرُونَ إِلَى آخِرِهِ، وَاسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ مِنْهُ عَلَى وَزْنِ مَفْعُولٍ، تَقُولُ: مَنْصُورٌ مَنْصُورَانِ مَنْصُورُونَ مَنْصُورَةٌ مَنْصُورَتَانِ مَنْصُورَاتٌ وَمَنَاصِرُ.
text.en: As for the active participle (ism al-fāʿil) and the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) of the bare triliteral: mostly its active participle comes on the measure fāʿilin; you say nāṣirun nāṣirāni nāṣirūna “a helper, two helpers, helpers” to its end; and its passive participle on the measure mafʿūlin; you say manṣūrun manṣūrāni manṣūrūna manṣūratun manṣūratāni manṣūrātun wa-manāṣiru “helped”.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي اللَّازِمِ: مَمْرُورٌ بِهِ، مَمْرُورٌ بِهِمَا، مَمْرُورٌ بِهِمْ، مَمْرُورٌ بِهَا، مَمْرُورٌ بِهِمَا، مَمْرُورٌ بِهِنَّ، فَتُثَنِّي وَتَجْمَعُ وَتُذَكِّرُ وَتُؤَنِّثُ الضَّمِيرَ فِيمَا يَتَعَدَّى بِحَرْفِ الْجَرِّ، لَا اسْمَ الْمَفْعُولِ. وَفَعِيلٌ قَدْ يَجِيءُ بِمَعْنَى الْفَاعِلِ كَالرَّحِيمِ، وَبِمَعْنَى الْمَفْعُولِ كَالْقَتِيلِ بِمَعْنَى الْمَقْتُولِ.
text.en: In the intransitive you say mamrūrun bi-hi, mamrūrun bi-himā, mamrūrun bi-him, mamrūrun bi-hā, mamrūrun bi-himā, mamrūrun bi-hinna “passed by him, by them two, by them, by her, by them two, by them (women)”: in what is made transitive by a preposition you put the pronoun in the dual and the plural, the masculine and the feminine, not the passive participle. faʿīlun sometimes comes in the meaning of the doer, as al-raḥīmi “the merciful”, and in the meaning of the one done to, as al-qatīli “the slain”, in the meaning of al-maqtūli “the killed”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا مَا زَادَ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَحْرُفٍ فَالضَّابِطُ فِيهِ أَنْ تَضَعَ فِي مُضَارِعِهِ الْمِيمَ الْمَضْمُومَةَ فِي مَوْضِعِ حَرْفِ الْمُضَارَعَةِ، وَتَكْسِرَ مَا قَبْلَ آخِرِهِ فِي الْفَاعِلِ، وَتَفْتَحَهُ فِي الْمَفْعُولِ فَرْقًا بَيْنَهُمَا، نَحْوُ: مُكْرِمٍ وَمُكْرَمٍ، وَمُدَحْرِجٍ وَمُدَحْرَجٍ، وَمُسْتَخْرِجٍ وَمُسْتَخْرَجٍ.
text.en: As for what has more than three letters, the rule for it is that you put in its muḍāriʿ a mīm with ḍamma in the place of the letter of the muḍāriʿ, and give the letter before its last kasra in the active participle and fatḥa in the passive participle, to tell them apart, as mukrimin “one who honours” and mukramin “one honoured”, mudaḥrijin and mudaḥrajin, mustakhrijin and mustakhrajin.

text.original: وَقَدْ يَسْتَوِي لَفْظُ الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ فِي بَعْضِ الْمَوَاضِعِ، كَمُحَابٍّ، وَمُجَابٍ، وَمُخْتَارٍ، وَمُضْطَرٍّ، وَمُعْتَدٍّ، وَمُنْصَبٍّ فِيهِ، وَمُتَحَابٍّ، وَمُتَحَابٍّ عَنْهُ، وَيَخْتَلِفُ التَّقْدِيرُ.
text.en: Sometimes the wording of the active and the passive participle is the same in some places, as muḥābbin, mujābin, mukhtārin, muḍṭarrin, muʿtaddin, munṣabbin fīhi, mutaḥābbin and mutaḥābbin ʿanhu; the underlying form (taqdīr) differs [mukhtayir for the doer, mukhtayar for the one done to].

lessons.title: The doubled verb
body: The doubled verb “is also called the deaf (al-aṣamm), because of its hardness”: the two like letters are pressed into one. In the triliteral, bare or augmented, it is the verb whose ʿayn and lām are of one kind: radda, “to send back”, and aʿadda, “to prepare”, whose originals are radada and aʿdada; “the first dāl was given sukūn and run into the second”.

In the bare quadriliteral it is the verb whose fāʾ and first lām are of one kind, and whose ʿayn and second lām are of one kind: zalzala zilzālan, “to shake”. It is also called “the matching” (al-muṭābiq): its two halves match, zal-zal.

Why is the doubled verb put among the weak verbs, though its letters are sound? “Because the doubled letter is subject to substitution”, as amlaytu for amlaltu, “I dictated”, a lām turned into yāʾ; “and to deletion”, as mastu and ẓaltu, said with fatḥa or kasra on the first letter, and aḥastu, for masistu, “I touched”, ẓaliltu, “I remained”, and aḥsastu, “I perceived”. Substitution and deletion are what happens to weak letters, so the doubled verb shares their chapter.

Know where these forms stand. Masistu, ẓaliltu, aḥsastu are the regular forms; mastu, ẓaltu, aḥastu are what the Arabs also said, and al-ʿIzzī cites them to show that doubled letters can drop. They are not patterns to imitate with every doubled verb.

A trap: count the radicals of a doubled verb correctly. Radda has three, r-d-d, though it is written with two letters and a shadda; zalzala has four, z-l-z-l. The shadda stands for two letters: the first quiescent, the second vowelled.

terms.en: the doubled verb, called the deaf
the matching: the doubled quadriliteral, as zalzala
substitution and deletion

zalzala zilzālan, “to shake”: the matching quadriliteral
amlaytu for amlaltu: substitution
mastu, ẓaltu for masistu, ẓaliltu: deletion

tasks.prompt: Give the originals of radda and aʿadda and say what happened.
tasks.answer: Radada and aʿdada. The first dāl was made quiescent and run into the second: one dāl with a shadda.

tasks.prompt: Why is zalzala called al-muṭābiq?
tasks.answer: Its fāʾ and first lām are the same letter (zāy), and its ʿayn and second lām are the same (lām): its two halves match.

tasks.prompt: Why does al-ʿIzzī treat the doubled verb with the weak verbs?
tasks.answer: Because the doubled letter undergoes what weak letters undergo: substitution, as amlaytu for amlaltu, and deletion, as mastu, ẓaltu, aḥastu for masistu, ẓaliltu, aḥsastu.

quiz.prompt: Why is the doubled verb called al-aṣamm?
quiz.explanation: “Li-shiddatihi”: the two like letters are pressed into one.

quiz.explanation: Afʿala on ʿ-d-d; the first dāl merged into the second.

quiz.prompt: What is ẓaltu short for?
quiz.explanation: A doubled letter deleted, as in mastu for masistu.

quiz.prompt: How many radicals has radda?
quiz.explanation: R-d-d: the shadda stands for two dāls.

text.original: وَيُقَالُ لَهُ الْأَصَمُّ لِشِدَّتِهِ، وَهُوَ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ وَالْمَزِيدِ فِيهِ مَا كَانَ عَيْنُهُ وَلَامُهُ مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ، كَرَدَّ وَأَعَدَّ، فَإِنَّ أَصْلَهُمَا رَدَدَ وَأَعْدَدَ، فَأُسْكِنَتِ الدَّالُ الْأُولَى فَأُدْرِجَتْ فِي الثَّانِيَةِ. وَمِنَ الرُّبَاعِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ مَا كَانَ فَاؤُهُ وَلَامُهُ الْأُولَى مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ، وَكَذَلِكَ عَيْنُهُ وَلَامُهُ الثَّانِيَةُ مِنْ جِنْسٍ وَاحِدٍ، وَيُقَالُ لَهُ الْمُطَابِقُ أَيْضًا، نَحْوُ: زَلْزَلَ زِلْزَالًا.
text.en: It is also called the deaf (al-aṣamm), because of its hardness. In the bare and the augmented triliteral it is the verb whose ʿayn and lām are of one kind, as radda “to send back” and aʿadda “to prepare”, for their originals are radada and aʿdada: the first dāl was given sukūn and run into the second. In the bare quadriliteral it is the verb whose fāʾ and first lām are of one kind, and likewise its ʿayn and second lām are of one kind; it is also called the matching (al-muṭābiq), as zalzala zilzālan “to shake”.

text.original: وَإِنَّمَا أُلْحِقَ الْمُضَاعَفُ بِالْمُعْتَلَّاتِ لِأَنَّ حَرْفَ التَّضْعِيفِ يَلْحَقُهُ الْإِبْدَالُ، كَقَوْلِهِمْ: أَمْلَيْتُ بِمَعْنَى أَمْلَلْتُ، وَالْحَذْفُ، كَمَا قَالُوا: مَسْتُ وَظَلْتُ بِفَتْحِ الْفَاءِ وَكَسْرِهَا، وَأَحَسْتُ، فِي مَسِسْتُ وَظَلِلْتُ وَأَحْسَسْتُ.
text.en: The doubled verb was joined to the weak verbs only because the doubled letter is subject to substitution, as their saying amlaytu in the meaning of amlaltu “I dictated”, and to deletion, as they said mastu and ẓaltu, with fatḥa and kasra on the fāʾ, and aḥastu, for masistu “I touched”, ẓaliltu “I remained” and aḥsastu “I perceived”.

lessons.title: Merging: necessary and impossible
body: Merging (idghām) “is that you give the first [letter] sukūn and run it into the second; the first is called the merged (mudgham) and the second the one merged into (mudgham fīhi)”. In madda the first dāl is the mudgham, the second the mudgham fīhi, and the shadda shows both.

It is necessary in such as madda yamuddu, “to stretch”, aʿadda yuʿiddu, inqadda yanqaddu, iʿtadda yaʿtaddu, iswadda yaswaddu, iswādda yaswāddu, istaʿadda yastaʿiddu, iṭmaʾanna yaṭmaʾinnu and tamādda yatamāddu: bare and augmented alike. In yamuddu, from yamdudu, the vowel of the first dāl went back to the mīm, as the Maqṣūd explained, and the two dāls met.

It is necessary too when these verbs are built for the one done to, mudda yumaddu; in such a maṣdar as madd; and when the alif, the wāw or the yāʾ of the pronoun is joined to the verb: maddā, maddū, muddī. In all of these the second dāl has a vowel.

It is impossible in madadna, madadnā, madadta and on to madadtunna, and in yamdudna, tamdudna, umdudna and lā tamdudna. Each of these ends in a pronoun beginning with a consonant (-na, -nā, -ta, -tunna), before which the last letter of the verb is always quiescent. The second dāl has no vowel, and nothing can be merged into a quiescent letter.

So one question settles every case: does the second of the two like letters have a vowel? If it does, they merge; if its sukūn is fixed by the pronoun, they stay apart. The next lesson takes up the third case, where the sukūn comes from the jussive and both are allowed.

terms.en: merging the first of two like letters into the second
the merged letter and the one merged into
merging necessary, impossible
