text.original: وَالْمُضَاعَفُ يَلْحَقُهُ الْإِدْغَامُ، وَهُوَ أَنْ تُسَكِّنَ الْأَوَّلَ وَتُدْرِجَ فِي الثَّانِي، وَيُسَمَّى الْأَوَّلُ مُدْغَمًا وَالثَّانِي مُدْغَمًا فِيهِ. وَذَلِكَ وَاجِبٌ فِي نَحْوِ: مَدَّ يَمُدُّ، وَأَعَدَّ يُعِدُّ، وَانْقَدَّ يَنْقَدُّ، وَاعْتَدَّ يَعْتَدُّ، وَاسْوَدَّ يَسْوَدُّ، وَاسْوَادَّ يَسْوَادُّ، وَاسْتَعَدَّ يَسْتَعِدُّ، وَاطْمَأَنَّ يَطْمَئِنُّ، وَتَمَادَّ يَتَمَادُّ.
text.en: The doubled verb is subject to merging (idghām), which is that you give the first [letter] sukūn and run it into the second; the first is called the merged (mudgham) and the second the one merged into (mudgham fīhi). This is necessary in such as madda yamuddu “to stretch”, aʿadda yuʿiddu “to prepare”, inqadda yanqaddu “to be split lengthwise”, iʿtadda yaʿtaddu “to reckon”, iswadda yaswaddu “to turn black”, iswādda yaswāddu “to turn deep black”, istaʿadda yastaʿiddu “to make ready”, iṭmaʾanna yaṭmaʾinnu “to be at rest” and tamādda yatamāddu “to stretch out”.

text.original: وَكَذَلِكَ هَذِهِ الْأَفْعَالُ إِذَا بَنَيْتَهَا لِلْمَفْعُولِ، نَحْوُ: مُدَّ يُمَدُّ، وَكَذَا نَظَائِرُهُ، وَفِي نَحْوِ: مَدٍّ مَصْدَرًا، وَكَذَلِكَ إِذَا اتَّصَلَ بِالْفِعْلِ أَلِفُ الضَّمِيرِ أَوْ وَاوُهُ أَوْ يَاؤُهُ، نَحْوُ: مَدَّا وَمَدُّوا وَمُدِّي. وَمُمْتَنِعٌ فِي نَحْوِ: مَدَدْنَ، وَمَدَدْنَا، وَمَدَدْتَ إِلَى مَدَدْتُنَّ، وَيَمْدُدْنَ، وَتَمْدُدْنَ، وَامْدُدْنَ، وَلَا تَمْدُدْنَ.
text.en: So too these verbs when you build them for the one done to, as mudda yumaddu, and likewise their like; and in such as maddin as a maṣdar; and likewise when the alif, the wāw or the yāʾ of the pronoun is joined to the verb, as maddā “they two stretched”, maddū “they stretched” and muddī “stretch! (f.)”. It is impossible in such as madadna “they (women) stretched”, madadnā “we stretched”, and madadta “you stretched” up to madadtunna, and yamdudna, tamdudna, umdudna and lā tamdudna.

lessons.title: Merging allowed: the jussive and the command
body: Merging is allowed, not required, “when the jussive particle comes before the verb of the singular”. If the ʿayn of the muḍāriʿ has kasra, as yafirru, “he flees”, or fatḥa, as yaʿaḍḍu, “he bites”, you say lam yafirra and lam yaʿaḍḍa, with fatḥa or kasra on the last letter, or you undo the merging: lam yafrir, lam yaʿḍaḍ. So too lam yaqshaʿirra, lam yaḥmarra, lam yaḥmārra.

“If the ʿayn has ḍamma, the three vowels are allowed with the merging, and undoing it as well”: lam yamudda, with fatḥa, ḍamma or kasra on the dāl, and lam yamdud. The ḍamma is allowed here and not with yafirru, because it follows the ḍamma of the ʿayn. The fatḥa is the lightest vowel; the kasra is the vowel a quiescent letter takes when it must be moved.

Why are both allowed? The jussive makes the last letter quiescent, as the pronoun did in madadtu; but this sukūn is not part of the word, it comes from a particle, so the letter may be moved to allow the merging. The commentators add that undoing is the speech of the Ḥijāz and merging that of Tamīm; the Qurʾān has both.

“Such is the rule of the command too”: firra and ʿaḍḍa, with kasra or fatḥa on the last letter, or ifrir and iʿḍaḍ; mudda with any of the three vowels on the dāl, or umdud. The command, built on the jussive, follows it exactly.

The participles: māddun māddāni māddūna māddatun māddatāni māddātun, with the broken plural mawāddu, all merged, for the second dāl always has a vowel; and the passive participle mamdūd, “like manṣūr”: in mafʿūl the long ū stands between the two dāls, so they never meet.

text.original: وَجَائِزٌ إِذَا دَخَلَ الْجَازِمُ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْوَاحِدِ: فَإِنْ كَانَ مَكْسُورَ الْعَيْنِ كَيَفِرُّ، أَوْ مَفْتُوحًا كَيَعَضُّ، فَتَقُولُ: لَمْ يَفِرَّ وَلَمْ يَعَضَّ، بِفَتْحِ اللَّامِ وَكَسْرِهَا، وَلَمْ يَفْرِرْ وَلَمْ يَعْضَضْ بِفَكِّ الْإِدْغَامِ، وَهَكَذَا حُكْمُ لَمْ يَقْشَعِرَّ وَلَمْ يَحْمَرَّ وَلَمْ يَحْمَارَّ. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْعَيْنُ مَضْمُومًا فَيَجُوزُ الْحَرَكَاتُ الثَّلَاثُ مَعَ الْإِدْغَامِ وَفَكُّهُ، فَتَقُولُ: لَمْ يَمُدَّ بِحَرَكَاتِ الدَّالِ، وَلَمْ يَمْدُدْ.
text.en: It is allowed when the jussive particle comes before the verb of the singular. If it has kasra on the ʿayn, as yafirru “he flees”, or fatḥa, as yaʿaḍḍu “he bites”, you say lam yafirra and lam yaʿaḍḍa, with fatḥa and kasra on the lām [of the verb], and lam yafrir and lam yaʿḍaḍ, undoing the merging; and such is the rule of lam yaqshaʿirra, lam yaḥmarra and lam yaḥmārra. If the ʿayn has ḍamma, the three vowels are allowed with the merging, and undoing it as well: you say lam yamudda, with any of the vowels on the dāl, and lam yamdud.

text.original: وَهَكَذَا حُكْمُ الْأَمْرِ، فَتَقُولُ: فِرَّ وَعَضَّ، بِكَسْرِ اللَّامِ وَفَتْحِهَا، وَافْرِرْ وَاعْضَضْ، وَمُدَّ بِحَرَكَاتِ الدَّالِ، وَامْدُدْ. وَتَقُولُ فِي اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ: مَادٌّ مَادَّانِ مَادُّونَ مَادَّةٌ مَادَّتَانِ مَادَّاتٌ وَمَوَادُّ، وَالْمَفْعُولُ مِنْهُ مَمْدُودٌ كَمَنْصُورٍ.
text.en: Such is the rule of the command too: you say firra and ʿaḍḍa, with kasra and fatḥa on the lām, and ifrir and iʿḍaḍ; and mudda, with any of the vowels on the dāl, and umdud. In the active participle you say māddun māddāni māddūna māddatun māddatāni māddātun wa-mawāddu, and its passive participle is mamdūdun, like manṣūrin.

parts.title: The mithāl and the hollow verb

lessons.title: The weak verb, and the mithāl with wāw
body: The weak verb is “the verb one of whose radicals is a letter of weakness”: the wāw, the yāʾ and the alif, called the letters of prolongation and softness. The alif is never a radical of its own: in a verb it “is changed from the wāw or the yāʾ”, as in qāla and ramā. The book counts seven kinds by where the weak letter stands, and takes them in turn.

The first is the verb weak in the fāʾ, called the mithāl, “the similar”, “because it resembles the sound verb in bearing the vowels”: its first letter takes vowels as a sound letter does. Its wāw “is deleted from the muḍāriʿ of the verb that is on yafʿilu, and from its maṣdar on fiʿla, and it stays in all its other forms”: waʿada yaʿidu ʿidatan wa-waʿdan, “to promise”, wāʿid, mawʿūd, the command ʿid, the prohibition lā taʿid; and wamiqa yamiqu, “to love”.

The cause is the kasra after the wāw, so “when the kasra of the letter after it is removed, the deleted wāw is brought back”: lam yūʿad, “he was not promised”, in the passive. With yafʿalu the wāw stays: wajila yawjalu, “to be afraid”, command ījal; there the quiescent wāw after the kasra of the hamza becomes a yāʾ. In speech it comes back after a ḍamma: yā Zaydu ūjal, “said with the wāw and written with the yāʾ”. With yafʿulu it stays too: wajuha yawjuhu, “to be eminent”, ūjuh, lā tawjuh.

What of yaṭaʾu, yasaʿu, yaḍaʿu, yaqaʿu and yadaʿu, which have fatḥa and still lose the wāw? “They are originally yafʿilu, with kasra, and were given fatḥa because of the letter of the throat”: the wāw dropped while the kasra was there. Yadharu, “he leaves”, has no throat letter and lost its wāw “because it has the meaning of yadaʿu”; and the Arabs let the past of both fall out of use.

The Maqṣūd listed three bābs in which the wāw drops; al-ʿIzzī gives one cause, the kasra, and explains the fatḥa cases from it. His last sentence is a tool: “the deletion of the fāʾ in the future is a proof that it is a wāw verb”. Meet yadaʿu with no past in sight, and the missing first letter tells you the root begins with wāw.

the verb weak in its fāʾ

tasks.answer: The wāw dropped because of the kasra after it. In the passive the letter after it has fatḥa, the kasra is gone, so the wāw returns, said as ū after the ḍamma of the prefix.

tasks.prompt: Yaḍaʿu has fatḥa, yet its wāw is gone. How does al-ʿIzzī explain this?
tasks.answer: It is originally yafʿilu, with kasra, and the wāw dropped then; the fatḥa came afterwards because of the throat letter, the ʿayn.

tasks.prompt: Why is ījal written with a yāʾ, but said ūjal after yā Zaydu?
tasks.answer: Alone, the quiescent wāw follows the kasra of the hamza and becomes a yāʾ. After yā Zaydu the hamza drops in connected speech, the wāw follows the ḍamma before it and returns in speech; the writing keeps the yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Which letters are the letters of weakness?
quiz.explanation: Also called the letters of prolongation and softness.

quiz.prompt: Why is the verb weak in the fāʾ called mithāl?
options: It resembles the sound verb in bearing the vowels
quiz.explanation: Its first letter takes the vowels as a sound letter does.

quiz.prompt: From which forms of waʿada does the wāw drop?
options: The muḍāriʿ and the maṣdar on fiʿla
quiz.explanation: Yaʿidu and ʿida; but waʿd, wāʿid and mawʿūd keep it.

quiz.prompt: The wāw stays in…
quiz.explanation: Its muḍāriʿ has fatḥa by origin, so there is no kasra after the wāw.

quiz.prompt: Why did yaṭaʾu lose its wāw despite its fatḥa?
options: It is irregular with no reason
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa came for the throat letter after the wāw was gone.

quiz.prompt: Why did yadharu lose its wāw?
options: It has the meaning of yadaʿu
quiz.explanation: It follows the verb of the same meaning.

quiz.prompt: What does al-ʿIzzī take as proof that a verb is a wāw verb?
options: The deletion of the fāʾ in the future
quiz.explanation: Yadaʿu has no past in use, yet its missing fāʾ shows the wāw.

text.original: وَهُوَ مَا كَانَ أَحَدُ أُصُولِهِ حَرْفَ عِلَّةٍ، وَهِيَ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْأَلِفُ، وَتُسَمَّى حُرُوفَ الْمَدِّ وَاللِّينِ، وَالْأَلِفُ حِينَئِذٍ تَكُونُ مُنْقَلِبَةً عَنِ الْوَاوِ وَالْيَاءِ. وَأَنْوَاعُهُ سَبْعَةٌ.
text.en: It is the verb one of whose radicals is a letter of weakness (ḥarf ʿilla), namely the wāw, the yāʾ and the alif; they are called the letters of prolongation and softness (ḥurūf al-madd wa-al-līn), and the alif in that case is changed from the wāw or the yāʾ. Its kinds are seven.

text.original: الْأَوَّلُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْفَاءِ، وَيُقَالُ لَهُ الْمِثَالُ لِمُمَاثَلَةِ الصَّحِيحِ فِي احْتِمَالِ الْحَرَكَاتِ. أَمَّا الْوَاوُ فَتُحْذَفُ مِنْ مُضَارِعِ الْفِعْلِ الَّذِي عَلَى يَفْعِلُ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ، وَمِنْ مَصْدَرِهِ الَّذِي عَلَى فِعْلَةٍ، وَتَسْلَمُ فِي سَائِرِ تَصَارِيفِهِ، فَتَقُولُ: وَعَدَ يَعِدُ عِدَةً وَوَعْدًا فَهُوَ وَاعِدٌ وَذَاكَ مَوْعُودٌ، وَالْأَمْرُ عِدْ، وَالنَّهْيُ لَا تَعِدْ، وَكَذَلِكَ وَمِقَ يَمِقُ.
text.en: The first is the verb weak in the fāʾ; it is called the similar (al-mithāl), because it resembles the sound verb in bearing the vowels. As for the wāw, it is deleted from the muḍāriʿ of the verb that is on yafʿilu, with kasra on the ʿayn, and from its maṣdar that is on fiʿlatin, and it stays in all its other derived forms. So you say waʿada yaʿidu ʿidatan wa-waʿdan “to promise”, so he is wāʿidun “one who promises” and that is mawʿūdun “promised”; the command is ʿid and the prohibition lā taʿid; and likewise wamiqa yamiqu “to love”.

text.original: فَإِذَا أُزِيلَتْ كَسْرَةُ مَا بَعْدَهَا أُعِيدَتِ الْوَاوُ الْمَحْذُوفَةُ، نَحْوُ: لَمْ يُوعَدْ. وَتَثْبُتُ فِي يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ، كَوَجِلَ يَوْجَلُ، وَالْأَمْرُ اِيجَلْ، قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً لِسُكُونِهَا وَانْكِسَارِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، فَإِنِ انْضَمَّ مَا قَبْلَهَا عَادَتِ الْوَاوُ، وَتَقُولُ: يَا زَيْدُ اِيجَلْ، تَلْفِظُ بِالْوَاوِ وَتَكْتُبُ بِالْيَاءِ.
text.en: When the kasra of the letter after it is removed, the deleted wāw is brought back, as lam yūʿad “he was not promised”. It stays in yafʿalu, with fatḥa on the ʿayn, as wajila yawjalu “to be afraid”; the command is ījal: the wāw was changed into yāʾ because it has sukūn and the letter before it has kasra. If the letter before it has ḍamma, the wāw comes back: you say yā Zaydu ījal “O Zayd, be afraid!” (said yā Zaydu ūjal), pronouncing it with the wāw and writing it with the yāʾ.

text.original: وَتَثْبُتُ فِي يَفْعُلُ بِضَمِّ الْعَيْنِ، كَوَجُهَ يَوْجُهُ، اُوجُهْ، لَا تَوْجُهْ. وَحُذِفَتِ الْوَاوُ مِنْ يَطَأُ وَيَسَعُ وَيَضَعُ وَيَقَعُ وَيَدَعُ؛ لِأَنَّهَا فِي الْأَصْلِ يَفْعِلُ بِالْكَسْرِ، وَفُتِحَتْ لِحَرْفِ الْحَلْقِ، وَمِنْ يَذَرُ لِكَوْنِهِ بِمَعْنَى يَدَعُ، وَأَمَاتُوا مَاضِيَ يَدَعُ وَيَذَرُ. وَحَذْفُ الْفَاءِ فِي الْمُسْتَقْبَلِ دَلِيلٌ عَلَى أَنَّهُ وَاوِيٌّ.
text.en: It stays in yafʿulu, with ḍamma on the ʿayn, as wajuha yawjuhu “to be eminent”, ūjuh, lā tawjuh. The wāw was deleted from yaṭaʾu “he treads”, yasaʿu “he holds”, yaḍaʿu “he puts”, yaqaʿu “he falls” and yadaʿu “he leaves”, because they are originally yafʿilu, with kasra, and were given fatḥa because of the letter of the throat; and from yadharu “he leaves”, because it has the meaning of yadaʿu; and they let the past of yadaʿu and yadharu fall out of use. The deletion of the fāʾ in the future is a proof that it is a wāw verb.

lessons.title: The mithāl with yāʾ, iftaʿala, and wadda
body: “As for the yāʾ, it stays in every case”: yamana yayminu, “to bring luck”, yasara yaysiru, “to play at maysir”, yaʾisa yayʾasu, “to despair”. The kasra that drives out the wāw does not touch the yāʾ: yaysiru keeps it.

But a quiescent yāʾ after a ḍamma does not stay a yāʾ. In afʿala from a yāʾ verb: aysara yūsiru īsāran, so he is mūsir, “to become rich; rich”: “the yāʾ was changed into wāw because it has sukūn and the letter before it has ḍamma”. In the maṣdar īsār it stays a yāʾ, after the kasra of the hamza.

In iftaʿala from wāw and yāʾ verbs alike, the weak fāʾ “is changed into tāʾ and merged into the tāʾ of iftaʿala”: ittaʿada yattaʿidu, muttaʿid, muttaʿad, “to accept a promise”, from w-ʿ-d; ittasara yattasiru, muttasir, from y-s-r. This is the rule already met with ittaqā. “It is sometimes said” otherwise: ītaʿada yātaʿidu mūtaʿid, ītasara yātasiru mūtasir, where the weak letter is kept and simply follows the vowel before it, ī after kasra, ā after fatḥa, ū after ḍamma.

Last, a verb that is both mithāl and doubled: wadda yawaddu, “to love”. “Its rule is the rule of ʿaḍḍa yaʿaḍḍu”: the doubling decides the merging, as in lesson 15, and the wāw stays because the present is on yafʿalu. In the command undone, the wāw after the kasra of the hamza becomes yāʾ: īdad, like iʿḍaḍ, and like ījal.

A trap for the ear: yūsiru and lam yūʿad both begin with yū-, from different roots. In yūsiru the ū is a yāʾ of y-s-r changed after the ḍamma; in yūʿad it is the wāw of w-ʿ-d come back. Before looking a word up, ask which letter the long vowel stands for.

a quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma turned into wāw
merging the changed fāʾ into the tāʾ of iftaʿala

tasks.prompt: Why is the muḍāriʿ of aysara yūsiru, with a wāw?
tasks.answer: Afʿala gives the prefix a ḍamma: the yāʾ of y-s-r is then quiescent after a ḍamma, and such a yāʾ is changed into a wāw.

tasks.prompt: Give the two ways of saying iftaʿala from waʿada, with the muḍāriʿ and the active participle.
tasks.answer: Ittaʿada yattaʿidu, muttaʿid (the wāw turned into tāʾ and merged); or ītaʿada yātaʿidu, mūtaʿid (the weak letter kept, following the vowel before it).

tasks.prompt: What is the command of wadda without merging, and why is it written with a yāʾ?
tasks.answer: Īdad, like iʿḍaḍ. The wāw, quiescent after the kasra of the hamza of joining, becomes a yāʾ, as in ījal.

quiz.prompt: In the mithāl with yāʾ, the yāʾ…
quiz.explanation: Yamana yayminu, yasara yaysiru, yaʾisa yayʾasu.

quiz.prompt: Why is there a wāw in mūsir?
options: A quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma became wāw
quiz.explanation: Mūsir is from aysara, root y-s-r: the quiescent yāʾ after ḍamma became wāw.

quiz.prompt: In ittaʿada, the doubled tāʾ comes from…
options: the wāw of the root and the tāʾ of iftaʿala
quiz.explanation: The wāw was changed into tāʾ and merged.

quiz.prompt: Ītasara yātasiru is…
quiz.explanation: “It is sometimes said”: the weak letter follows the vowel before it.

quiz.prompt: Wadda yawaddu follows the rule of…
quiz.explanation: A doubled verb with fatḥa in its present.

quiz.prompt: The command of wadda without merging is…
quiz.explanation: Like iʿḍaḍ, with the wāw written yāʾ after kasra.

quiz.prompt: In īsār, the yāʾ is kept because…
quiz.explanation: Only after a ḍamma does the quiescent yāʾ become a wāw.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْيَاءُ فَتَثْبُتُ عَلَى كُلِّ حَالٍ، نَحْوُ: يَمَنَ يَيْمِنُ، وَيَسَرَ يَيْسِرُ، وَيَئِسَ يَيْئَسُ. تَقُولُ فِي أَفْعَلَ مِنَ الْيَائِيِّ: أَيْسَرَ يُوسِرُ إِيسَارًا فَهُوَ مُوسِرٌ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْيَاءُ وَاوًا لِسُكُونِهَا وَانْضِمَامِ مَا قَبْلَهَا. وَفِي افْتَعَلَ مِنْهُمَا تُقْلَبَانِ تَاءً وَتُدْغَمَانِ فِي تَاءِ افْتَعَلَ، نَحْوُ: اتَّعَدَ يَتَّعِدُ فَهُوَ مُتَّعِدٌ وَذَاكَ مُتَّعَدٌ، وَاتَّسَرَ يَتَّسِرُ فَهُوَ مُتَّسِرٌ.
text.en: As for the yāʾ, it stays in every case, as yamana yayminu “to bring luck”, yasara yaysiru “to play at maysir” and yaʾisa yayʾasu “to despair”. You say in afʿala from the yāʾ verb: aysara yūsiru īsāran, so he is mūsirun “to become rich; rich”: the yāʾ was changed into wāw because it has sukūn and the letter before it has ḍamma. In iftaʿala from both, they are changed into tāʾ and merged into the tāʾ of iftaʿala, as ittaʿada yattaʿidu, so he is muttaʿidun and that is muttaʿadun “to accept a promise”, and ittasara yattasiru, so he is muttasirun “to play at maysir”.

text.original: وَقَدْ يُقَالُ: اِيتَعَدَ يَاتَعِدُ فَهُوَ مُوتَعِدٌ، وَاِيتَسَرَ يَاتَسِرُ فَهُوَ مُوتَسِرٌ. وَحُكْمُ وَدَّ يَوَدُّ حُكْمُ عَضَّ يَعَضُّ، وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ: اِيدَدْ، كَاعْضَضْ.
text.en: It is sometimes said ītaʿada yātaʿidu, so he is mūtaʿidun, and ītasara yātasiru, so he is mūtasirun. The rule of wadda yawaddu “to love” is the rule of ʿaḍḍa yaʿaḍḍu “to bite”; you say in the command īdad, like iʿḍaḍ.

lessons.title: The hollow verb: the past
body: The second kind is the verb weak in the ʿayn, called the hollow (al-ajwaf), and also “the one of three” (dhū al-thalātha), “because its past has three letters when you speak about yourself”: ṣuntu, “I guarded”, has three letters, the ʿayn having gone. In the bare verb “its ʿayn is changed into alif in the past, whether it is wāw or yāʾ, because they are vowelled and the letter before them has fatḥa”: ṣāna, “to guard”, and bāʿa, “to sell”.

When a pronoun beginning with a consonant is joined to it (of the speaker, of the one addressed, or of the absent women), faʿala is moved “to faʿula in the wāw verb and to faʿila in the yāʾ verb, to point to them”. Then the ḍamma or kasra is moved to the fāʾ, and the ʿayn is deleted because two sukūns meet, the ʿayn and the last letter. A verb already faʿula or faʿila by origin is not moved; it keeps its own vowel.

So you say ṣāna ṣānā ṣānū ṣānat ṣānatā, with the alif, and then ṣunna ṣunta ṣuntumā ṣuntum ṣunti ṣuntumā ṣuntunna ṣuntu ṣunnā, without it; and bāʿa bāʿā bāʿū bāʿat bāʿatā biʿna. The vowel on the first letter tells the root: ḍamma for the wāw of ṣ-w-n, kasra for the yāʾ of b-y-ʿ. In ṣunna and ṣunnā the nūn of the root meets the nūn of the pronoun and the two are merged.

Built for the one done to, “you give the fāʾ kasra in all of them”: ṣīna, “it was guarded”, whose change is “by moving and changing”, and bīʿa, “it was sold”, “by moving only”. In both the kasra of the ʿayn moves back to the fāʾ; in ṣīna the wāw, now quiescent after kasra, must also change into yāʾ, while in bīʿa the yāʾ is already at home after the kasra.

The Maqṣūd reached qulna by turning the wāw into alif, dropping it, and then changing the vowel. Al-ʿIzzī goes another way: first move faʿala to faʿula or faʿila, then move the vowel, then drop. The road differs, the form is the same; what both teach is that the vowel left on the first letter is the trace of the letter that has gone.

tasks.prompt: Why is the hollow verb called dhū al-thalātha?
tasks.answer: Because its past has three letters when you speak about yourself: ṣuntu is ṣād, nūn, tāʾ; the ʿayn has gone.

tasks.prompt: Explain ṣuntu step by step, as al-ʿIzzī does.
tasks.answer: Before the pronoun -tu, faʿala of the wāw verb is moved to faʿula; the ḍamma of the ʿayn moves to the fāʾ; the ʿayn, now quiescent, meets the quiescent nūn and is deleted: ṣuntu.

tasks.prompt: Why does the form for the absent women have a doubled nūn: ṣunna?
tasks.answer: The root ends in nūn. Its nūn, quiescent before the pronoun, meets the nūn of the women, and the two are merged.

tasks.prompt: Make the passive of ṣāna and bāʿa and name the change in each.
tasks.answer: Ṣīna: by moving (the kasra to the ṣād) and changing (the quiescent wāw after kasra into yāʾ). Bīʿa: by moving only, since a yāʾ after kasra needs no change.

quiz.prompt: Why does the ʿayn of ṣāna become alif?
options: It is vowelled after a fatḥa
quiz.explanation: Wāw or yāʾ alike: qāla, ṣāna, bāʿa.

quiz.prompt: With the pronoun of the speaker, faʿala of a wāw verb is moved to…
quiz.explanation: So that the ḍamma left on the fāʾ points to the wāw: ṣuntu.

quiz.prompt: Biʿna has a kasra on the bāʾ because…
quiz.explanation: Faʿala of the yāʾ verb is moved to faʿila.

quiz.prompt: Why is the ʿayn deleted in ṣuntu?
options: It is a weak letter at the end
quiz.explanation: The ʿayn, quiescent after its vowel moved, meets the quiescent nūn.

quiz.prompt: The passive of bāʿa is…
quiz.explanation: The kasra moved to the fāʾ: change by moving only.

quiz.prompt: Ṣīna is changed by…
quiz.explanation: The kasra moves back, and the wāw after kasra becomes yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Which forms of ṣāna keep the alif?
quiz.explanation: The pronouns beginning with a vowel or the tāʾ of the feminine leave the ʿayn vowelled.

text.original: الثَّانِي الْمُعْتَلُّ الْعَيْنِ، وَيُقَالُ لَهُ الْأَجْوَفُ وَذُو الثَّلَاثَةِ لِكَوْنِ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَحْرُفٍ إِذَا أَخْبَرْتَ عَنْ نَفْسِكَ. فَالْمُجَرَّدُ تُقْلَبُ عَيْنُهُ فِي الْمَاضِي أَلِفًا، سَوَاءٌ كَانَ وَاوًا أَوْ يَاءً، لِتَحَرُّكِهِمَا وَانْفِتَاحِ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، نَحْوُ: صَانَ وَبَاعَ.
text.en: The second is the verb weak in the ʿayn; it is called the hollow (al-ajwaf) and the one of three (dhū al-thalātha), because its past has three letters when you speak about yourself. In the bare verb its ʿayn is changed into alif in the past, whether it is wāw or yāʾ, because they are voweled and the letter before them has fatḥa, as ṣāna “to guard” and bāʿa “to sell”.

text.original: فَإِنِ اتَّصَلَ بِهِ ضَمِيرُ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ أَوِ الْمُخَاطَبِ وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ الْغَائِبَةِ نُقِلَ فَعَلَ مِنَ الْوَاوِيِّ إِلَى فَعُلَ، وَمِنَ الْيَائِيِّ إِلَى فَعِلَ، دَلَالَةً عَلَيْهِمَا، وَلَمْ يُغَيَّرْ فَعُلَ وَلَا فَعِلَ إِذَا كَانَا أَصْلِيَّيْنِ، وَنُقِلَتِ الضَّمَّةُ وَالْكَسْرَةُ إِلَى الْفَاءِ، وَحُذِفَتِ الْعَيْنُ لِالْتِقَاءِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ.
text.en: If the pronoun of the speaker, of the one addressed or of the plural of the absent feminine is joined to it, faʿala is moved to faʿula in the wāw verb and to faʿila in the yāʾ verb, to point to them; faʿula and faʿila are not changed when they are original. The ḍamma and the kasra are moved to the fāʾ, and the ʿayn is deleted because two sukūns meet.

text.original: فَتَقُولُ: صَانَ صَانَا صَانُوا صَانَتْ صَانَتَا صُنَّ صُنْتَ صُنْتُمَا صُنْتُمْ صُنْتِ صُنْتُمَا صُنْتُنَّ صُنْتُ صُنَّا، وَتَقُولُ: بَاعَ بَاعَا بَاعُوا بَاعَتْ بَاعَتَا بِعْنَ إِلَى آخِرِهِ. وَإِذَا بَنَيْتَهُ لِلْمَفْعُولِ كَسَرْتَ الْفَاءَ مِنَ الْجَمِيعِ، فَقُلْتَ: صِينَ، وَإِعْلَالُهُ بِالنَّقْلِ وَالْقَلْبِ، وَبِيعَ، وَإِعْلَالُهُ بِالنَّقْلِ فَقَطْ.
text.en: So you say ṣāna ṣānā ṣānū ṣānat ṣānatā ṣunna ṣunta ṣuntumā ṣuntum ṣunti ṣuntumā ṣuntunna ṣuntu ṣunnā “he guarded” etc., and you say bāʿa bāʿā bāʿū bāʿat bāʿatā biʿna “he sold” to its end. When you build it for the one done to, you give the fāʾ kasra in all of them and say ṣīna, whose change (iʿlāl) is by moving [the vowel] and changing [the letter], and bīʿa, whose change is by moving only.

lessons.title: The hollow verb: muḍāriʿ, jussive and command
body: In the muḍāriʿ: yaṣūnu and yabīʿu, “whose change is by moving”; yakhāfu, “he fears”, and yahābu, “he dreads”, “whose change is by moving and changing”. In yaṣūnu the vowel of the wāw goes back to the quiescent ṣād and the wāw becomes the long ū; in yakhāfu the fatḥa goes back and the wāw, now quiescent after fatḥa, is changed into alif.

Then the jussive: “the ʿayn drops when the letter after it has sukūn, and stays when the letter after it is vowelled”. Lam yaṣun, lam yaṣūnā, lam yaṣūnū, lam taṣun, lam taṣūnā, lam yaṣunna, lam taṣun, lam taṣūnā, lam taṣūnū, lam taṣūnī, lam taṣūnā, lam taṣunna, lam aṣun, lam naṣun. So lam yabiʿ lam yabīʿā lam yabīʿū … lam yabiʿna, and lam yakhaf lam yakhāfā lam yakhāfū.

The rule is one you know: two quiescent letters cannot meet. In lam yaṣun the long ū meets the quiescent nūn, and the ū is shortened; in lam yaṣūnā the nūn has a vowel for the alif of the dual, and the ū stays. Where a pronoun beginning with a consonant follows, as -na, the nūn is quiescent again and the vowel short: lam yaṣunna.

“Measure the command on it”: ṣun ṣūnā ṣūnū ṣūnī ṣūnā ṣunna, “guard!”; biʿ bīʿā bīʿū bīʿī bīʿā biʿna; khaf khāfā khāfū khāfī khāfā khafna. With the nūn of emphasis the last letter takes a vowel, so the long vowel returns: ṣūnanna ṣūnānni ṣūnunna ṣūninna ṣūnānni ṣunnānni; bīʿanna … biʿnānni; khāfanna … khafnānni. Only the women's form stays short, for its nūn is still quiescent before the nūn of the women.

A trap: ṣun and ṣūnanna are the same command to one man, short alone and long with emphasis. Do not take ṣūnanna for a different verb. The rule decides each case: is the letter after the ʿayn vowelled or not?

tasks.prompt: Why does the wāw drop in lam yaṣun but stay in lam yaṣūnā?
tasks.answer: In lam yaṣun the nūn is quiescent, and the long ū before it would make two sukūns meet, so it drops. In lam yaṣūnā the nūn has a vowel for the alif of the dual, so the ū stays.

tasks.prompt: Give the command of khāfa in the six persons.
tasks.answer: Khaf, khāfā, khāfū, khāfī, khāfā, khafna.

tasks.prompt: Why does ṣun become ṣūnanna with the nūn of emphasis?
tasks.answer: The nūn of emphasis gives the last letter a vowel; the nūn of the root is no longer quiescent, so the long ū returns.

tasks.prompt: Name the change in yabīʿu and in yahābu.
tasks.answer: Yabīʿu: by moving only (the kasra of the yāʾ goes back to the bāʾ). Yahābu: by moving and changing (the fatḥa goes back, the yāʾ becomes alif).

quiz.prompt: Yaṣūnu is changed by…
quiz.explanation: The ḍamma of the wāw goes back to the ṣād.

quiz.prompt: Yakhāfu is changed by…
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa goes back and the wāw becomes alif.

quiz.prompt: In the jussive the ʿayn drops when…
options: the letter after it is vowelled
the letter after it is quiescent
quiz.explanation: When the letter after the ʿayn is quiescent, the ʿayn drops: lam yaṣun, but lam yaṣūnā.

quiz.prompt: Lam yaṣunna is…
quiz.explanation: The root's nūn merged with the nūn of the women.

quiz.explanation: The ʿayn stays because the letter after it is vowelled.

quiz.prompt: With the nūn of emphasis, the command ṣun becomes…
quiz.explanation: The last letter takes a vowel and the long ū returns.

quiz.prompt: Which emphasised command stays short?
quiz.explanation: The nūn of the root is still quiescent before the women's nūn.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْمُضَارِعِ: يَصُونُ وَيَبِيعُ، وَإِعْلَالُهُمَا بِالنَّقْلِ، وَيَخَافُ وَيَهَابُ، وَإِعْلَالُهُمَا بِالنَّقْلِ وَالْقَلْبِ.
text.en: You say in the muḍāriʿ yaṣūnu and yabīʿu, whose change is by moving, and yakhāfu “he fears” and yahābu “he dreads”, whose change is by moving and changing.

text.original: وَيَدْخُلُ الْجَازِمُ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ الْمُضَارِعِ فَيَسْقُطُ الْعَيْنُ إِذَا سَكَنَ مَا بَعْدَهُ، وَتَثْبُتُ إِذَا تَحَرَّكَ مَا بَعْدَهُ، تَقُولُ: لَمْ يَصُنْ لَمْ يَصُونَا لَمْ يَصُونُوا لَمْ تَصُنْ لَمْ تَصُونَا لَمْ يَصُنَّ لَمْ تَصُنْ لَمْ تَصُونَا لَمْ تَصُونُوا لَمْ تَصُونِي لَمْ تَصُونَا لَمْ تَصُنَّ لَمْ أَصُنْ لَمْ نَصُنْ. وَهَكَذَا قِيَاسُ لَمْ يَبِعْ لَمْ يَبِيعَا لَمْ يَبِيعُوا لَمْ تَبِعْ لَمْ تَبِيعَا لَمْ يَبِعْنَ إِلَى آخِرِهِ، وَلَمْ يَخَفْ لَمْ يَخَافَا لَمْ يَخَافُوا.
text.en: The jussive particle comes before the muḍāriʿ, and then the ʿayn drops when the letter after it has sukūn, and stays when the letter after it is voweled. You say lam yaṣun lam yaṣūnā lam yaṣūnū lam taṣun lam taṣūnā lam yaṣunna lam taṣun lam taṣūnā lam taṣūnū lam taṣūnī lam taṣūnā lam taṣunna lam aṣun lam naṣun “he did not guard” etc. So goes the rule of lam yabiʿ lam yabīʿā lam yabīʿū lam tabiʿ lam tabīʿā lam yabiʿna to its end, and of lam yakhaf lam yakhāfā lam yakhāfū.

text.original: وَقِسْ عَلَيْهِ الْأَمْرَ، نَحْوُ: صُنْ صُونَا صُونُوا صُونِي صُونَا صُنَّ، وَبِالتَّأْكِيدِ: صُونَنَّ صُونَانِّ صُونُنَّ صُونِنَّ صُونَانِّ صُنَّانِّ، وَبِعْ بِيعَا بِيعُوا بِيعِي بِيعَا بِعْنَ، وَخَفْ خَافَا خَافُوا خَافِي خَافَا خَفْنَ، وَالتَّأْكِيدُ: بِيعَنَّ بِيعَانِّ بِيعُنَّ بِيعِنَّ بِيعَانِّ بِعْنَانِّ، وَخَافَنَّ خَافَانِّ خَافُنَّ خَافِنَّ خَافَانِّ خَفْنَانِّ.
text.en: Measure the command on it, as ṣun ṣūnā ṣūnū ṣūnī ṣūnā ṣunna “guard!”, and with emphasis ṣūnanna ṣūnānni ṣūnunna ṣūninna ṣūnānni ṣunnānni; biʿ bīʿā bīʿū bīʿī bīʿā biʿna “sell!”; khaf khāfā khāfū khāfī khāfā khafna “fear!”; and the emphasis: bīʿanna bīʿānni bīʿunna bīʿinna bīʿānni biʿnānni and khāfanna khāfānni khāfunna khāfinna khāfānni khafnānni.

lessons.title: The augmented hollow verb, the sound exceptions and the participles
lessons.arabic: الْأَجْوَفُ الْمَزِيدُ فِيهِ وَاسْمَا الْفَاعِلِ وَالْمَفْعُولِ
lessons.transliteration: al-ajwaf al-mazīd fīhi wa-ismā al-fāʿil wa-l-mafʿūl
body: “In the augmented triliteral only four patterns are weak”: ajāba yujību ijābatan, “to answer”; istaqāma yastaqīmu istiqāmatan, “to be straight”; ikhtāra yakhtāru ikhtiyāran, “to choose”; inqāda yanqādu inqiyādan, “to comply”. The maṣdar ijāba is explained: its original is ijwāb; “it was changed by moving and changing, so two alifs came together; one of them was deleted, and the tāʾ at its end was put in its place”.

Built for the one done to: ujība yujābu, ustuqīma yustaqāmu, ikhtīra yukhtāru, inqīda yunqādu. The command: ajib ajībā ajībū ajībī ajībā ajibna; istaqim … istaqimna; ikhtar … ikhtarna; inqad … inqadna. These follow the bare hollow verb exactly: the long vowel is shortened where a quiescent letter follows (ajib, ajibna) and kept where a vowel follows (ajībā).

The other augmented patterns stay sound: qāwala, taqāwala, taqawwala, zayyana, tazayyana, sāyara, tasāyara, iswadda, iswādda, ibyaḍḍa, ibyāḍḍa, “and so in all their derived forms”. The book gives no reason; look at the patterns and the cause is missing. In qāwala and sāyara an alif, not a fatḥa, stands before the weak letter; in zayyana and taqawwala the first of the doubled letters has its own sukūn; in iswadda the wāw is quiescent by the pattern. None has a vowelled weak letter after a fatḥa.

The active participle of the bare verb “is changed with the hamza”: ṣāʾin, bāʾiʿ, as the Maqṣūd explained for qāʾil; that of the augmented verb follows its muḍāriʿ: mujīb, mustaqīm, munqād, mukhtār. The passive participle of the bare verb “is changed by deletion and moving”: maṣūn, mabīʿ. Two letters were quiescent after the moving, the ʿayn and the wāw of mafʿūl, and one went: “the wāw of mafʿūl according to Sībawayh, and the ʿayn of the verb according to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash”.

“The Banū Tamīm keep the yāʾ and say mabyūʿ”: the full form, unchanged. The passive participle of the augmented verb is changed by moving and changing, “if its verb is changed”: mujāb, mustaqām, munqād, mukhtār. Note mukhtār and munqād again: as in lesson 12, the active and passive participle have one wording.

tasks.prompt: Explain the maṣdar ijāba from its original ijwāb.
tasks.answer: The fatḥa of the wāw moved to the jīm and the wāw became alif (moving and changing); two alifs met, one was deleted, and a tāʾ was put at the end in its place: ijāba.

tasks.prompt: Why is the wāw of qāwala and the yāʾ of zayyana left unchanged?
tasks.answer: The cause of the change is missing. In qāwala an alif, not a fatḥa, stands before the wāw; in zayyana the first yāʾ has its own sukūn and the second follows it. No weak letter there is vowelled after a fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: Give the active and passive participles of ikhtāra. Why are they the same?
tasks.answer: Mukhtār and mukhtār. The yāʾ became alif in both, and with it went the kasra or fatḥa that tells the doer from the one done to; only the underlying forms differ.

tasks.prompt: On what did Sībawayh and al-Akhfash disagree in maṣūn?
tasks.answer: On which of two quiescent letters was deleted after the vowel moved: Sībawayh says the wāw of mafʿūl, al-Akhfash the ʿayn of the verb.

quiz.prompt: How many augmented patterns of the hollow verb are weak?
quiz.explanation: Ajāba, istaqāma, ikhtāra, inqāda.

quiz.prompt: What does the tāʾ of ijāba replace?
quiz.explanation: Two alifs met; one was deleted and the tāʾ put in its place.

quiz.prompt: The passive of istaqāma is…
quiz.explanation: Ḍamma on the first vowelled letter, the hamza following it, and kasra before the last: ustuqīma yustaqāmu.

quiz.prompt: Which verb stays sound?
quiz.explanation: An alif, not a fatḥa, stands before its yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Ṣāʾin, “guarding”, is changed with…
quiz.explanation: The active participle of the bare hollow verb.

quiz.prompt: According to Sībawayh, what was deleted in maṣūn?
quiz.explanation: Sībawayh says the wāw of mafʿūl was deleted; al-Akhfash says the ʿayn of the verb.

quiz.explanation: The Banū Tamīm keep the yāʾ unchanged and say mabyūʿ for mabīʿ.

text.original: وَالْمَزِيدُ الثُّلَاثِيُّ لَا يَعْتَلُّ مِنْهُ إِلَّا أَرْبَعَةُ أَبْنِيَةٍ، وَهِيَ: أَجَابَ يُجِيبُ إِجَابَةً، وَالْأَصْلُ إِجْوَابًا، أُعِلَّ بِالنَّقْلِ وَالْقَلْبِ، فَاجْتَمَعَ أَلِفَانِ، فَحُذِفَ إِحْدَاهُمَا، وَعُوِّضَ عَنْهُ التَّاءُ فِي آخِرِهِ، وَاسْتَقَامَ يَسْتَقِيمُ اسْتِقَامَةً، وَاخْتَارَ يَخْتَارُ اخْتِيَارًا، وَانْقَادَ يَنْقَادُ انْقِيَادًا.
text.en: In the augmented triliteral only four patterns are weak: ajāba yujību ijābatan “to answer”, whose original is ijwāban: it was changed by moving and changing, so two alifs came together; one of them was deleted, and the tāʾ at its end was put in its place; istaqāma yastaqīmu istiqāmatan “to be straight”; ikhtāra yakhtāru ikhtiyāran “to choose”; and inqāda yanqādu inqiyādan “to comply”.

text.original: وَإِذَا بَنَيْتَهَا لِلْمَفْعُولِ قُلْتَ: أُجِيبَ يُجَابُ، وَاسْتُقِيمَ يُسْتَقَامُ، وَاخْتِيرَ يُخْتَارُ، وَانْقِيدَ يُنْقَادُ. وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهَا: أَجِبْ أَجِيبَا أَجِيبُوا أَجِيبِي أَجِيبَا أَجِبْنَ، وَاسْتَقِمْ اسْتَقِيمَا اسْتَقِيمُوا اسْتَقِيمِي اسْتَقِيمَا اسْتَقِمْنَ، وَاخْتَرْ اخْتَارَا اخْتَارُوا اخْتَارِي اخْتَارَا اخْتَرْنَ، وَانْقَدْ انْقَادَا انْقَادُوا انْقَادِي انْقَادَا انْقَدْنَ.
text.en: When you build them for the one done to, you say ujība yujābu, ustuqīma yustaqāmu, ikhtīra yukhtāru and inqīda yunqādu. The command from them: ajib ajībā ajībū ajībī ajībā ajibna, istaqim istaqīmā istaqīmū istaqīmī istaqīmā istaqimna, ikhtar ikhtārā ikhtārū ikhtārī ikhtārā ikhtarna and inqad inqādā inqādū inqādī inqādā inqadna.

text.original: وَيَصِحُّ نَحْوُ: قَاوَلَ، وَتَقَاوَلَ، وَتَقَوَّلَ، وَزَيَّنَ، وَتَزَيَّنَ، وَسَايَرَ، وَتَسَايَرَ، وَاسْوَدَّ، وَاسْوَادَّ، وَابْيَضَّ، وَابْيَاضَّ، وَكَذَا فِي سَائِرِ تَصَارِيفِهَا.
text.en: Sound are such as qāwala “to converse”, taqāwala “to talk together”, taqawwala “to make up words”, zayyana “to adorn”, tazayyana “to adorn oneself”, sāyara “to go along with”, tasāyara “to go along together”, iswadda, iswādda, ibyaḍḍa “to turn white” and ibyāḍḍa “to turn pure white”; and so in all their derived forms.

text.original: وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ مِنَ الْمُجَرَّدِ يَعْتَلُّ بِالْهَمْزَةِ، كَصَائِنٍ وَبَائِعٍ، وَمِنَ الْمَزِيدِ فِيهِ يَعْتَلُّ بِمَا اعْتَلَّ بِهِ الْمُضَارِعُ، كَمُجِيبٍ وَمُسْتَقِيمٍ وَمُنْقَادٍ وَمُخْتَارٍ. وَاسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ يَعْتَلُّ بِالْحَذْفِ وَالنَّقْلِ، كَمَصُونٍ وَمَبِيعٍ، وَالْمَحْذُوفُ وَاوُ الْمَفْعُولِ عِنْدَ سِيبَوَيْهِ، وَعَيْنُ الْفِعْلِ عِنْدَ أَبِي الْحَسَنِ الْأَخْفَشِ.
text.en: The active participle of the bare verb is changed with the hamza, as ṣāʾinin “guarding” and bāʾiʿin “selling”; of the augmented verb it is changed with what the muḍāriʿ is changed with, as mujībin, mustaqīmin, munqādin and mukhtārin. The passive participle of the bare triliteral is changed by deletion and moving, as maṣūnin “guarded” and mabīʿin “sold”; what is deleted is the wāw of [the pattern] mafʿūl according to Sībawayh, and the ʿayn of the verb according to Abū al-Ḥasan al-Akhfash.

text.original: وَبَنُو تَمِيمٍ يُثْبِتُونَ الْيَاءَ فَيَقُولُونَ: مَبْيُوعٌ. وَمِنَ الْمَزِيدِ فِيهِ يَعْتَلُّ بِالنَّقْلِ وَالْقَلْبِ إِنِ اعْتَلَّ فِعْلُهُ، كَمُجَابٍ وَمُسْتَقَامٍ وَمُنْقَادٍ وَمُخْتَارٍ.
text.en: The Banū Tamīm keep the yāʾ and say mabyūʿun. Of the augmented verb it is changed by moving and changing, if its verb is changed, as mujābin, mustaqāmin, munqādin and mukhtārin.

parts.title: The defective verb and the lafīf

lessons.title: The defective verb: the past
body: The third kind is the verb weak in the lām, called the defective (al-nāqiṣ) and “the one of four” (dhū al-arbaʿa), “because its past has four letters when you speak about yourself”: sarūtu, “I was noble”, has four, s-r-w-t. The wāw and the yāʾ “are changed into alif when they are vowelled and the letter before them has fatḥa”: ghazā, “to raid”, ramā, “to throw”, and in nouns ʿaṣan, “a stick”, raḥan, “a millstone”.

So too in the verb of more than three letters, aʿṭā, “to give”, ishtarā, “to buy”, istaqṣā, “to go to the utmost”; in their passive participles, al-muʿṭā, al-mushtarā, al-mustaqṣā; and in the passive muḍāriʿ: yuʿṭā, yughzā, yurmā. Wherever the last weak letter is vowelled after a fatḥa, it is an alif.

In the past “the lām is deleted in the form faʿalū in every case, and in faʿalat and faʿalatā when the ʿayn has fatḥa; it stays in the others”: ghazā ghazawā ghazaw ghazat ghazatā ghazawna; ramā ramayā ramaw ramat ramatā ramayna; raḍiya raḍiyā raḍū raḍiyat raḍiyatā raḍīna. Saruwa, “to be noble”, keeps its wāw throughout except in sarū: saruwa saruwā sarū saruwat saruwatā sarūna sarūta … sarūtu sarūnā.

Why a fatḥa before the wāw of ghazaw and ramaw, but a ḍamma in raḍū and sarū? When the wāw of the pronoun follows a defective verb whose lām has dropped, a fatḥa before it is kept, and a kasra or ḍamma becomes a ḍamma. “The original of raḍū is raḍiyū: the ḍamma of the yāʾ was moved to the ḍād, and the yāʾ was deleted because two sukūns met.” So the vowel before the wāw tells the bāb: ghazaw is faʿala, raḍū faʿila.

Two traps. Raḍiyat keeps its yāʾ while ghazat loses its wāw: after a kasra the yāʾ never became alif, so there is nothing to drop before the tāʾ. And ghazaw and ghazawna both show a wāw: in ghazaw, “they (men) raided”, the wāw is the pronoun; in ghazawna, “they (women) raided”, it is the lām of the root, before the pronoun -na.

tasks.prompt: Why is the defective verb called dhū al-arbaʿa?
tasks.answer: Because its past has four letters when you speak about yourself: sarūtu is s-r-w-t. The hollow verb loses its ʿayn and has three (ṣuntu); the defective keeps its lām there.

tasks.prompt: Explain raḍū from raḍiyū.
tasks.answer: The ḍamma of the yāʾ was moved to the ḍād (in place of its kasra); the yāʾ, now quiescent, met the quiescent wāw of the pronoun and was deleted: raḍū.

tasks.prompt: Why does the lām drop in ghazat but stay in raḍiyat?
tasks.answer: In ghazat the wāw, vowelled after a fatḥa, became alif, and the alif dropped before the quiescent tāʾ. In raḍiyat the yāʾ follows a kasra and never becomes alif, so it stays with its fatḥa.

tasks.prompt: In ghazaw and ghazawna, which wāw is the root's and which the pronoun's?
tasks.answer: In ghazaw the wāw is the pronoun of the men; the root's wāw has dropped. In ghazawna the wāw is the root's lām, quiescent before the pronoun -na of the women.

quiz.prompt: When do the wāw and yāʾ become alif?
options: When vowelled with a fatḥa before them
quiz.explanation: A wāw or yāʾ with a vowel and a fatḥa before it becomes alif: ghazā, ramā, ʿaṣan, raḥan.

quiz.prompt: In which past form is the lām deleted in every case?
quiz.explanation: In faʿalū the lām drops in every case: ghazaw, ramaw, raḍū, sarū.

quiz.prompt: Ramat has lost its yāʾ because…
quiz.explanation: The lām drops in faʿalat when the ʿayn has fatḥa; raḍiyat keeps it.

quiz.prompt: The original of raḍū is…
quiz.explanation: The ḍamma of the yāʾ moved to the ḍād and the yāʾ dropped.

quiz.prompt: Why a fatḥa before the wāw of ghazaw?
options: A fatḥa before the pronoun is kept
quiz.explanation: A kasra or ḍamma there becomes a ḍamma, as in raḍū.

quiz.prompt: Which is passive?
quiz.explanation: In the passive muḍāriʿ the lām after fatḥa becomes alif.

quiz.prompt: Ghazawna means…
quiz.explanation: The wāw is the lām, before the women's -na.

text.original: الثَّالِثُ الْمُعْتَلُّ اللَّامِ، وَيُقَالُ لَهُ النَّاقِصُ وَذُو الْأَرْبَعَةِ لِكَوْنِ مَاضِيهِ عَلَى أَرْبَعَةِ أَحْرُفٍ إِذَا أَخْبَرْتَ عَنْ نَفْسِكَ. تُقْلَبُ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ أَلِفًا إِذَا تَحَرَّكَتَا وَانْفَتَحَ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا، كَغَزَا وَرَمَى وَعَصًا وَرَحًى، وَكَذَلِكَ الْفِعْلُ الزَّائِدُ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَحْرُفٍ، كَأَعْطَى وَاشْتَرَى وَاسْتَقْصَى، وَاسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ مِنْهُ، كَالْمُعْطَى وَالْمُشْتَرَى وَالْمُسْتَقْصَى، وَكَذَلِكَ مَا لَمْ يُسَمَّ فَاعِلُهُ مِنَ الْمُضَارِعِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: يُعْطَى وَيُغْزَى وَيُرْمَى.
text.en: The third is the verb weak in the lām; it is called the defective (al-nāqiṣ) and the one of four (dhū al-arbaʿa), because its past has four letters when you speak about yourself. The wāw and the yāʾ are changed into alif when they are voweled and the letter before them has fatḥa, as ghazā “to raid”, ramā “to throw”, ʿaṣan “a stick” and raḥan “a millstone”; and likewise in the verb with more than three letters, as aʿṭā “to give”, ishtarā “to buy” and istaqṣā “to go to the utmost”, and in its passive participle, as al-muʿṭā, al-mushtarā and al-mustaqṣā; and likewise in the muḍāriʿ whose doer is not named, as when you say yuʿṭā, yughzā and yurmā.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَاضِي فَتُحْذَفُ اللَّامُ مِنْهُ فِي مِثَالِ فَعَلُوا مُطْلَقًا، وَفِي مِثَالِ فَعَلَتْ وَفَعَلَتَا إِذَا انْفَتَحَ الْعَيْنُ، وَتَثْبُتُ فِي غَيْرِهَا، فَتَقُولُ: غَزَا غَزَوَا غَزَوْا غَزَتْ غَزَتَا غَزَوْنَ إِلَى آخِرِهِ، وَرَمَى رَمَيَا رَمَوْا رَمَتْ رَمَتَا رَمَيْنَ إِلَخْ، وَرَضِيَ رَضِيَا رَضُوا رَضِيَتْ رَضِيَتَا رَضِينَ إِلَخْ.
text.en: As for the past, the lām is deleted from it in the form faʿalū in every case, and in the forms faʿalat and faʿalatā when the ʿayn has fatḥa; it stays in the others. So you say ghazā ghazawā ghazaw ghazat ghazatā ghazawna “he raided” to its end, ramā ramayā ramaw ramat ramatā ramayna “he threw” etc., and raḍiya raḍiyā raḍū raḍiyat raḍiyatā raḍīna “he was pleased” etc.

text.original: وَكَذَلِكَ سَرُوَ سَرُوَا سَرُوا سَرُوَتْ سَرُوَتَا سَرُونَ سَرُوتَ سَرُوتُمَا سَرُوتُمْ سَرُوتِ سَرُوتُمَا سَرُوتُنَّ سَرُوتُ سَرُونَا.
text.en: So too saruwa saruwā sarū saruwat saruwatā sarūna sarūta sarūtumā sarūtum sarūti sarūtumā sarūtunna sarūtu sarūnā “he was noble”.

text.original: وَإِنَّمَا فُتِحَ مَا قَبْلَ وَاوِ الضَّمِيرِ فِي غَزَوْا وَرَمَوْا، وَضُمَّ فِي رَضُوا وَسَرُوا؛ لِأَنَّ وَاوَ الضَّمِيرِ إِذَا اتَّصَلَ بِالْفِعْلِ النَّاقِصِ بَعْدَ حَذْفِ اللَّامِ، فَإِنْ كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَفْتُوحًا أُبْقِيَ عَلَى الْفَتْحَةِ، نَحْوُ: غَزَوْا وَرَمَوْا، وَإِنْ كَانَ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَكْسُورًا أَوْ مَضْمُومًا ضُمَّتْ، نَحْوُ: رَضُوا وَسَرُوا، وَأَصْلُ رَضُوا رَضِيُوا، فَنُقِلَتْ ضَمَّةُ الْيَاءِ إِلَى الضَّادِ، وَحُذِفَتِ الْيَاءُ لِالْتِقَاءِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ.
text.en: The letter before the wāw of the pronoun was given fatḥa in ghazaw and ramaw, and ḍamma in raḍū and sarū, because when the wāw of the pronoun is joined to the defective verb after the deletion of the lām, if the letter before it has fatḥa, it is left on the fatḥa, as ghazaw and ramaw; and if the letter before it has kasra or ḍamma, it is given ḍamma, as raḍū and sarū. The original of raḍū is raḍiyū: the ḍamma of the yāʾ was moved to the ḍād, and the yāʾ was deleted because two sukūns met.

lessons.title: The defective muḍāriʿ in rafʿ, naṣb and jazm
body: In the muḍāriʿ of the defective verb “the wāw, the yāʾ and the alif have sukūn in the rafʿ”: yaghzū, “he raids”, yarmī, “he throws”, yakhshā, “he fears”; “and they are deleted in the state of jazm”. In naṣb “the wāw and the yāʾ are given fatḥa, because the fatḥa is light, and the alif stays with sukūn in naṣb as in rafʿ”.

This is three different behaviours in one table. The wāw and the yāʾ refuse a ḍamma but take a fatḥa; the alif takes no vowel at all; all three drop in jazm. The Ājurrūmiyya named this: the jazm of the verb whose last letter is weak is by deletion, and its rafʿ is by an assumed ḍamma.

The jussive: lam yaghzu, lam yaghzuwā; lam yarmi, lam yarmiyā, lam yarmū; and in full, lam yarḍa lam yarḍayā lam yarḍaw lam tarḍa lam tarḍayā lam yarḍayna lam tarḍa lam tarḍayā lam tarḍaw lam tarḍay lam tarḍayā lam tarḍayna lam arḍa lam narḍa. The particles of jazm and naṣb “drop the nūns, except the nūn of the feminine plural”, as in the sound verb.

The naṣb: lan yaghzuwa, lan yaghzuwā, lan yaghzū; lan yarmiya, lan yarmiyā, lan yarmū; lan yarḍā lan yarḍayā lan yarḍaw lan tarḍā lan tarḍayā lan yarḍayna … lan tarḍay … lan arḍā lan narḍā. Compare lan yarḍā with lam yarḍa: the alif stays in naṣb and drops in jazm.

A trap: lam tarḍay and lam tarḍa are two persons. In lam tarḍa, “you (man) were not pleased”, the alif of the lām has dropped. In lam tarḍay, “you (woman) were not pleased”, the yāʾ is the pronoun of the woman, left when the jussive took its nūn from tarḍayna.

tasks.prompt: Why does the alif of yarḍā show no fatḥa in lan yarḍā?
tasks.answer: An alif cannot bear any vowel. The book says it “stays with sukūn in the state of naṣb as in the state of rafʿ”: the fatḥa is assumed on it.

tasks.prompt: Put tarḍā in jazm for “you (man)”, and tarḍayna for “you (woman)”. Explain the yāʾ of the second.
tasks.answer: Lam tarḍa and lam tarḍay. In the first the alif of the lām is deleted. In the second the jussive takes the nūn of tarḍayna, and the yāʾ that remains is the pronoun of the woman, not the root's letter.

tasks.prompt: Give the jussive of yarmī for he, they two and they (men).
tasks.answer: Lam yarmi, lam yarmiyā, lam yarmū.

quiz.prompt: In rafʿ the last weak letter of the muḍāriʿ is…
quiz.explanation: Yaghzū, yarmī, yakhshā: the ḍamma is assumed.

quiz.prompt: Why do the wāw and yāʾ take a fatḥa in naṣb?
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa is light enough for the wāw and the yāʾ to bear: lan yaghzuwa, lan yarmiya.

quiz.prompt: In naṣb the alif…
quiz.explanation: An alif bears no vowel, so it stays quiescent in naṣb: lan yarḍā, lan yakhshā.

quiz.prompt: The jazm of the defective verb is by…
quiz.explanation: Lam yaghzu, lam yarmi, lam yarḍa.

quiz.prompt: Lam yarmū means…
quiz.explanation: Lam took the nūn of yarmūna; what is left, yarmū, is the men's plural.

quiz.prompt: Lam tarḍay is said to…
quiz.explanation: The yāʾ is her pronoun; the nūn has gone.

quiz.prompt: Which nūn is kept in jazm and naṣb?
options: The nūn of the feminine plural
The nūn of the men's plural
quiz.explanation: The nūn of the feminine plural is a pronoun, so it stays: lam yarḍayna, lan yarḍayna.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمُضَارِعُ مِنَ النَّاقِصِ فَتُسَكَّنُ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْأَلِفُ فِي الرَّفْعِ، نَحْوُ: يَغْزُو وَيَرْمِي وَيَخْشَى، فَتُحْذَفُ فِي حَالَةِ الْجَزْمِ، وَتُفْتَحُ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ فِي النَّصْبِ لِخِفَّةِ الْفَتْحَةِ، وَتَثْبُتُ الْأَلِفُ سَاكِنَةً فِي حَالَةِ النَّصْبِ كَمَا فِي حَالِ الرَّفْعِ، وَيُسْقِطُ الْجَازِمُ وَالنَّاصِبُ النُّونَاتِ إِلَّا نُونَ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ.
text.en: As for the muḍāriʿ of the defective verb, the wāw, the yāʾ and the alif have sukūn in the rafʿ, as yaghzū “he raids”, yarmī “he throws” and yakhshā “he fears”, and they are deleted in the state of jazm. The wāw and the yāʾ are given fatḥa in the naṣb, because the fatḥa is light, and the alif stays with sukūn in the state of naṣb as in the state of rafʿ. The jussive particle and the particle of naṣb drop the nūns, except the nūn of the feminine plural.

text.original: فَتَقُولُ: لَمْ يَغْزُ لَمْ يَغْزُوَا، وَكَذَا لَمْ يَرْمِ لَمْ يَرْمِيَا لَمْ يَرْمُوا، وَلَمْ يَرْضَ لَمْ يَرْضَيَا لَمْ يَرْضَوْا لَمْ تَرْضَ لَمْ تَرْضَيَا لَمْ يَرْضَيْنَ لَمْ تَرْضَ لَمْ تَرْضَيَا لَمْ تَرْضَوْا لَمْ تَرْضَيْ لَمْ تَرْضَيَا لَمْ تَرْضَيْنَ لَمْ أَرْضَ لَمْ نَرْضَ.
text.en: So you say lam yaghzu lam yaghzuwā, and likewise lam yarmi lam yarmiyā lam yarmū, and lam yarḍa lam yarḍayā lam yarḍaw lam tarḍa lam tarḍayā lam yarḍayna lam tarḍa lam tarḍayā lam tarḍaw lam tarḍay lam tarḍayā lam tarḍayna lam arḍa lam narḍa.

text.original: فَتَقُولُ فِي النَّصْبِ: لَنْ يَغْزُوَ لَنْ يَغْزُوَا لَنْ يَغْزُوا، لَنْ يَرْمِيَ لَنْ يَرْمِيَا لَنْ يَرْمُوا، وَلَنْ يَرْضَى لَنْ يَرْضَيَا لَنْ يَرْضَوْا لَنْ تَرْضَى لَنْ تَرْضَيَا لَنْ يَرْضَيْنَ لَنْ تَرْضَى لَنْ تَرْضَيَا لَنْ تَرْضَوْا لَنْ تَرْضَيْ لَنْ تَرْضَيَا لَنْ تَرْضَيْنَ لَنْ أَرْضَى لَنْ نَرْضَى.
text.en: And you say in the naṣb: lan yaghzuwa lan yaghzuwā lan yaghzū, lan yarmiya lan yarmiyā lan yarmū, and lan yarḍā lan yarḍayā lan yarḍaw lan tarḍā lan tarḍayā lan yarḍayna lan tarḍā lan tarḍayā lan tarḍaw lan tarḍay lan tarḍayā lan tarḍayna lan arḍā lan narḍā.

lessons.title: The paradigms of yaghzū, yarmī and yarḍā
body: “The lām of the verb stays in the verb of the two and of the group of women, and is deleted from the verb of the group of men and from the verb of the feminine singular addressed.” So: yaghzū yaghzuwāni yaghzūna taghzū taghzuwāni yaghzūna taghzū taghzuwāni taghzūna taghzīna taghzuwāni taghzūna aghzū naghzū.

Look at yaghzūna: it stands twice in the list, for the men and for the women. “The wording … is the same, … but the underlying form differs: the measure of the masculine is yafʿūna and tafʿūna, and the measure of the feminine plural is yafʿulna and tafʿulna.” For the men the lām is gone and the ū is the pronoun, with -na the sign of rafʿ; for the women the ū is the lām and -na is the pronoun. The jussive shows it: lam yaghzū for the men, yaghzūna unchanged for the women.

Yarmī: yarmī yarmiyāni yarmūna tarmī tarmiyāni yarmīna tarmī tarmiyāni tarmūna tarmīna tarmiyāni tarmīna armī narmī. “The original of yarmūna is yarmiyūna, and with it was done what was done with raḍū”: the ḍamma of the yāʾ moved to the mīm, and the yāʾ dropped before the wāw.

“Such is the rule of every verb in which the letter before its lām has kasra”: yahdī, “he guides”, yunājī, “he speaks in secret”, yartajī, “he hopes”, yashtarī, yastadʿī, yarʿawī, yaʿrawrī. Several of these have a wāw root (yunājī, yartajī, yastadʿī), and still end like yarmī: what decides is the kasra before the lām, after which a wāw becomes yāʾ.

Yarḍā: yarḍā yarḍayāni yarḍawna tarḍā tarḍayāni yarḍayna tarḍā tarḍayāni tarḍawna tarḍayna tarḍayāni tarḍayna arḍā narḍā. Here the plural of the men is yarḍawna, with fatḥa before the wāw, and the women's yarḍayna keeps the yāʾ: the three tables differ exactly at the men, the woman addressed and the women.

tasks.answer: For the men yafʿūna: the lām is gone, the ū is the pronoun, -na is the sign of rafʿ (it drops in jazm). For the women yafʿulna: the ū is the lām, -na is the pronoun (it stays in jazm).

tasks.prompt: Explain yarmūna from yarmiyūna.

text.original: وَتَثْبُتُ لَامُ الْفِعْلِ فِي فِعْلِ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَجَمَاعَةِ الْإِنَاثِ، وَتُحْذَفُ مِنْ فِعْلِ جَمَاعَةِ الذُّكُورِ وَفِعْلِ الْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُخَاطَبَةِ، فَتَقُولُ: يَغْزُو يَغْزُوَانِ يَغْزُونَ تَغْزُو تَغْزُوَانِ يَغْزُونَ تَغْزُو تَغْزُوَانِ تَغْزُونَ تَغْزِينَ تَغْزُوَانِ تَغْزُونَ أَغْزُو نَغْزُو.
text.en: The lām of the verb stays in the verb of the two and of the group of women, and is deleted from the verb of the group of men and from the verb of the feminine singular addressed. So you say yaghzū yaghzuwāni yaghzūna taghzū taghzuwāni yaghzūna taghzū taghzuwāni taghzūna taghzīna taghzuwāni taghzūna aghzū naghzū.

text.original: وَيَسْتَوِي فِيهِ لَفْظُ جَمَاعَةِ الذُّكُورِ وَالْإِنَاثِ فِي الْخِطَابِ وَالْغَيْبَةِ جَمِيعًا، لَكِنِ التَّقْدِيرُ مُخْتَلِفٌ؛ فَوَزْنُ الْمُذَكَّرِ يَفْعُونَ وَتَفْعُونَ، وَوَزْنُ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ يَفْعُلْنَ وَتَفْعُلْنَ.
text.en: In it the wording of the group of men and of women is the same, in addressing and in the absent alike, but the underlying form differs: the measure of the masculine is yafʿūna and tafʿūna, and the measure of the feminine plural is yafʿulna and tafʿulna.

text.original: فَتَقُولُ: يَرْمِي يَرْمِيَانِ يَرْمُونَ تَرْمِي تَرْمِيَانِ يَرْمِينَ تَرْمِي تَرْمِيَانِ تَرْمُونَ تَرْمِينَ تَرْمِيَانِ تَرْمِينَ أَرْمِي نَرْمِي، وَأَصْلُ يَرْمُونَ يَرْمِيُونَ، فَفُعِلَ فِيهِ كَمَا فُعِلَ بِرَضُوا، وَهَكَذَا حُكْمُ كُلِّ مَا كَانَ مَا قَبْلَ لَامِهِ مَكْسُورًا، كَيَهْدِي وَيُنَاجِي وَيَرْتَجِي وَيَشْتَرِي وَيَسْتَدْعِي وَيَرْعَوِي وَيَعْرَوْرِي.
text.en: So you say yarmī yarmiyāni yarmūna tarmī tarmiyāni yarmīna tarmī tarmiyāni tarmūna tarmīna tarmiyāni tarmīna armī narmī. The original of yarmūna is yarmiyūna, and with it was done what was done with raḍū. Such is the rule of every verb in which the letter before its lām has kasra, as yahdī “he guides”, yunājī “he speaks in secret”, yartajī “he hopes”, yashtarī “he buys”, yastadʿī “he summons”, yarʿawī “he desists” and yaʿrawrī “he rides bareback”.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ: يَرْضَى يَرْضَيَانِ يَرْضَوْنَ تَرْضَى تَرْضَيَانِ يَرْضَيْنَ تَرْضَى تَرْضَيَانِ تَرْضَوْنَ تَرْضَيْنَ تَرْضَيَانِ تَرْضَيْنَ أَرْضَى نَرْضَى.
text.en: And you say yarḍā yarḍayāni yarḍawna tarḍā tarḍayāni yarḍayna tarḍā tarḍayāni tarḍawna tarḍayna tarḍayāni tarḍayna arḍā narḍā.

lessons.title: Fatḥa before the lām; the woman and the women
body: “Such is the rule of every verb in which [the letter] before its lām has fatḥa”: it goes like yarḍā. The book writes out four in full: yatamaṭṭā, “he stretches himself”; yataṣābā, “he behaves like a youth”; yataqalsā, “he puts on a cap”; and yataṣaddā, “he turns to”. Tafaʿʿala, tafāʿala and tafaʿlala all have fatḥa before the lām in their muḍāriʿ, so all their defective verbs end in alif.

Set this beside the previous lesson. There, yunājī, yartajī and yastadʿī had a wāw root and went like yarmī because of the kasra; here, yataṣaddā and the others go like yarḍā because of the fatḥa. The root letter does not decide the muḍāriʿ of a longer defective verb; the vowel before the lām does.

Read the paradigm of yatamaṭṭā as a pattern: yatamaṭṭā yatamaṭṭayāni yatamaṭṭawna tatamaṭṭā tatamaṭṭayāni yatamaṭṭayna … atamaṭṭā natamaṭṭā. Every ending is the ending of yarḍā: -ā, -ayāni, -awna, -ayna. A student who knows yarḍā knows all four.

Then a warning: “the wording of the feminine singular in addressing is like the wording of the feminine plural in the bāb of yarmī and yarḍā, but the underlying form differs: the measure of the feminine singular is tafʿīna and tafʿayna, and the measure of the plural tafʿilna and tafʿalna.” Tarmīna and tarḍayna each mean both “you (woman)” and “you (women)”.

The jussive separates them, as with yaghzūna. For the woman the lām is gone and the nūn is the sign of rafʿ: lam tarḍay. For the women the yāʾ is the lām and the nūn is the pronoun: lam tarḍayna, unchanged. If a form keeps its nūn after lam, it is the women's.

tasks.prompt: Why do yataṣaddā and yatamaṭṭā go like yarḍā and not like yarmī?
tasks.answer: The letter before their lām has fatḥa (the muḍāriʿ of tafaʿʿala), and every verb with fatḥa before its lām goes like yarḍā.

tasks.prompt: Tarḍayna: show by the jussive whether it is said to the woman or to the women.
tasks.answer: If lam leaves lam tarḍay, it was the woman's (tafʿayna: the nūn was the sign of rafʿ). If lam leaves lam tarḍayna, it was the women's (tafʿalna: the nūn is their pronoun).

tasks.answer: For the woman tafʿīna (the lām gone, the ī the pronoun); for the women tafʿilna (the ī the lām, -na the pronoun).

text.original: وَلَفْظُ الْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فِي الْخِطَابِ كَلَفْظِ جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فِي بَابِ يَرْمِي وَيَرْضَى، وَالتَّقْدِيرُ مُخْتَلِفٌ؛ فَوَزْنُ الْوَاحِدَةِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ تَفْعِينَ وَتَفْعَيْنَ، وَوَزْنُ الْجَمْعِ تَفْعِلْنَ وَتَفْعَلْنَ.
text.en: The wording of the feminine singular in addressing is like the wording of the feminine plural in the bāb of yarmī and yarḍā, but the underlying form differs: the measure of the feminine singular is tafʿīna and tafʿayna, and the measure of the plural tafʿilna and tafʿalna.

lessons.title: The command of the defective verb
body: “The command from them”: ughzu ughzuwā ughzū ughzī ughzuwā ughzūna, “raid!”; irmi irmiyā irmū irmī irmiyā irmīna, “throw!”; irḍa irḍayā irḍaw irḍay irḍayā irḍayna, “be pleased!”. Each is the jussive with the prefix taken away and a hamza of joining before the quiescent first radical, ḍamma after yaghzū, kasra after yarmī and yarḍā.

To one man the last radical has gone, as in the jussive: ughzu, irmi, irḍa. To the two and to the women it stays: ughzuwā, ughzūna. To the men and to the woman the endings are those of the muḍāriʿ without its nūn: ughzū and ughzī, irmū and irmī, irḍaw and irḍay.

“When you bring the nūn of emphasis on it, the deleted lām is brought back”: ughzuwanna ughzuwānni ughzunna ughzinna ughzuwānni ughzūnānni; irmiyanna irmiyānni irmunna irminna irmiyānni irmīnānni; irḍayanna irḍayānni irḍawunna irḍayinna irḍayānni irḍaynānni. The reason is the one met in ṣūnanna: the last letter must take a vowel before the nūn, so the lām that dropped for want of a vowel returns.

In the forms of the men and the woman the rules of lesson 11 apply. In ughzunna and irmunna, ughzinna and irminna, the pronoun's wāw or yāʾ is dropped and its ḍamma or kasra left, for the letter before it had ḍamma or kasra. In irḍawunna and irḍayinna the letter before has fatḥa, so the wāw and yāʾ stay and take a vowel, as in lā takhshawunna.

A trap: ughzūna and irmīna, to the women, keep the long vowel because it is the lām, not a pronoun; the pronoun is the -na. Compare ughzū, to the men, where the ū is the pronoun. The same long vowel, two different letters, exactly as in yaghzūna.

tasks.prompt: Why does the wāw come back in ughzuwanna?
tasks.answer: The wāw of ughzu dropped because the last letter was in jazm. Before the nūn of emphasis the last letter takes a fatḥa, and a wāw can bear a fatḥa, so the deleted lām is brought back.

tasks.prompt: Explain irḍawunna and irḍayinna.
tasks.answer: They are irḍaw and irḍay with the heavy nūn. The letter before the pronoun's wāw and yāʾ has fatḥa, so these are not dropped but given a vowel, ḍamma and kasra, before the nūn.

tasks.prompt: Ughzūna: to whom is it said, and what is its ū?
tasks.answer: To the women. The ū is the lām of the root, kept because the nūn of the women follows; the -na is their pronoun.

quiz.prompt: The command of ghazā to one man is…
quiz.explanation: The lām drops as in the jussive lam yaghzu.

quiz.prompt: The command of raḍiya to the men is…
quiz.explanation: The fatḥa before the wāw stays: like yarḍawna.

quiz.prompt: What happens to the deleted lām before the nūn of emphasis?
quiz.explanation: Ughzuwanna, irmiyanna, irḍayanna.

quiz.prompt: Irmunna is said to…
quiz.explanation: The pronoun's wāw dropped, its ḍamma left.

quiz.prompt: Why is the yāʾ kept in irḍayinna?
options: The letter before it has fatḥa
quiz.explanation: The letter before it has fatḥa, so the yāʾ takes a vowel instead of dropping, as in immā tarayinna.

quiz.prompt: The ū of ughzūna is…
quiz.explanation: The -na is the women's pronoun.

quiz.prompt: Ughzinna is said to…
quiz.explanation: From ughzī: the yāʾ dropped and its kasra left.

text.original: وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهَا: اُغْزُ اُغْزُوَا اُغْزُوا اُغْزِي اُغْزُوَا اُغْزُونَ، وَارْمِ ارْمِيَا ارْمُوا ارْمِي ارْمِيَا ارْمِينَ، وَارْضَ ارْضَيَا ارْضَوْا ارْضَيْ ارْضَيَا ارْضَيْنَ.
text.en: The command from them: ughzu ughzuwā ughzū ughzī ughzuwā ughzūna “raid!”, irmi irmiyā irmū irmī irmiyā irmīna “throw!” and irḍa irḍayā irḍaw irḍay irḍayā irḍayna “be pleased!”.

text.original: فَإِذَا أَدْخَلْتَ عَلَيْهِ نُونَ التَّأْكِيدِ أُعِيدَتِ اللَّامُ الْمَحْذُوفَةُ، فَقُلْتَ: اُغْزُوَنَّ اُغْزُوَانِّ اُغْزُنَّ اُغْزِنَّ اُغْزُوَانِّ اُغْزُونَانِّ، وَارْمِيَنَّ ارْمِيَانِّ ارْمُنَّ ارْمِنَّ ارْمِيَانِّ ارْمِينَانِّ، وَارْضَيَنَّ ارْضَيَانِّ ارْضَوُنَّ ارْضَيِنَّ ارْضَيَانِّ ارْضَيْنَانِّ.
text.en: When you bring the nūn of emphasis on it, the deleted lām is brought back, and you say ughzuwanna ughzuwānni ughzunna ughzinna ughzuwānni ughzūnānni, irmiyanna irmiyānni irmunna irminna irmiyānni irmīnānni and irḍayanna irḍayānni irḍawunna irḍayinna irḍayānni irḍaynānni.

lessons.title: Participles of the defective verb; the longer defective verbs
body: The active participle: ghāzin ghāziyāni ghāzūna ghāziyatun ghāziyatāni ghāziyātun, with the broken plurals ghuzātun, ghuzzan, ghuzzāʾun and ghawāzin, “a raider”; rāmin rāmiyāni rāmūna, rumātun wa-rumman, rāmiyatun rāmiyatāni rāmiyātun wa-rawāmin, “a thrower”; and rāḍin, “pleased”.

“The original of ghāzin is ghāziwun: the wāw was changed into yāʾ because it is at the end and the letter before it has kasra, as it was changed in ghuziya.” Then “they said ghāziyatun, because the feminine is a branch of the masculine, and the tāʾ is something that comes after”. With the tāʾ the wāw would no longer be at the end; but the feminine is built on the masculine, which already has the yāʾ, so the yāʾ stays.

The passive participle: maghzuww, “raided”, from the wāw verb, and marmiyy, “thrown”, from the yāʾ verb. In marmiyy “the wāw was changed into yāʾ and merged into the second yāʾ, and the letter before it was given kasra; for when the wāw and the yāʾ come together in one word and the first of them has sukūn, the wāw is changed into yāʾ”. In maghzuww two wāws meet and merge with no change.

Two noun patterns follow the same rules: faʿūl gives ʿaduww, “an enemy”, from a wāw root, and baghiyy, “a harlot”, from a yāʾ root; faʿīl gives ṣabiyy, “a boy”, from a wāw root, and shariyy, “bought”, from a yāʾ root. In baghiyy and ṣabiyy a wāw met a yāʾ and became yāʾ, whichever came first.

In the augmented verb “its wāw is changed into yāʾ, because every wāw that stands fourth or further on, while the letter before it has no ḍamma, is changed into yāʾ”: aʿṭā yuʿṭī, iʿtadā yaʿtadī, istarshā yastarshī, and with the pronoun aʿṭaytu, iʿtadaytu, istarshaytu, taghāzaynā, tarajjaynā. Aʿṭā is from a wāw root, yet aʿṭaytu shows a yāʾ: in a longer verb the wāw at the end always yields to the yāʾ.

the tāʾ that comes after, added to a finished word
a wāw and a yāʾ together, the first quiescent: both become yāʾ

the passive participle: two wāws merged; wāw and yāʾ merged as yāʾ

tasks.prompt: Why does one say ghāziyatun, with a yāʾ, though the root has a wāw and the tāʾ keeps it from the end?
tasks.answer: The feminine is a branch of the masculine, and the tāʾ comes after it: the feminine is built on ghāzin, whose wāw has already become yāʾ, so the yāʾ stays.

tasks.prompt: Explain marmiyy step by step.
tasks.answer: Marmūy on mafʿūl: a quiescent wāw meets a yāʾ in one word; the wāw becomes a yāʾ, the letter before it takes a kasra, and the two yāʾs are merged: marmiyy.

tasks.prompt: Aʿṭā is from a wāw root. Why does aʿṭaytu have a yāʾ?
tasks.answer: Its wāw stands fourth (a-ʿ-ṭ-w) with no ḍamma before it, and every such wāw is changed into a yāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Give the broken plurals of ghāzin that the book lists.
tasks.answer: Ghuzātun, ghuzzan, ghuzzāʾun and ghawāzin.

quiz.prompt: The original of ghāzin is…
quiz.explanation: The final wāw after kasra became yāʾ, as in ghuziya.

quiz.prompt: Why does ghāziyatun keep the yāʾ?
options: The feminine is a branch of the masculine
quiz.explanation: The tāʾ comes after the masculine is complete.

quiz.prompt: Maghzuww has…
quiz.explanation: Mafʿūl of gh-z-w: the wāw of mafʿūl and the lām.

quiz.prompt: In marmiyy, the wāw of mafʿūl…
quiz.explanation: A quiescent wāw before a yāʾ becomes yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Ṣabiyy, “a boy”, is on…
quiz.explanation: From a wāw root: the wāw merged as yāʾ.

quiz.prompt: When does a final wāw become yāʾ in the augmented verb?
options: When fourth or further, with no ḍamma before
quiz.explanation: A wāw fourth or further, with no ḍamma before it, becomes yāʾ: aʿṭā yuʿṭī, iʿtadā yaʿtadī.

quiz.prompt: Taghāzaynā means…
quiz.explanation: Tafāʿala of gh-z-w: the wāw, fifth, became yāʾ.

text.original: وَاسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ مِنْهَا: غَازٍ غَازِيَانِ غَازُونَ غَازِيَةٌ غَازِيَتَانِ غَازِيَاتٌ غُزَاةٌ وَغُزًّى وَغُزَّاءٌ وَغَوَازٍ، وَكَذَا رَامٍ رَامِيَانِ رَامُونَ رُمَاةٌ وَرُمًّى، رَامِيَةٌ رَامِيَتَانِ رَامِيَاتٌ وَرَوَامٍ، وَرَاضٍ. وَأَصْلُ غَازٍ غَازِوٌ، قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً لِتَطَرُّفِهَا وَانْكِسَارِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، كَمَا قُلِبَتْ فِي غُزِيَ، ثُمَّ قَالُوا: غَازِيَةٌ؛ لِأَنَّ الْمُؤَنَّثَ فَرْعُ الْمُذَكَّرِ، وَالتَّاءُ طَارِئَةٌ.
text.en: The active participle from them: ghāzin ghāziyāni ghāzūna ghāziyatun ghāziyatāni ghāziyātun ghuzātun wa-ghuzzan wa-ghuzzāʾun wa-ghawāzin “a raider” etc.; likewise rāmin rāmiyāni rāmūna rumātun wa-rumman, rāmiyatun rāmiyatāni rāmiyātun wa-rawāmin “a thrower”, and rāḍin “pleased”. The original of ghāzin is ghāziwun: the wāw was changed into yāʾ because it is at the end and the letter before it has kasra, as it was changed in ghuziya “he was raided”; then they said ghāziyatun, because the feminine is a branch of the masculine, and the tāʾ is something that comes after.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْمَفْعُولِ مِنَ الْوَاوِيِّ: مَغْزُوٌّ، وَمِنَ الْيَائِيِّ: مَرْمِيٌّ، قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً وَأُدْغِمَتْ فِي الْيَاءِ الثَّانِي، وَكُسِرَ مَا قَبْلَهَا؛ لِأَنَّ الْوَاوَ وَالْيَاءَ إِذَا اجْتَمَعَتَا فِي كَلِمَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ وَالْأُولَى مِنْهُمَا سَاكِنَةٌ قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً وَأُدْغِمَتِ الْيَاءُ فِي الْيَاءِ.
text.en: You say in the passive participle of the wāw verb maghzuwwun “raided”, and of the yāʾ verb marmiyyun “thrown”: the wāw was changed into yāʾ and merged into the second yāʾ, and the letter before it was given kasra; for when the wāw and the yāʾ come together in one word and the first of them has sukūn, the wāw is changed into yāʾ and the yāʾ is merged into the yāʾ.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي فَعُولٍ مِنَ الْوَاوِيِّ: عَدُوٌّ، وَمِنَ الْيَائِيِّ: بَغِيٌّ، وَفِي فَعِيلٍ مِنَ الْوَاوِيِّ: صَبِيٌّ، وَمِنَ الْيَائِيِّ: شَرِيٌّ.
text.en: You say in faʿūlin from the wāw verb ʿaduwwun “an enemy”, and from the yāʾ verb baghiyyun “a harlot”; and in faʿīlin from the wāw verb ṣabiyyun “a boy”, and from the yāʾ verb shariyyun “bought”.

text.original: وَالْمَزِيدُ فِيهِ تُقْلَبُ وَاوُهُ يَاءً؛ لِأَنَّ كُلَّ وَاوٍ إِذَا وَقَعَتْ رَابِعَةً فَصَاعِدًا وَلَمْ يَكُنْ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَضْمُومًا قُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً، فَتَقُولُ: أَعْطَى يُعْطِي، وَاعْتَدَى يَعْتَدِي، وَاسْتَرْشَى يَسْتَرْشِي، وَتَقُولُ مَعَ الضَّمِيرِ: أَعْطَيْتُ وَاعْتَدَيْتُ وَاسْتَرْشَيْتُ، وَكَذَلِكَ تَغَازَيْنَا وَتَرَجَّيْنَا.
text.en: In the augmented verb its wāw is changed into yāʾ, because every wāw that stands fourth or further on, while the letter before it has no ḍamma, is changed into yāʾ. So you say aʿṭā yuʿṭī “to give”, iʿtadā yaʿtadī “to transgress” and istarshā yastarshī “to ask for a bribe”; and with the pronoun you say aʿṭaytu, iʿtadaytu and istarshaytu, and likewise taghāzaynā “we raided each other” and tarajjaynā “we hoped”.

lessons.title: The two lafīfs and the last two kinds
body: The fourth kind, weak in the ʿayn and the lām, is the joined lafīf (al-lafīf al-maqrūn). Its ʿayn is treated as sound and its lām as defective: shawā yashwī shayyan, “to roast”, like ramā yarmī ramyan; qawiya yaqwā quwwatan, “to be strong”; rawiya yarwā riyyan, “to drink one's fill”, like raḍiya yarḍā riḍan, so he is rayyān and she rayyā, like ʿaṭshān and ʿaṭshā; and arwā, “to quench the thirst of”, like aʿṭā.

Ḥayiya, “to live”, is like raḍiya; and it is also said ḥayya yaḥyā ḥayātan, “to live”, so he is ḥayy, “alive”, with ḥayyā (ḥayyāni) and ḥayyū (aḥyāʾ); “and ḥayū, without doubling, is allowed, like raḍū”. The command is iḥya, like irḍa. In the augmented verb: aḥyā yuḥyī iḥyāʾan, “to give life”; ḥāyā yuḥāyī muḥāyātan, “to favour”; istaḥyā yastaḥyī, “to be ashamed”, command istaḥyi; “some of them say istaḥā yastaḥī istaḥi, and that is because of much use, as they said lā adri for lā adrī”.

The fifth kind, weak in the fāʾ and the lām, is the separated lafīf (al-lafīf al-mafrūq): waqā yaqī, “to protect”, like ramā yarmī, yaqiyāni, yaqūna and so on. Its fāʾ drops as in waʿada yaʿidu; its lām follows yarmī. “The command from it is qi, so the command comes to be a single letter, and in a pause the hāʾ is necessary to it”: qih; then qiyā qū qī qiyā qīna. With emphasis: qiyanna qiyānni qunna qinna qiyānni qīnānni, and light qiyan qun qin.

Wajiya yawjā, “to have worn hoofs”, is like raḍiya yarḍā, and its command is īja, like irḍa. Here the fāʾ stays: the present is on yafʿalu, and lesson 16 taught that the wāw stays with yafʿalu. In īja the wāw, after the kasra of the hamza, is written yāʾ, as in ījal.

The sixth kind, weak in the fāʾ and the ʿayn, exists only in nouns: yayn, the name of a place, yawm, “a day”, wayl, “woe”; “no verb is built from it”. The seventh, weak in all three, is wāw and yāʾ, the names of the two letters. With these the seven kinds of the weak verb are complete.

the separated lafīf: weak fāʾ and lām
the hāʾ of pause: qih
because of much use: istaḥā, lā adri

tasks.prompt: Which weak letter of shawā behaves as weak, and how?
tasks.answer: Only the lām: shawā yashwī goes like ramā yarmī. The ʿayn, the wāw, is treated as a sound letter and does not change.

tasks.prompt: Why is the command of waqā a single letter, and what is added in the pause?
tasks.answer: Its fāʾ drops in the muḍāriʿ, as in yaʿidu, and its lām drops in the command, as in irmi; only the qāf is left. In the pause a hāʾ is necessary: qih.

tasks.prompt: Waqā loses its wāw in the present, but wajiya keeps it. Why?
tasks.answer: Yaqī is on yafʿilu, and the wāw of the mithāl drops before a kasra. Yawjā is on yafʿalu, and with yafʿalu the wāw stays.

tasks.prompt: Name the sixth and seventh kinds of the weak, with their examples.
tasks.answer: The sixth, weak in the fāʾ and the ʿayn: yayn, yawm, wayl, from which no verb is built. The seventh, weak in all three: wāw and yāʾ, the names of the letters.

quiz.prompt: The joined lafīf is weak in…
quiz.explanation: Its weak letters stand side by side in the ʿayn and the lām: shawā, qawiya, rawiya.

quiz.prompt: Rawiya yarwā goes like…
quiz.explanation: Faʿila yafʿalu of a defective verb.

quiz.prompt: Why do some say istaḥā for istaḥyā?
options: By the rule of the hamza
quiz.explanation: Much use wears words down: istaḥā for istaḥyā, as lā adri for lā adrī.

quiz.prompt: The command of waqā to the men is…
quiz.explanation: Qiyā to two, qū to men, qī to a woman, qīna to women.

quiz.prompt: Qih is…
options: qi with the hāʾ of pause
quiz.explanation: A one-letter command needs the hāʾ when one pauses on it.

quiz.prompt: The command of wajiya is…
quiz.explanation: Like irḍa, with the wāw kept and written yāʾ after kasra.

quiz.prompt: From which kind is no verb built?
options: Weak in the ʿayn and the lām
Weak in the fāʾ and the ʿayn
Weak in the fāʾ and the lām
quiz.explanation: Weak in the fāʾ and the ʿayn are only nouns, yayn, yawm, wayl; no verb is built from them.

text.original: النَّوْعُ الرَّابِعُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْعَيْنِ وَاللَّامِ، وَيُقَالُ لَهُ اللَّفِيفُ الْمَقْرُونُ، فَتَقُولُ: شَوَى يَشْوِي شَيًّا مِثْلُ رَمَى يَرْمِي رَمْيًا، وَقَوِيَ يَقْوَى قُوَّةً، وَرَوِيَ يَرْوَى رِيًّا مِثْلُ رَضِيَ يَرْضَى رِضًا، فَهُوَ رَيَّانُ، وَامْرَأَةٌ رَيَّا، مِثْلُ عَطْشَانَ وَعَطْشَى، وَأَرْوَى كَأَعْطَى.
text.en: The fourth kind is the verb weak in the ʿayn and the lām; it is called the joined lafīf (al-lafīf al-maqrūn). So you say shawā yashwī shayyan “to roast”, like ramā yarmī ramyan; qawiya yaqwā quwwatan “to be strong”; and rawiya yarwā riyyan “to drink one's fill”, like raḍiya yarḍā riḍan, so he is rayyānu and a woman rayyā “whose thirst is quenched”, like ʿaṭshāna and ʿaṭshā “thirsty”; and arwā “to quench the thirst of”, like aʿṭā.

text.original: وَحَيِيَ كَرَضِيَ، وَحَيَّ يَحْيَى حَيَاةً فَهُوَ حَيٌّ، وَحَيَّا فَهُمَا حَيَّانِ، وَحَيُّوا فَهُمْ أَحْيَاءٌ، وَيَجُوزُ حَيُوا بِالتَّخْفِيفِ كَرَضُوا. وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهَا: اِحْيَ كَارْضَ. وَأَحْيَا يُحْيِي إِحْيَاءً، وَحَايَا يُحَايِي مُحَايَاةً، وَاسْتَحْيَا يَسْتَحْيِي، وَالْأَمْرُ اسْتَحْيِ، وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ: اسْتَحَى يَسْتَحِي اسْتَحِ، وَذَلِكَ لِكَثْرَةِ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ، كَمَا قَالُوا: لَا أَدْرِ، فِي لَا أَدْرِي.
text.en: ḥayiya “to live” is like raḍiya; and ḥayya yaḥyā ḥayātan, so he is ḥayyun “alive”; ḥayyā, so they two are ḥayyāni; ḥayyū, so they are aḥyāʾun; and ḥayū, without doubling, is allowed, like raḍū. The command from it is iḥya, like irḍa. And aḥyā yuḥyī iḥyāʾan “to give life”, ḥāyā yuḥāyī muḥāyātan “to favour”, and istaḥyā yastaḥyī “to be ashamed”, the command being istaḥyi; some of them say istaḥā yastaḥī istaḥi, and that is because of much use, as they said lā adri for lā adrī “I do not know”.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْفَاءِ وَاللَّامِ، وَيُقَالُ لَهُ اللَّفِيفُ الْمَفْرُوقُ، فَتَقُولُ: وَقَى يَقِي كَرَمَى يَرْمِي، يَقِيَانِ يَقُونَ إِلَى آخِرِهِ، وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهُ قِ، فَيَصِيرُ الْأَمْرُ عَلَى حَرْفٍ وَاحِدٍ، وَيَلْزَمُهُ الْهَاءُ فِي الْوَقْفِ، فَيُقَالُ: قِهْ، قِيَا قُوا قِي قِيَا قِينَ.
text.en: And the fifth is the verb weak in the fāʾ and the lām; it is called the separated lafīf (al-lafīf al-mafrūq). So you say waqā yaqī “to protect”, like ramā yarmī, yaqiyāni yaqūna to its end. The command from it is qi, so the command comes to be a single letter, and in a pause the hāʾ is necessary to it: one says qih; qiyā qū qī qiyā qīna.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي التَّأْكِيدِ: قِيَنَّ قِيَانِّ قُنَّ قِنَّ قِيَانِّ قِينَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: قِيَنْ قُنْ قِنْ. وَتَقُولُ: وَجِيَ يَوْجَى كَرَضِيَ يَرْضَى، وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهُ: اِيجَ كَارْضَ.
text.en: In the emphasis you say qiyanna qiyānni qunna qinna qiyānni qīnānni, and with the light one qiyan qun qin. And you say wajiya yawjā “to have worn hoofs”, like raḍiya yarḍā; the command from it is īja, like irḍa.

text.original: وَالسَّادِسُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْفَاءِ وَالْعَيْنِ، كَيَيْنَ اسْمِ مَكَانٍ، وَيَوْمٍ، وَوَيْلٍ، وَلَا يُبْنَى مِنْهُ فِعْلٌ. وَالسَّابِعُ الْمُعْتَلُّ الْفَاءِ وَالْعَيْنِ وَاللَّامِ، وَذَلِكَ وَاوٌ وَيَاءٌ لِاسْمَيِ الْحَرْفَيْنِ.
text.en: The sixth is the verb weak in the fāʾ and the ʿayn, as yayna, the name of a place, yawmin “a day” and waylin “woe”; no verb is built from it. The seventh is the verb weak in the fāʾ, the ʿayn and the lām, and that is wāwun and yāʾun, as the names of the two letters.

lessons.title: The hamzated verb: two hamzas, and khudh, kul, mur
body: “The rule of the hamzated verb in the derived forms of its verb is the rule of the sound verb, because the hamza is a sound letter; but it is sometimes lightened when it does not stand first, because it is a hard letter from the farthest part of the throat.” The hamza is not a weak letter; it changes only because it is heavy to say, and only where a rule allows.

So amala yaʾmulu, “to hope”, goes like naṣara yanṣuru, and its command is ūmul, like unṣur. Here two hamzas meet: the hamza of joining and the radical hamza. “When two hamzas meet in one word and the second of them has sukūn, it must be changed into the kind of the vowel before it”, as in āmana, ūmina and īmān: after fatḥa an alif, after ḍamma a wāw, after kasra a yāʾ.

“If the first is a hamza of connection, the second goes back to a hamza in connected speech when the letter before it has fatḥa”: wa-ʾmul, “and hope!”. The hamza of joining falls in connected speech, so there are no longer two hamzas, and the radical hamza returns. Ūmul alone, wa-ʾmul after wa-: one command, two shapes.

“They deleted the hamza in khudh, “take!”, kul, “eat!”, and mur, “command!”, against the rule, because of much use.” But “wa-ʾmur sometimes comes on the original in connected speech”, as in the verse wa-ʾmur ahlaka bi-l-ṣalāti, “and command your family to pray” (Q 20:132). Both shapes stand side by side in one verse: khudhi al-ʿafwa wa-ʾmur bi-l-ʿurfi, “take to pardon, and command what is right” (Q 7:199).

A trap: do not count ūmul as a hollow verb because of its long ū. Its root is ʾ-m-l, and the ū is a hamza turned into wāw after the ḍamma of the hamza of joining. The test is the past: amala, with the hamza in the fāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Why is the command of amala ūmul, with a wāw?

tasks.prompt: Why does the hamza come back in wa-ʾmul?

tasks.prompt: What does al-ʿIzzī say of khudh, kul and mur, and what does Q 20:132 show?
