text.original: حُكْمُ الْمَهْمُوزِ فِي تَصَارِيفِ فِعْلِهِ حُكْمُ الصَّحِيحِ؛ لِأَنَّ الْهَمْزَةَ حَرْفٌ صَحِيحٌ، لَكِنَّهَا قَدْ تُخَفَّفُ إِذَا وَقَعَتْ غَيْرَ أَوَّلٍ؛ لِأَنَّهَا حَرْفٌ شَدِيدٌ مِنْ أَقْصَى الْحَلْقِ.
text.en: The rule of the hamzated verb in the derived forms of its verb is the rule of the sound verb, because the hamza is a sound letter; but it is sometimes lightened when it does not stand first, because it is a hard letter from the farthest part of the throat.

text.original: فَتَقُولُ: أَمَلَ يَأْمُلُ مِثْلُ نَصَرَ يَنْصُرُ، وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهَا: اُومُلْ كَانْصُرْ، تُقْلَبُ الْهَمْزَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَاوًا؛ لِأَنَّ الْهَمْزَتَيْنِ إِذَا الْتَقَتَا فِي كَلِمَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ وَثَانِيهِمَا سَاكِنَةٌ وَجَبَ قَلْبُهَا بِجِنْسِ حَرَكَةِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، كَآمَنَ وَأُومِنَ وَإِيمَانًا، فَإِنْ كَانَتِ الْأُولَى هَمْزَةَ وَصْلٍ تَعُودُ الثَّانِيَةُ هَمْزَةً عِنْدَ الْوَصْلِ إِذَا انْفَتَحَ مَا قَبْلَهَا، مِثْلُ: وَأْمُلْ.
text.en: So you say amala yaʾmulu “to hope”, like naṣara yanṣuru; the command from it is ūmul, like unṣur: the second hamza is changed into wāw, because when two hamzas meet in one word and the second of them has sukūn, it must be changed into the kind of the vowel before it, as āmana, ūmina and īmānan. If the first is a hamza of connection, the second goes back to a hamza in connected speech when the letter before it has fatḥa, as wa-ʾmul “and hope!”.

text.original: وَحَذَفُوا الْهَمْزَةَ فِي خُذْ وَكُلْ وَمُرْ عَلَى غَيْرِ الْقِيَاسِ لِكَثْرَةِ الِاسْتِعْمَالِ، وَقَدْ يَجِيءُ وَأْمُرْ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ عِنْدَ الْوَصْلِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَأْمُرْ أَهْلَكَ بِالصَّلَاةِ﴾.
text.en: They deleted the hamza in khudh “take!”, kul “eat!” and mur “command!” against the rule, because of much use; and wa-ʾmur sometimes comes on the original in connected speech, as in His saying, exalted is He: wa-ʾmur ahlaka bi-al-ṣalāti “and command your family to pray” [20:132].

lessons.title: Hamzated verbs on the models of others
body: Al-ʿIzzī now names, for each hamzated verb, the verb it goes like. Adaba yaʾdibu, “to invite to a feast”, and hanaʾa yahniʾu, “to give”, go like ḍaraba yaḍribu; their command is īdib, the radical hamza turned into yāʾ after the kasra of the hamza of joining. Aduba yaʾdubu, “to be well-mannered”, goes like karuma yakrumu, command ūdub. Saʾala yasʾalu, “to ask”, goes like manaʿa yamnaʿu, command isʾal; “and sāla yasālu, with sal, is allowed, with lightening; its original is isʾal”.

Some verbs are hamzated and weak at once. Āba yaʾūbu awban, “to return”, and sāʾa yasūʾu, “to be bad”, go like ṣāna yaṣūnu; jāʾa yajīʾu, “to come”, like kāla yakīlu, “to measure”; and their doers are sāʾin and jāʾin. Here the hamza stands in the lām, and the participle ends like ghāzin.

Asā yaʾsū, “to treat a wound”, goes like ʿadā yaʿdū, “to run”; atā yaʾtī, “to come”, like ramā yarmī, with the command iʾti; “and some of them say ti, likening it to khudh”. Waʾā yaʾī, “to promise”, goes like waqā yaqī; awā yaʾwī ayyan, “to take refuge”, like shawā yashwī shayyan, with the command īwi, like ishwi; and naʾā yanʾā, “to be far”, like raʿā yarʿā, “to graze”.

This is the Maqṣūd's method made into a list: find the model, conjugate the verb like it, and let the hamza follow its own few rules. Waʾā is the separated lafīf with a hamza for its ʿayn; awā is the joined lafīf with a hamza for its fāʾ; atā is the defective; jāʾa is the hollow. Every verb of the chapter lands on a model already learnt.

A trap: ti, from atā, and qi, from waqā, look alike: one letter and a kasra. Ti is a shortening that some Arabs used, “likening it to khudh”, beside the regular iʾti; qi is the regular command of the separated lafīf.

tasks.prompt: Why is the command of adaba īdib, but that of aduba ūdub?
tasks.answer: Adaba yaʾdibu has kasra on its ʿayn, so the hamza of joining has kasra and the radical hamza after it becomes yāʾ. Aduba yaʾdubu has ḍamma, so the hamza of joining has ḍamma and the radical hamza becomes wāw.

tasks.prompt: What is sal, and where does it come from?
tasks.answer: The command of saʾala with the hamza lightened: its original is isʾal. With the hamza gone, the sīn has a vowel and needs no hamza of joining.

tasks.prompt: Name the model of waʾā, awā, atā and jāʾa, and the kind of weak verb each follows.
tasks.answer: Waʾā like waqā (the separated lafīf); awā like shawā (the joined lafīf); atā like ramā (the defective); jāʾa like kāla (the hollow).

text.original: وَأَدَبَ يَأْدِبُ، وَهَنَأَ يَهْنِئُ، كَضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ، وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهَا: إِيدِبْ. وَأَدُبَ يَأْدُبُ، كَكَرُمَ يَكْرُمُ، وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهَا: اُودُبْ. وَسَأَلَ يَسْأَلُ كَمَنَعَ يَمْنَعُ، وَالْأَمْرُ اسْأَلْ، وَيَجُوزُ سَالَ يَسَالُ سَلْ بِالتَّخْفِيفِ، أَصْلُهُ اسْأَلْ.
text.en: adaba yaʾdibu “to invite to a feast” and hanaʾa yahniʾu “to give” are like ḍaraba yaḍribu; the command from them is īdib. aduba yaʾdubu “to be well-mannered” is like karuma yakrumu; the command from it is ūdub. saʾala yasʾalu “to ask” is like manaʿa yamnaʿu; the command is isʾal; and sāla yasālu, with sal, is allowed, with lightening; its original is isʾal.

text.original: وَآبَ يَؤُوبُ أَوْبًا، وَسَاءَ يَسُوءُ، كَصَانَ يَصُونُ، وَجَاءَ يَجِيءُ كَكَالَ يَكِيلُ، فَهُوَ سَاءٍ وَجَاءٍ، وَأَسَا يَأْسُو كَعَدَا يَعْدُو، وَأَتَى يَأْتِي كَرَمَى يَرْمِي، وَالْأَمْرُ مِنْهُ: ائْتِ، وَمِنْهُمْ مَنْ يَقُولُ: تِ، تَشْبِيهًا بِخُذْ.
text.en: āba yaʾūbu awban “to return” and sāʾa yasūʾu “to be bad” are like ṣāna yaṣūnu; jāʾa yajīʾu “to come” is like kāla yakīlu “to measure”, so he is sāʾin and jāʾin; asā yaʾsū “to treat a wound” is like ʿadā yaʿdū “to run”; and atā yaʾtī “to come” is like ramā yarmī; the command from it is iʾti, and some of them say ti, likening it to khudh.

text.original: وَوَأَى يَئِي كَوَقَى يَقِي، وَأَوَى يَأْوِي أَيًّا كَشَوَى يَشْوِي شَيًّا، وَالْأَمْرُ اِيوِ كَاشْوِ، وَنَأَى يَنْأَى كَرَعَى يَرْعَى.
text.en: waʾā yaʾī “to promise” is like waqā yaqī; awā yaʾwī ayyan “to take refuge” is like shawā yashwī shayyan, the command being īwi, like ishwi; and naʾā yanʾā “to be far” is like raʿā yarʿā “to graze”.

lessons.title: Raʾā and arā
body: By rule raʾā, “to see”, would go like naʾā: raʾā yarʾā. “But the Arabs agreed on deleting the hamza from its muḍāriʿ”: yarā yarayāni yarawna tarā tarayāni yarayna tarā tarayāni tarawna tarayna tarayāni tarayna arā narā. The endings are those of yarḍā; only the hamza, the ʿayn of the verb, is gone. For the woman and the women addressed the wording agrees, tarayna, “but the singular is tafayna and the plural tafalna”: the measures of tarḍayna with the ʿayn left out.

The command: on the original irʾa, like irʿa; and with the deletion, ra, a single letter, which needs the hāʾ in a pause: rah. Then rayā raw ray rayā rayna; with emphasis rayanna rayānni rawunna rayinna rayānni raynānni; with the light nūn rayan rawun rayin. These are the commands of yarā exactly as irḍa was the command of yarḍā, without the hamza.

The participles keep the hamza: rāʾin, like rāʿin, with rāʾiyāni and rāʾūna, like rāʿiyāni and rāʿūna; and the passive participle marʾiyy, like marʿiyy. Deletion belongs to the muḍāriʿ and its command; it does not reach the nouns.

“The pattern afʿala from it also differs from its sisters”: arā yurī irāʾatan, “to show”, with the hamza gone from all its forms. Its doer is murin muriyāni murūna muriyatun muriyatāni muriyātun, like a defective participle; its one done to is muran murayāni murawna, like al-muʿṭā. The command: ari ariyā arū arī ariyā arīna, and with emphasis ariyanna … arīnānni; the prohibition: lā turi lā turiyā lā turū lā turī lā turiyā lā turīna.

Last, iftaʿala from a verb with hamza as its fāʾ: ītāla, like ikhtāra, and ītalā, like iqtaḍā. The radical hamza, quiescent after the hamza of joining, has become a yāʾ, as in īdib. With this the chapter of the hamzated verb ends, and with it the conjugation of every kind of verb.

text.original: وَكَذَلِكَ قِيَاسُ رَأَى يَرْأَى، لَكِنَّ الْعَرَبَ قَدِ اجْتَمَعَتْ عَلَى حَذْفِ الْهَمْزَةِ مِنْ مُضَارِعِهِ، فَقَالُوا: يَرَى يَرَيَانِ يَرَوْنَ تَرَى تَرَيَانِ يَرَيْنَ تَرَى تَرَيَانِ تَرَوْنَ تَرَيْنَ تَرَيَانِ تَرَيْنَ أَرَى نَرَى. وَاتَّفَقَ فِي خِطَابِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ لَفْظُ الْوَاحِدَةِ وَالْجَمْعِ، لَكِنِ الْوَاحِدَةُ تَفَيْنَ وَالْجَمْعُ تَفَلْنَ.
text.en: Such too is the rule of raʾā yarʾā “to see”; but the Arabs agreed on deleting the hamza from its muḍāriʿ, and said yarā yarayāni yarawna tarā tarayāni yarayna tarā tarayāni tarawna tarayna tarayāni tarayna arā narā. In addressing the feminine, the wording of the singular and of the plural agree, but the singular is tafayna and the plural tafalna.

text.original: فَإِذَا أَمَرْتَ مِنْهُ قُلْتَ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ: ارْأَ كَارْعَ، وَعَلَى الْحَذْفِ: رَ، وَيَلْزَمُهُ الْهَاءُ فِي الْوَقْفِ، فَتَقُولُ: رَهْ رَيَا رَوْا رَيْ رَيَا رَيْنَ، وَبِالتَّأْكِيدِ: رَيَنَّ رَيَانِّ رَوُنَّ رَيِنَّ رَيَانِّ رَيْنَانِّ، وَبِالْخَفِيفَةِ: رَيَنْ رَوُنْ رَيِنْ.
text.en: When you command from it, you say on the original irʾa, like irʿa, and with the deletion ra; in a pause the hāʾ is necessary to it, so you say rah rayā raw ray rayā rayna “see!”; with emphasis rayanna rayānni rawunna rayinna rayānni raynānni; and with the light one rayan rawun rayin.

text.original: فَهُوَ رَاءٍ كَرَاعٍ، رَائِيَانِ رَاءُونَ كَرَاعِيَانِ رَاعُونَ، وَذَاكَ مَرْئِيٌّ كَمَرْعِيٍّ.
text.en: So he is rāʾin, like rāʿin, rāʾiyāni rāʾūna, like rāʿiyāni rāʿūna; and that is marʾiyyun, like marʿiyyin.

text.original: وَبِنَاءُ أَفْعَلَ مِنْهُ مُخَالِفٌ لِأَخَوَاتِهِ أَيْضًا، فَتَقُولُ: أَرَى يُرِي إِرَاءَةً، فَهُوَ مُرٍ مُرِيَانِ مُرُونَ مُرِيَةٌ مُرِيَتَانِ مُرِيَاتٌ، وَذَاكَ مُرًى مُرَيَانِ مُرَوْنَ مُرَيَةٌ مُرَيَتَانِ مُرَيَاتٌ.
text.en: The pattern afʿala from it also differs from its sisters: you say arā yurī irāʾatan “to show”, so he is murin muriyāni murūna muriyatun muriyatāni muriyātun, and that is muran murayāni murawna murayatun murayatāni murayātun.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي الْأَمْرِ: أَرِ أَرِيَا أَرُوا أَرِي أَرِيَا أَرِينَ، وَبِالتَّأْكِيدِ: أَرِيَنَّ أَرِيَانِّ أَرُنَّ أَرِنَّ أَرِيَانِّ أَرِينَانِّ. وَتَقُولُ فِي النَّهْيِ: لَا تُرِ لَا تُرِيَا لَا تُرُوا لَا تُرِي لَا تُرِيَا لَا تُرِينَ، وَبِالتَّأْكِيدِ: لَا تُرِيَنَّ لَا تُرِيَانِّ لَا تُرُنَّ لَا تُرِنَّ لَا تُرِيَانِّ لَا تُرِينَانِّ.
text.en: In the command you say ari ariyā arū arī ariyā arīna “show!”, and with emphasis ariyanna ariyānni arunna arinna ariyānni arīnānni. In the prohibition you say lā turi lā turiyā lā turū lā turī lā turiyā lā turīna, and with emphasis lā turiyanna lā turiyānni lā turunna lā turinna lā turiyānni lā turīnānni.

text.original: وَتَقُولُ فِي افْتَعَلَ مِنَ الْمَهْمُوزِ الْفَاءِ: اِيتَالَ كَاخْتَارَ، وَاِيتَلَى كَاقْتَضَى.
text.en: You say in iftaʿala from the verb hamzated in the fāʾ: ītāla, like ikhtāra, and ītalā, like iqtaḍā.

parts.title: The nouns of time, place, instrument and once

lessons.title: The nouns of time and place
body: The nouns of time and place are formed “from yafʿilu, with kasra, on mafʿil, with kasra on the ʿayn, as al-majlis, “the place of sitting”, and al-mabīt, “the place to spend the night”; and from yafʿalu, with fatḥa or ḍamma on the ʿayn, on mafʿal, with fatḥa, as al-madhhab, “the way to go”, al-mashrab, “the place of drinking”, and al-maqām, “the place of standing””. As in the Maqṣūd, the rule looks at the muḍāriʿ, not the past.

“Irregular are al-masjid, “the place of prostration”, al-mashriq, “the east”, al-maghrib, “the west”, al-maṭliʿ, al-majzir, al-mafriq, al-maskin, al-manbit, al-masqiṭ, al-mansik and al-marfiq, “the elbow””: all with kasra, though their muḍāriʿ has ḍamma (yasjudu, yashruqu). “Fatḥa is reported in some of them, and allowed in all of them.” The Maqṣūd's list was nearly the same, but not quite: al-ʿIzzī has al-maghrib and al-marfiq, the Maqṣūd al-mankhir and al-majmiʿ. Such lists are learnt by hearing.

“This is when the verb is sound in the fāʾ and the lām.” From the verb weak in the fāʾ the noun “always has kasra”: al-mawʿid, “the appointed time”, al-mawḍiʿ, “the place”, al-mawsim, “the season”; even waḍaʿa, whose muḍāriʿ yaḍaʿu has fatḥa, gives al-mawḍiʿ. From the verb weak in the lām it “always has fatḥa”: al-marmā, “the target”, al-maʾwā, “the refuge”, al-marʿā, al-marḍā, al-maghzā; even ramā, whose muḍāriʿ yarmī has kasra, gives al-marmā.

“The tāʾ of the feminine sometimes comes on some of them”: al-maẓinna, “the likely place”, al-maqbara, “the graveyard”, al-mashraqa, “the sunny place”; “and al-maqbura and al-mashruqa, with ḍamma in both, are irregular”. The tāʾ here does not make the noun feminine in meaning; it is only part of the word as heard.

So the weak letters override the vowel of the muḍāriʿ. A wāw at the start pulls the noun to mafʿil; a weak letter at the end pulls it to mafʿal, where it can end in alif. The student who asks first “is the fāʾ or the lām weak?” and only then “what is the muḍāriʿ?” will form these nouns rightly.

tasks.answer: Its muḍāriʿ is yasjudu, with ḍamma, so the rule gives mafʿal; yet it is heard with kasra. Fatḥa is reported in some such words and allowed in all.

text.original: بِنَاءُ اسْمَيِ الزَّمَانِ وَالْمَكَانِ مِنْ يَفْعِلُ بِالْكَسْرِ عَلَى مَفْعِلٍ بِكَسْرِ الْعَيْنِ، كَالْمَجْلِسِ وَالْمَبِيتِ، وَمِنْ يَفْعَلُ بِفَتْحِ الْعَيْنِ وَضَمِّهَا عَلَى مَفْعَلٍ بِالْفَتْحِ، كَالْمَذْهَبِ وَالْمَشْرَبِ وَالْمَقَامِ.
text.en: The nouns of time and place are formed from yafʿilu, with kasra, on mafʿilin, with kasra on the ʿayn, as al-majlisi “the place of sitting” and al-mabīti “the place to spend the night”; and from yafʿalu, with fatḥa or ḍamma on the ʿayn, on mafʿalin, with fatḥa, as al-madhhabi “the way to go”, al-mashrabi “the place of drinking” and al-maqāmi “the place of standing”.

text.original: وَشَذَّ الْمَسْجِدُ، وَالْمَشْرِقُ، وَالْمَغْرِبُ، وَالْمَطْلِعُ، وَالْمَجْزِرُ، وَالْمَفْرِقُ، وَالْمَسْكِنُ، وَالْمَنْبِتُ، وَالْمَسْقِطُ، وَالْمَنْسِكُ، وَالْمَرْفِقُ، وَحُكِيَ الْفَتْحُ فِي بَعْضِهَا، وَأُجِيزَ فِي كُلِّهَا. هَذَا إِذَا كَانَ الْفِعْلُ صَحِيحَ الْفَاءِ وَاللَّامِ.
text.en: Irregular are al-masjidu “the place of prostration”, al-mashriqu “the east”, al-maghribu “the west”, al-maṭliʿu “the place of rising”, al-majziru “the place of slaughter”, al-mafriqu “the parting [of the hair]”, al-maskinu “the dwelling”, al-manbitu “the place of growing”, al-masqiṭu “the place of falling”, al-mansiku “the place of the rites” and al-marfiqu “the elbow”; fatḥa is reported in some of them, and allowed in all of them. This is when the verb is sound in the fāʾ and the lām.

text.original: وَمِنَ الْمُعْتَلِّ الْفَاءِ مَكْسُورٌ أَبَدًا، كَالْمَوْعِدِ وَالْمَوْضِعِ وَالْمَوْسِمِ، وَمِنَ الْمُعْتَلِّ اللَّامِ مَفْتُوحٌ أَبَدًا، كَالْمَرْمَى وَالْمَأْوَى وَالْمَرْعَى وَالْمَرْضَى وَالْمَغْزَى. وَقَدْ تَدْخُلُ عَلَى بَعْضِهَا تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ، كَالْمَظِنَّةِ وَالْمَقْبَرَةِ وَالْمَشْرَقَةِ، وَشَذَّ الْمَقْبُرَةُ وَالْمَشْرُقَةُ بِالضَّمِّ فِيهِمَا.
text.en: From the verb weak in the fāʾ it always has kasra, as al-mawʿidi “the appointed time”, al-mawḍiʿi “the place” and al-mawsimi “the season”; and from the verb weak in the lām it always has fatḥa, as al-marmā “the target”, al-maʾwā “the refuge”, al-marʿā “the pasture”, al-marḍā and al-maghzā “the aim”. The tāʾ of the feminine sometimes comes on some of them, as al-maẓinnati “the likely place”, al-maqbarati “the graveyard” and al-mashraqati “the sunny place”; and al-maqburatu and al-mashruqatu, with ḍamma in both, are irregular.

lessons.title: Longer verbs, abundance, the instrument, once and manner
body: “What has more than three [letters] is like the passive participle”: al-mudkhal, “the entrance”, al-muqām, “the place of staying”. The same word serves as the passive participle and as the noun of place: mudkhal is “one made to enter” and “the entrance”. Compare al-maqām of the last lesson: from qāma, with fatḥa, the place of standing; al-muqām, from aqāma, with ḍamma, the place of staying.

“When a thing is plentiful in a place, one says of it mafʿala, with fatḥa, from the bare triliteral”: arḍun masbaʿatun, “a land full of beasts of prey”, maʾsada, “full of lions”, madhʾaba, “full of wolves”, mabṭakha, “full of melons”, maqthaʾa, “full of cucumbers”. These are made from nouns, sabʿ, asad, dhiʾb, biṭṭīkh, qiththāʾ, not from verbs.

The noun of the instrument (ism al-āla) is “that with which the doer works on the one done to, for the effect to reach it”. It comes on the pattern of miḥlab, “a milking pail”, miksaḥa, “a broom”, miftāḥ, “a key”, miṣfāh, “a strainer”: mifʿal, mifʿala, mifʿāl, always with kasra on the mīm. “They said mirqāt, a ladder, on this, and whoever gives the mīm fatḥa means the place.” Irregular, “with ḍamma on the mīm and the ʿayn”: mudhun, musʿuṭ, muduqq, munkhul, mukḥula, muḥruḍa; while midaqq and midaqqa “came according to the rule”.

A closing note (tanbīh). The noun of once (al-marra) from the maṣdar of the bare triliteral is on faʿla: ḍarabtu ḍarbatan, “I hit once”, qumtu qawmatan, “I stood up once”. From longer verbs it is made by adding the tāʾ: al-iʿṭāʾa, al-inṭilāqa. Where the maṣdar already has the tāʾ, “the description with “one” is necessary”: raḥimtuhu raḥmatan wāḥidatan, daḥrajtuhu daḥrajatan wāḥidatan, since raḥma alone would not show that it happened once.

“And al-fiʿla, with kasra, is for the kind of the action”: ḥasanu al-ṭiʿmati wa-l-jilsati, “good in his way of eating and of sitting”. One vowel separates the two: faʿla counts the act, fiʿla describes its manner. With these two patterns al-ʿIzzī ends his book.

tasks.prompt: Al-maqām and al-muqām: from which verbs, and what does each mean?
tasks.answer: Al-maqām from qāma yaqūmu, on mafʿal: the place of standing. Al-muqām from aqāma, on the passive participle: the place of staying.

tasks.prompt: What does arḍun maʾsadatun mean, and from what is maʾsada made?
tasks.answer: “A land full of lions”. Maʾsada is mafʿala made from the noun asad, “lion”, for a place where the thing is plentiful.

tasks.prompt: Why does one say raḥimtuhu raḥmatan wāḥidatan, and not simply raḥmatan?
tasks.answer: The maṣdar raḥma already ends in the tāʾ, so raḥmatan alone cannot show “once”; the word wāḥidatan must be added.

tasks.prompt: What separates the noun of once from the noun of manner? Use the book's examples.
tasks.answer: The first vowel: faʿla with fatḥa counts the act (ḍarabtu ḍarbatan, “I hit once”); fiʿla with kasra describes the manner (ḥasanu al-ṭiʿmati, “good in his way of eating”).

text.original: وَمَا زَادَ عَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ كَاسْمِ الْمَفْعُولِ، كَالْمُدْخَلِ وَالْمُقَامِ. وَإِذَا كَثُرَ الشَّيْءُ بِالْمَكَانِ قِيلَ فِيهِ: مَفْعَلَةٌ بِالْفَتْحِ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ، فَيُقَالُ: أَرْضٌ مَسْبَعَةٌ، وَمَأْسَدَةٌ، وَمَذْأَبَةٌ، وَمَبْطَخَةٌ، وَمَقْثَأَةٌ.
text.en: What has more than three [letters] is like the passive participle, as al-mudkhali “the entrance” and al-muqāmi “the place of staying”. When a thing is plentiful in a place, one says of it mafʿalatun, with fatḥa, from the bare triliteral: one says arḍun masbaʿatun “a land full of beasts of prey”, maʾsadatun “full of lions”, madhʾabatun “full of wolves”, mabṭakhatun “full of melons” and maqthaʾatun “full of cucumbers”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا اسْمُ الْآلَةِ، وَهُوَ مَا يُعَالِجُ بِهِ الْفَاعِلُ الْمَفْعُولَ لِوُصُولِ الْأَثَرِ إِلَيْهِ، فَيَجِيءُ عَلَى مِثَالِ مِحْلَبٍ وَمِكْسَحَةٍ وَمِفْتَاحٍ وَمِصْفَاةٍ، وَقَالُوا: مِرْقَاةٌ عَلَى هَذِهِ، وَمَنْ فَتَحَ الْمِيمَ أَرَادَ الْمَكَانَ. وَشَذَّ مُدْهُنٌ، وَمُسْعُطٌ، وَمُدُقٌّ، وَمُنْخُلٌ، وَمُكْحُلَةٌ، وَمُحْرُضَةٌ، مَضْمُومَةَ الْمِيمِ وَالْعَيْنِ، وَجَاءَ مِدَقٌّ وَمِدَقَّةٌ عَلَى الْقِيَاسِ.
text.en: As for the noun of the instrument (ism al-āla), which is that with which the doer works on the one done to, for the effect to reach it, it comes on the pattern of miḥlabin “a milking pail”, miksaḥatin “a broom”, miftāḥin “a key” and miṣfātin “a strainer”; they said mirqātun “a ladder” on this [pattern], and whoever gives the mīm fatḥa means the place. Irregular are mudhunun “an oil flask”, musʿuṭun “a vessel for nose drops”, muduqqun “a pestle”, munkhulun “a sieve”, mukḥulatun “a kohl pot” and muḥruḍatun “a vessel for washing soda”, with ḍamma on the mīm and the ʿayn; and midaqqun and midaqqatun came according to the rule.

text.original: الْمَرَّةُ مِنْ مَصْدَرِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ عَلَى فَعْلَةٍ بِالْفَتْحِ، تَقُولُ: ضَرَبْتُ ضَرْبَةً، وَقُمْتُ قَوْمَةً، وَمِمَّا زَادَ عَلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ بِزِيَادَةِ الْهَاءِ، كَالْإِعْطَاءَةِ وَالِانْطِلَاقَةِ، إِلَّا مَا فِيهِ تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ مِنْهُمَا فَالْوَصْفُ فِيهِ بِالْوَاحِدَةِ وَاجِبٌ، كَقَوْلِكَ: رَحِمْتُهُ رَحْمَةً وَاحِدَةً، وَدَحْرَجْتُهُ دَحْرَجَةً وَاحِدَةً. وَالْفِعْلَةُ بِالْكَسْرِ لِلنَّوْعِ مِنَ الْفِعْلِ، تَقُولُ: حَسَنُ الطِّعْمَةِ وَالْجِلْسَةِ.
text.en: The noun of once (al-marra) from the maṣdar of the bare triliteral is on faʿlatin, with fatḥa; you say ḍarabtu ḍarbatan “I hit once” and qumtu qawmatan “I stood up once”; and from what has more than three [letters] it is made by adding the hāʾ, as al-iʿṭāʾati “one giving” and al-inṭilāqati “one setting off”; except the maṣdar of either that has the tāʾ of the feminine: in it the description with “one” is necessary, as when you say raḥimtuhu raḥmatan wāḥidatan “I had mercy on him once” and daḥrajtuhu daḥrajatan wāḥidatan “I rolled it once”. al-fiʿlatu, with kasra, is for the kind of the action; you say ḥasanu al-ṭiʿmati wa-al-jilsati “good in his way of eating and of sitting”.
